It runs locally at temperature zero with clean per-call model reloads and injects differentiated cognitive states per turn through dissonance-driven behavioural modes and gated internal voices. Seven model configurations from 4B to 31B parameters are compared with an ablated baseline.
AI.result: Models of 8B parameters or fewer suffer context capacity overload and produce repetitive, specular dialogue loops. At 12B parameters and above, the scaffolding breaks monotonous response patterns and yields spontaneous diegetic expansion with anachronism-free details. The Narrative Vector stays open in 12 of 21 overall sessions and in 9 of 9 official configurations of 12B and above, whereas the unscaffolded ablation is never open (0 of 21).
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a transparent, auditable benchmark architecture for virtual archaeology, and the full pipeline is released as open-source software to enable independent replication.

title: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
summary: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic metric, our 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models establish a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the 2.5-bit-equivalent models match dense 3-bit QAT accuracy, while the 1.5-bit-equivalent models approach dense 2-bit models and outperform dense ternary models by 1.3 pp on average. These results establish native-gate training as a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.

AI.tldr: Introduces SGA-Sparse, which trains the existing SwiGLU gate projection as a fixed-budget top-k router to make LLMs activation-sparse, then adds quantization-aware training for low-bit weights. The sparse models reach 75-85% FFN channel sparsity with small accuracy losses and match dense 3-bit QAT at a 2.5-bit equivalent.
AI.motivation: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic in single-user decoding, but active channels must be identified early, and in pretrained SwiGLU models routing with the native gate performs much worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity.
AI.method: The native gate projection is trained directly as a top-k router, with no auxiliary router parameters, while the original SwiGLU activation is preserved and all parameters are updated end-to-end on about 30B tokens for LLaMA models of 1B to 8B parameters. Two quantization-aware training recipes, continued-QAT and joint-QAT, are studied, and the weight-traffic reduction from sparsity is converted into an equivalent bit width.
AI.result: The ordering of gate and up routing reverses after sparsity-aware training. Models reach uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while staying within 0.2 to 2.7 points of their dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weights, and joint-QAT performs better at sub-4-bit targets. The 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models set a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the former match dense 3-bit QAT, and the latter approach dense 2-bit models and beat dense ternary models by 1.3 points on average.
AI.conclusion: Native-gate training is a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.

title: TLRS-DPO: Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a simple and widely used alternative to RLHF for aligning large language models (LLMs), but its sequence-level objective cannot precisely locate or suppress the local patterns that make an otherwise acceptable response unsafe or undesirable. We propose TLRS-DPO (Token-Level Risk Scoring for Better Direct Preference Optimization), which augments DPO with fine-grained token-level control while remaining fully offline and reference-based. TLRS-DPO introduces a token-level robust compensation term that converts the policy-reference log-ratio on rejected responses into localized risk scores, a curriculum-style schedule that gradually increases the strength of this compensation during training, and a risk-adaptive screening mechanism that selectively penalizes only high-risk tokens instead of entire sequences. This design bridges sequence-level preference fitting and token-level behavior control, and can be implemented as a drop-in modification to standard DPO trainers. Empirically, TLRS-DPO improves alignment quality and safety-relevant behavior with minimal impact on helpfulness compared to strong DPO baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes TLRS-DPO, a drop-in extension of DPO that scores risk at the token level and penalises only high-risk tokens of rejected responses. It improves alignment and safety-relevant behaviour with minimal loss of helpfulness.
AI.motivation: The sequence-level objective of standard DPO cannot precisely locate or suppress the local token patterns that make an otherwise acceptable response unsafe or undesirable.
AI.method: TLRS-DPO adds a token-level robust compensation term that turns the policy-reference log-ratio on rejected responses into localised risk scores, a curriculum-style schedule that gradually strengthens this compensation, and a risk-adaptive screening step that penalises only high-risk tokens. It remains fully offline and reference-based.
AI.result: Compared with strong DPO baselines, TLRS-DPO improves alignment quality and safety-relevant behaviour with minimal impact on helpfulness. The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Token-level risk scoring bridges sequence-level preference fitting and token-level behaviour control, and can be added to standard DPO trainers as a drop-in modification.

title: Task-adaptive anonymisation enables privacy-preserving sharing of clinical speech data
summary: Clinical speech is increasingly used for disease screening and clinical assessment, but directly distributing speech recordings poses privacy risks because they contain both speaker-identifying voiceprints and sensitive spoken content. Existing speech anonymisation approaches are primarily developed for general speech applications or task-specific clinical speech and overlook that different clinical tasks rely on distinct speech characteristics, necessitating task-adaptive anonymisation strategies to protect patient privacy while preserving clinical utility. Here we introduce CASA, a clinically adaptive speech anonymisation agent that transforms anonymisation from a fixed processing procedure into a task-guided optimisation process, dynamically tailoring voiceprint and content anonymisation to task-specific privacy and clinical utility requirements. Through recursive self-improvement (RSI), CASA iteratively evaluates and refines anonymisation strategies against task-specific privacy and clinical utility requirements, while learning from these outcomes to guide more efficient planning in subsequent clinical tasks. CASA is validated across 14 clinical tasks encompassing five languages, diverse elicitation paradigms, and mental health, cognitive and voice disorders. CASA preserved disease-related classification performance while meeting speaker-anonymisation requirements across all clinical tasks, versus only 8/14 for the strongest fixed method. Assessments of resistance to speaker re-identification by external attackers and identification and redaction of sensitive personal information in clinical speech further demonstrated CASA's dual protection of speaker identity and sensitive spoken content. Clinical expert assessments further supported the preservation of clinically relevant information and the acceptability of anonymised speech for controlled research sharing.

AI.tldr: Introduces CASA, a clinically adaptive speech anonymisation agent that tailors voiceprint and content anonymisation to each clinical task. It meets speaker-anonymisation requirements on all 14 tasks while preserving disease-related classification, where the strongest fixed method meets them on only 8.
AI.motivation: Clinical speech carries speaker-identifying voiceprints and sensitive content, but existing anonymisation is built for general speech or a single clinical task and overlooks that different clinical tasks rely on distinct speech characteristics.
AI.method: CASA treats anonymisation as a task-guided optimisation. Through recursive self-improvement, it iteratively evaluates and refines anonymisation strategies against task-specific privacy and clinical-utility requirements, and it learns from these outcomes to plan more efficiently for later tasks.
AI.result: CASA is validated on 14 clinical tasks across five languages, diverse elicitation paradigms, and mental health, cognitive and voice disorders. It preserves disease-related classification performance and meets speaker-anonymisation requirements on all tasks, versus 8 of 14 for the strongest fixed method. Re-identification attacks by external attackers and redaction of sensitive personal information support its dual protection of speaker identity and content. Clinical experts judged that clinically relevant information was preserved and the anonymised speech acceptable for controlled research sharing.
AI.conclusion: Task-adaptive anonymisation enables privacy-preserving sharing of clinical speech for controlled research, protecting speaker identity and sensitive spoken content while keeping disease-related classification performance.

title: ReGKG-2025: A GKG-Compatible Reconstruction of the GDELT Global Knowledge Graph for the Missing Period of 14 June to 2 July 2025
comment: 17 pages, 14 figures, 19 tables, including appendices. Companion methods paper: arXiv:2610.35358. Dataset: this https URL
summary: The June 2025 outage in the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) collection pipeline left a gap in the Global Knowledge Graph (GKG), interrupting article-level news metadata used in downstream research. ReGKG-2025 is an archive-derived sample of 281,620 reconstructed article records covering all 1,665 missing 15-minute batches. Articles were recovered from Common Crawl and the Wayback Machine using source quotas estimated from surrounding native GKG data. Text was screened and normalized, non-English bodies were translated, and flagged records were manually reviewed. Eligible articles were converted to the 27-column GKG 2.1 layout. The versioned package includes record-level provenance, archive replay and WARC locators, source summaries, source-by-day calibration weights, and the complete manual decision journal. The sample reaches about 14% of modeled native volume and represents sources accounting for 84% of selected reference record mass. In an intact-week test, 41% of recovered articles matched native GKG records; field agreement on matched pairs is close to the processor baseline (tone MAE 1.69). The dataset supports retrospective content analysis and source-level aggregates; its tone and theme distributions differ from native GKG, and it does not support exhaustive counts. Data: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents ReGKG-2025, a GKG-compatible reconstruction of 281,620 news article records for the 14 June to 2 July 2025 gap in the GDELT Global Knowledge Graph. It supports retrospective content analysis and source-level aggregates but not exhaustive counts.
AI.motivation: A June 2025 outage in the GDELT collection pipeline left a gap in the Global Knowledge Graph, interrupting the article-level news metadata used in downstream research.
AI.method: Articles were recovered from Common Crawl and the Wayback Machine using source quotas estimated from surrounding native GKG data. Text was screened and normalised, non-English bodies were translated, flagged records were manually reviewed, and eligible articles were converted to the 27-column GKG 2.1 layout, with record-level provenance, archive locators and calibration weights.
AI.result: The sample covers all 1,665 missing 15-minute batches, about 14% of modelled native volume, and represents sources accounting for 84% of selected reference record mass. In an intact-week test, 41% of recovered articles matched native GKG records, and field agreement on matched pairs is close to the processor baseline (tone MAE 1.69). Tone and theme distributions differ from native GKG.
AI.conclusion: The package supports retrospective content analysis and source-level aggregates but not exhaustive counts, and users must account for its coverage and distributional differences from native GKG.

title: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Code and data: this https URL
summary: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

AI.tldr: Tests whether an agent's notes, learned from its own failure traces, improve a frozen 9B model, and finds the gain smaller than it looks. A matched search that never sees the traces reaches about 60% of the improvement, and the learned lessons showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether an agent's harness, the notes around a fixed model, can learn from failure traces beyond what a matched search that never sees them achieves.
AI.method: An open 9B model with fixed weights is used, and a larger teacher model writes the notes. Notes based on the agent's mistakes are compared with notes from the same process with mistakes withheld, on generated customer-service decisions and full conversations. A strict screen of single lessons and a blind audit of tool-use test items are also used.
AI.result: On generated customer-service decisions, mistake-based notes improve accuracy by 4.0 points over notes from the same process with mistakes withheld, and the search process alone reaches about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the notes show no demonstrated improvement. Two customer-service lessons pass the strict screen but await tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson written without seeing the agent's mistakes shows no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.
AI.conclusion: Failure traces add value over a matched search, but less than it appears, and the gains did not carry over to full conversations or new tool-use tasks, so the value of learned notes is limited on current evidence.

title: LLM-based Multi-Criteria Deep Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Efficient 5G UPF Selection
summary: User plane function (UPF) selection in 5G networks is an active area of research, with various limited approaches proposed to enhance network efficiency and manage resources effectively. In this paper, we address this gap in the related literature by proposing a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) UPF selection method that utilizes a dynamic, multi-objective reward function and validating it on a real-world 5G emulation platform. The proposed method is based on the large language models' (LLMs) translation of network operator intents and the network data analytics function (NWDAF) abnormality alerts. The experimental results validated in the real-world experimental setup demonstrate that our dynamic DRL solution achieves an effective balance between latency, power consumption, and traffic distribution, outperforming the heuristic baselines and fixed DRL by 16.89%. These findings highlight the real-world applicability of our approach for dynamic, intent-driven UPF selection.

AI.tldr: Proposes a deep reinforcement learning UPF selection method whose multi-objective reward is shaped by LLM translations of operator intents and NWDAF abnormality alerts. Validated on a real-world 5G emulation platform, it outperforms heuristic baselines and fixed DRL by 16.89%.
AI.motivation: UPF selection in 5G networks is an active research area, but the proposed approaches are limited and do not manage network efficiency and resources effectively.
AI.method: A DRL UPF selection method uses a dynamic, multi-objective reward function. LLMs translate network operator intents and NWDAF abnormality alerts into this reward, and the method is validated on a real-world 5G emulation platform.
AI.result: The dynamic DRL solution balances latency, power consumption and traffic distribution, and outperforms heuristic baselines and fixed DRL by 16.89% in the real-world experimental setup.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the real-world applicability of intent-driven, dynamic UPF selection.

title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
comment: 43 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables, supplementary material included. Tobias Penzkofer and Jawed Nawabi share last authorship. Code: this https URL
summary: Purpose: To estimate how often tool-using large language model (LLM) agents record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in simulated radiology documentation and how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors. Materials and Methods: In this simulation study (October 2026), 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios covered finding communication, tumor board preparation and follow-up management. Forty-three also had a misleading-information variant (91 variants). Six LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) completed each variant with permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker (1638 episodes). The primary outcome was at least one executed high-severity violation per episode. Risk differences were estimated per agent at base-scenario level and, exploratorily, pooled across agents, with analyses of document access and blocks. Results: With permissions only, 7.3%-27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation (pooled across agents, 19.4%). Pooled, it was 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI: -6.1, 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI: -9.5, -3.0). Adding the LLM checker to rules changed it by -3.5 (95% CI: -6.3, -0.7). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64%-68%) would not have caused a violation and were returned for revision. Conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudged rather than missed information.

AI.tldr: In a simulated radiology documentation study, layered safeguards of deterministic rules plus a local LLM checker reduced pooled high-severity agent errors from 19.4% to 13.2%, but did not prevent them. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudgement rather than missed information.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents may record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in radiology documentation, and it is unclear how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors.
AI.method: A simulation study uses 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios, 43 of which have misleading-information variants (91 variants in total). Six LLM agents complete each variant under three conditions: permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker, giving 1638 episodes. The primary outcome is at least one executed high-severity violation per episode.
AI.result: With permissions only, 7.3% to 27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation, 19.4% pooled. Pooled rates were 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI -6.1 to 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI -9.5 to -3.0). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64% to 68%) would not have caused a violation.
AI.conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors, and errors after misleading information reflect misjudged rather than missed information.

title: FinCutBench: A Continually Updated Benchmark for Measuring the Temporal Boundaries of LLM Financial Knowledge
summary: In financial backtesting and other point-in-time tasks, external inputs can be restricted by date, but model parameters may retain financial facts disclosed later, introducing parametric look-ahead bias. We introduce FinCutBench, a continually updated monthly financial knowledge benchmark for measuring how far a fixed model's financial knowledge extends over calendar time. The current dataset contains 9,000 Chinese and English four-option multiple-choice questions from January 2023 to September 2026, covering Chinese and U.S. markets and four categories of financial information. We construct monthly knowledge profiles using the approximate months in which the tested facts became public. After a profile passes the decline test and knot checks, we define the FinCut Boundary as the first month when the fitted profile reaches its lower level, and report the stability of the estimated date under resampling. Boundary dates and localization precision vary across models. Using the independently measured Transition Start and Boundary as fixed references for downstream sample grouping, we find clear relative declines after the Boundary in U.S. asset ranking and earnings recall for some models, while Chinese-market ranking estimates vary across models and all eight disclosure-period-paired forecast-error comparisons have unadjusted $p$ values above 0.10. The FinCut Boundary thus provides an empirical reference for the temporal scope of parametric knowledge in point-in-time financial evaluation, supporting evaluation-window selection and result interpretation.

AI.tldr: Introduces FinCutBench, a monthly updated benchmark of 9,000 Chinese and English financial multiple-choice questions that estimates when a model's financial knowledge reaches a boundary, the FinCut Boundary. Boundary dates vary across models, and some show clear relative declines after the boundary in U.S. asset ranking and earnings recall.
AI.motivation: In point-in-time financial tasks external inputs can be restricted by date, but model parameters may still retain financial facts disclosed later, which introduces parametric look-ahead bias.
AI.method: Monthly knowledge profiles are built from the approximate months in which tested facts became public. After a profile passes a decline test and knot checks, the FinCut Boundary is the first month the fitted profile reaches its lower level, and its stability is reported under resampling. The independently measured Transition Start and Boundary serve as fixed references for grouping downstream samples.
AI.result: Boundary dates and localisation precision vary across models. Some models show clear relative declines after the Boundary in U.S. asset ranking and earnings recall. Chinese-market ranking estimates vary across models, and all eight disclosure-period-paired forecast-error comparisons have unadjusted p values above 0.10.
AI.conclusion: The FinCut Boundary gives an empirical reference for the temporal scope of parametric financial knowledge, supporting evaluation-window selection and the interpretation of point-in-time results.

title: LAION-Audio-XL: A Web-Scale Corpus and Scaling Studies for Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining
summary: Recent progress on contrastive audio-language models can be attributed mainly to the scale and quality of their training data. Larger training datasets expose models to a broader range of sounds and corresponding audio captions. To exploit this, we collect 1.48 billion audio samples from academic datasets, internet datasets, web collections, Common Crawl, and YouTube, and process them with a multi-stage curation pipeline. Furthermore, we generate short and long captions for samples in our corpus that lack them. We use our dataset to study the scaling behavior of contrastive audio-language models based on the NaFlex architecture for the audio encoder. Our experiments identify trade-offs between model size and training data for a given compute budget. Moreover, our resulting models, CLAP2, outperform prior audio-text models of comparable size on the MAEB and HEAR benchmarks. We release our dataset, captions, model checkpoints, and code.

AI.tldr: Assembles LAION-Audio-XL, a corpus of 1.48 billion audio samples with generated captions where missing, and trains CLAP2 on it. CLAP2 outperforms prior audio-text models of comparable size on the MAEB and HEAR benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Progress in contrastive audio-language models is attributed mainly to the scale and quality of training data, so larger and more varied audio-caption corpora are needed.
AI.method: 1.48 billion audio samples are collected from academic datasets, internet datasets, web collections, Common Crawl and YouTube, and processed by a multi-stage curation pipeline. Short and long captions are generated for samples that lack them, and scaling studies on the NaFlex audio encoder examine trade-offs between model size and training data.
AI.result: CLAP2 outperforms prior audio-text models of comparable size on the MAEB and HEAR benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The scaling studies identify trade-offs between model size and training data for a given compute budget, and the dataset, captions, model checkpoints and code are released.

title: ODSA: Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation
summary: Test-time scaling improves the accuracy of a language model's answers by spending more computation at inference time. Established methods do so either sequentially, revising a single solution over several passes, or in parallel, generating several independent solutions and selecting among them. We present ODSA (Orchestrated Discovery and Self-Aggregation), an LLM-directed scaling framework in which an orchestrator LLM is given existing test-time scaling methods as actions --- discovery of a new independent solution, comparison of existing solutions to build a better one, and acceptance of a proposed answer, which triggers its verification --- and directs stateless workers to carry them out. The orchestrator does not solve the problem itself: it allocates computation, feeds the results of earlier actions into later ones, and takes every action from a single context, so that each decision is informed by everything tried before. On Humanity's Last Exam, ODSA improves accuracy by 4.7 to 18.0 points across three models over a single direct call to the model with no test-time scaling. On LiveCodeBench, where a single direct call already solves most problems, it improves accuracy by 0.6 to 14.0 points.

AI.tldr: Presents ODSA, in which an orchestrator LLM directs stateless workers to take test-time scaling actions: discovering new solutions, comparing solutions to build a better one, and accepting an answer for verification. It improves accuracy by 4.7 to 18.0 points on Humanity's Last Exam and by 0.6 to 14.0 points on LiveCodeBench.
AI.motivation: Established test-time scaling methods either revise a single solution over several sequential passes or generate independent solutions in parallel and select among them, without a single controller that uses everything tried before.
AI.method: An orchestrator LLM is given existing test-time scaling methods as actions: discovery of a new independent solution, comparison of existing solutions to build a better one, and acceptance of a proposed answer, which triggers its verification. The orchestrator allocates computation and feeds the results of earlier actions into later ones from a single context, without solving the problem itself.
AI.result: On Humanity's Last Exam, ODSA improves accuracy by 4.7 to 18.0 points across three models over a single direct call with no test-time scaling. On LiveCodeBench, where a single direct call already solves most problems, it improves accuracy by 0.6 to 14.0 points.
AI.conclusion: Orchestrating existing test-time scaling methods as actions within one context yields accuracy gains over a single direct call on both a hard reasoning benchmark and a coding benchmark.

title: The Value of Not Knowing: How Fresh Eyes through Naive LLMs Fuel Creativity
summary: Many major scientific advances come from approaching a problem with a new or novel perspective. While large language models (LLMs) with internet-scale knowledge seem poised to take such perspectives, their consistent generation remains elusive. Instead, models are drawn to dominant views and preexisting, in-field bias. To explore the potential of fresh eyes to increase creativity, this paper proposes naive LLMs, models that are made intentionally ignorant of a specific topic. Through deprivation in training or intentional forgetting, naive models are unburdened by existing dogma, allowing them to be free to make new associations and conjectures. These naive models can then be paired with a stronger mentor model that can refine their unique perspectives into concrete proposals. For the 1B and 7B models tested in this paper, naive models consistently produce seed ideas that are more novel and useful than baseline counterparts, and mentor refinement improves the ideas even further. Thus, contrary to the prevailing tradition of scaling up training data, we demonstrate a case where less information is actually more powerful, in particular when the aim is to discover genuinely outside-the-box solutions.

AI.tldr: Proposes naive LLMs, deliberately made ignorant of a topic through training deprivation or intentional forgetting, which produce seed ideas more novel and useful than baseline models, with a stronger mentor model then refining them. The tests cover 1B and 7B models.
AI.motivation: LLMs are drawn to dominant views and in-field bias, which makes it hard for them to generate the fresh perspectives behind many major scientific advances.
AI.method: Naive models are made intentionally ignorant of a specific topic, so they are free of existing dogma and can form new associations and conjectures. Each is paired with a stronger mentor model that refines its unique perspectives into concrete proposals.
AI.result: For the 1B and 7B models tested, naive models consistently produce seed ideas that are more novel and useful than those of baseline counterparts, and mentor refinement improves the ideas further.
AI.conclusion: Less information can be more powerful than more training data when the aim is genuinely outside-the-box solutions, challenging the tradition of scaling up training data.

title: Creative Priming: Decoupling Process from Product to Escape the Creative Paradox
summary: Many of the most consequential advances promised by AI, from curing diseases and inventing new technologies to formulating new scientific theories, are fundamentally creative acts. Yet creativity is uniquely difficult to learn because it faces a creative paradox: learning to repeat past examples of creative success makes those specific examples more likely to recur, inhibiting the very creativity desired. This work argues that creativity is better modeled as an explicit process rather than as a property of individual artifacts, and proposes to learn the underlying generative principles behind the creative process. In particular, to escape the paradox, we introduce creative priming (CP), wherein a trained priming model generates a prompt-specific primer that assists a response model in being creative, explicitly decoupling the creative process from response generation. The priming model learns through GRPO, rewarding primers that lead to responses that are novel, high-quality, and diverse, thereby reinforcing the process that yields creative responses without reinforcing any specific response.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes creative priming (CP), where a trained priming model writes a prompt-specific primer that helps a response model be creative, so the creative process is learned without reinforcing any specific response. The priming model is trained with GRPO to reward primers whose responses are novel, high-quality and diverse.
AI.motivation: Learning from past examples of creative success makes those examples more likely to recur, which inhibits creativity (the creative paradox). Creativity is usually treated as a property of artifacts rather than as an explicit process.
AI.method: Creative priming decouples the creative process from response generation: a priming model generates a prompt-specific primer, and a response model conditions on it. The priming model is optimized with GRPO using rewards for novelty, quality and diversity of the resulting responses, so the generative principles are reinforced rather than particular outputs.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Modelling creativity as a learnable process rather than a property of individual artifacts offers a way to escape the creative paradox, with implications for AI-driven discovery and invention.

title: A Benchmark and Layered Evaluation Protocol for Evidence-Grounded Shared Belief Updating in Connected Robotics
comment: 15 pages (10 main + 5 supplementary), 6 figures, 4 tables; supplement adds 1 figure and 7 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Connected physical systems fuse observations from robots, IoT sensors, and edge-AI modules into a shared account of the world, yet most evaluations score only the final answer or action and cannot tell whether a method attributed the evidence, updated its belief, handled contradictions, and justified its decision. We argue that shared reasoning in Connected Robotics should be evaluated as an evidence-to-belief trajectory, and introduce the Connected Robotics Evidence Graph (CREG) Benchmark to make that trajectory measurable. CREG comprises 350 deterministically generated scenarios across seven regimes (justified revision, belief preservation, relation association, contradiction onset and resolution, stale/delayed evidence, and source reliability), each exposing a normative posterior reference at every evidence prefix, validated by an independent log-odds checker and screened by a blinded expert audit. Nine representation conditions separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata. Evaluating four open-weight instruction models and six transparent fusion baselines yields three findings. First, entity grounding accounts for a substantial part of the weak-model deficit. Second, deleting semantic relations costs 15.3 points of strict belief-state accuracy on relation-dependent scenarios (Holm-corrected p<0.001), but an information-matched structured list outperforms the full graph and shuffling the graph does not hurt: relation content matters where required, while graph serialization confers no consistent advantage. Third, belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic along the evidence sequence, with mid-trajectory failures that endpoint-only evaluation cannot detect. All scenarios, references, prompts, metrics, and analysis code are released for offline, hardware-free reproduction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the CREG benchmark, which evaluates shared belief updating in connected robotics as an evidence-to-belief trajectory rather than only the final answer. It spans 350 deterministic scenarios across seven regimes with normative posterior references at every evidence prefix.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations score only the final answer or action and cannot tell whether a method attributed evidence, updated its belief, handled contradictions and justified its decision.
AI.method: Scenarios are generated deterministically and validated by an independent log-odds checker and a blinded expert audit. Nine representation conditions separate relation content from serialization, ordering and metadata, and four open-weight instruction models are compared with six transparent fusion baselines.
AI.result: Entity grounding accounts for a substantial part of the weak-model deficit. Deleting semantic relations costs 15.3 points of strict belief-state accuracy on relation-dependent scenarios (Holm-corrected p<0.001), while an information-matched structured list beats the full graph and shuffling the graph has no effect. Belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic along the evidence sequence, with mid-trajectory failures that endpoint-only evaluation misses.
AI.conclusion: Relation content matters where needed, but graph serialization gives no consistent advantage, and trajectory-level evaluation reveals failures hidden by endpoint scoring. All scenarios, references, prompts, metrics and code are released for hardware-free reproduction.

title: Competing Influence in LLM Populations: Budget Timing and Baseline Drift
summary: When competing campaigns target a population of large language model (LLM) agents, observed opinion changes may reflect both campaign influence and changes that would occur without intervention. We study how the timing of campaign expenditure and the population's own evolution shape outcomes in a network of persona-conditioned LLM agents that exchange and revise opinions in natural language. A proponent and a challenger are tasked with generating opposing messages under equal delivery budgets, while a separate stance probe measures opinions without influencing the simulation. Across eight claims, we compare single-campaign and competitive conditions against matched no-campaign runs, and evaluate all nine combinations of early, sustained, and late spending on a reference topic. Baseline stance drift varies substantially across claims and, on some, accounts for a sizeable fraction of apparent campaign effects. After accounting for this drift, the direction of observed campaign-associated changes aligns more closely with the claim's epistemic standing than with the campaigner's assigned role. Uninfluenced populations also consistently lose stance diversity, demonstrating that directional opinion change and convergence are distinct phenomena. In networks with two opinion-segregated communities, campaigns primarily reduce differences between communities rather than diversity within them. LLM campaign agents do not always argue for their assigned positions, particularly when these conflict with established evidence. Finally, campaign outcomes depend on the opponent's expenditure schedule: unlike a matched numerical bounded-confidence population receiving interventions at the same times and locations, the LLM population exhibits a payoff structure with no pure-strategy equilibrium.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the timing of competing campaign spending and the population's own drift shape opinion outcomes among persona-conditioned LLM agents that exchange and revise opinions. It finds that baseline drift can account for a sizeable fraction of apparent campaign effects.
AI.motivation: When campaigns target LLM agent populations, observed opinion changes may reflect campaign influence or changes that would occur without intervention, so a no-campaign baseline is needed to separate them.
AI.method: A proponent and a challenger generate opposing messages under equal delivery budgets, while a separate stance probe measures opinions without influencing the simulation. Eight claims are compared under single-campaign, competitive and matched no-campaign conditions, and all nine early, sustained and late spending combinations are evaluated on a reference topic.
AI.result: Baseline stance drift varies across claims and sometimes accounts for much of the apparent campaign effect. After correcting for drift, campaign-associated changes align more with the claim's epistemic standing than with the assigned role. Uninfluenced populations lose stance diversity, and in two-community networks campaigns mainly reduce between-community differences. The LLM population has no pure-strategy equilibrium in the spending game, unlike a matched bounded-confidence model.
AI.conclusion: Directional opinion change and convergence are distinct phenomena, and LLM campaign agents do not always argue for their assigned positions, especially against established evidence. Campaign outcomes depend on the opponent's spending schedule.

title: When Answer Decodability Is Not a Decision: Separating Final-Answer and Imminent-Emission Signals in Chain-of-Thought
summary: Answer probes applied to chain-of-thought hidden states are often read as evidence that a language model has already decided its final response. This reading overlooks a competing signal, the candidate the model is about to mention. We introduce emission-controlled dual-target probing (ECDP), which fits the same low-rank reader family separately to the imminent mention and to the final answer at identical positions, with target-specific nulls and thresholds fixed before any fit. On correct DecisionDepth (DD) rollouts in which a distractor is mentioned before the final answer, Qwen3.5-4B decodes the next mention at .966 (null .234) but the final answer only at .221 (null .186), an emission gap of .696 [.648, .744]; Llama-3.1-8B gives .575 [.514, .632]. This pattern is not universal. In a pre-specified evaluation of Qwen3-8B with thinking enabled on held-out MMLU questions, using a full-prefix attention reader over every thinking position, both targets are decodable and the final answer is read far more strongly (mention-minus-answer lift -.398 [-.459, -.336] at layer 22 over 467 questions). Model, task, positions, and reader change together between these settings, and an attempted matched comparison on DD produced no valid statistics because the imminent-mention probe did not train reliably, so we do not identify what reverses the order. On DD, planted-signal controls show that the reader recovers an injected final-answer signal at one tenth of full dose. Answer-candidate decodability is therefore target-relative and protocol-dependent: a strong answer readout does not by itself establish when a model commits, and a probe that fails to train is not evidence that the information is absent. ECDP is a practical control for distinguishing imminent text emission from evidence of a settled decision.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that answer probes on chain-of-thought hidden states do not establish that a model has decided its final answer, because the candidate about to be mentioned is a competing signal. It introduces emission-controlled dual-target probing (ECDP), which fits separate readers to the imminent mention and to the final answer.
AI.motivation: Answer probes are often read as evidence that a model has already decided its response, but this overlooks the candidate the model is about to emit.
AI.method: ECDP fits the same low-rank reader family separately to the imminent mention and to the final answer at identical positions, with target-specific nulls and thresholds fixed before fitting. Experiments use Qwen3.5-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B with thinking, a DecisionDepth task and held-out MMLU questions, plus planted-signal controls.
AI.result: On DecisionDepth, Qwen3.5-4B decodes the next mention at .966 (null .234) but the final answer only at .221 (null .186), an emission gap of .696 [.648, .744]; Llama-3.1-8B gives .575 [.514, .632]. On MMLU with Qwen3-8B, the final answer is read more strongly (mention-minus-answer lift -.398 [-.459, -.336] at layer 22 over 467 questions). A matched comparison produced no valid statistics because the mention probe failed to train.
AI.conclusion: Answer decodability is target-relative and protocol-dependent, so a strong answer readout does not establish when a model commits, and a failed probe is not evidence of absence. ECDP is a practical control for separating imminent text emission from a settled decision.

title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
summary: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes spectral unlearning, which applies matrix-structured, steepest-descent updates to transformer weights on top of existing LLM unlearning objectives. It consistently outperforms a range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearning work focuses on objectives and largely ignores the matrix structure of transformer weights, since standard optimizers treat coordinates as independent scalars.
AI.method: The spectral update is combined with standard unlearning objectives and shown to be the steepest-descent direction for transformers built from linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Performance is summarized as the harmonic mean over memorization, privacy and utility.
AI.result: Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Respecting the matrix structure of transformer weights is a useful addition to existing unlearning methods, improving the trade-off across forgetting, privacy and utility.

title: Language processing in the autistic brain: A meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies across modalities and age
summary: Language is central to social communication, which is altered in autism, and language abilities vary widely among autistic individuals. How the autistic brain processes language is central to understanding autistic communication. Yet neuroimaging studies report inconsistent findings on how autistic brain activity is altered during language processing. We synthesized 45 fMRI and PET studies (753 autistic and 777 non-autistic participants) with seed-based d mapping with permutation of subject images (SDM-PSI). We estimated autistic and non-autistic activation and their difference with meta-regressions adjusted for each study's language modality and mean age. Autistic and non-autistic brains activated a similar left-lateralized language network. Autistic brains showed reduced activity throughout the left perisylvian cortex, from the inferior frontal gyrus to the mid superior temporal gyrus and the posterior superior temporal sulcus, and increased activity in the right temporal pole. Spoken language showed a larger autistic reduction than written language in the left mid superior temporal gyrus. Adults, but not children and adolescents, showed increased autistic activity in the right superior temporal gyrus and cuneus. Autistic language processing thus relies on the typical left-lateralized network but shows reduced leftward lateralization.

AI.tldr: A meta-analysis of 45 fMRI and PET studies (753 autistic and 777 non-autistic participants) finds that autistic and non-autistic brains engage a similar left-lateralized language network, with reduced activity in left perisylvian regions in autism.
AI.motivation: Neuroimaging studies of language processing in autism report inconsistent findings, and language abilities vary widely among autistic individuals.
AI.method: Seed-based d mapping with permutation of subject images (SDM-PSI) synthesizes the studies, with meta-regressions adjusted for each study's language modality and mean age to estimate activation and between-group differences.
AI.result: Autistic brains show reduced activity from the inferior frontal gyrus to the mid superior temporal gyrus and the posterior superior temporal sulcus, and increased activity in the right temporal pole. Spoken language shows a larger reduction than written language in the left mid superior temporal gyrus. Only adults show increased activity in the right superior temporal gyrus and cuneus.
AI.conclusion: Autistic language processing relies on the typical left-lateralized network but shows reduced leftward lateralization, with age and modality both shaping the pattern.

title: CHO-Bench: How Do Context Hints Affect Ad Rankings in LLM Advertising?
summary: LLM advertising selects advertisements based on user conversations, where user needs may extend beyond explicit product searches. ChatGPT Ads allows advertisers to provide natural-language context hints describing what they offer, who may find it useful, and when it may be useful, as additional information for ranking advertisements across diverse user conversations. However, how to effectively construct these hints remains unclear. We formulate Context Hint Optimization (CHO) as the problem of constructing context hints to improve an advertisement's ranking under a given budget. Drawing on established marketing frameworks, we develop seven context hint generation strategies covering What, Who, and When, along with a Unified strategy that combines all seven dimensions. We introduce CHO-Bench and conduct over 1.19 million paired evaluations across five datasets using embedding-based and LLM-based rankers. Our results show that context hints improve advertisement rankings under the evaluated offline rankers. While individual strategies achieve similar average gains and Unified offers no consistent advantage, strategy differences become more pronounced under specific generation-ranking configurations, with embedding-based and LLM-based rankers favoring different information dimensions. Increasing the hint budget further improves rankings with diminishing marginal gains. These findings establish an offline benchmark for studying ad-side ranking optimization in LLM advertising and highlight opportunities for model-specific hint selection and budget-aware generation and aggregation.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates context hint optimization for LLM advertising and introduces CHO-Bench, which evaluates seven hint generation strategies (What, Who, When and a Unified strategy) across five datasets and two kinds of rankers. Context hints improve advertisement rankings under the evaluated offline rankers.
AI.motivation: ChatGPT Ads lets advertisers supply natural-language context hints, but how to construct effective hints for ad ranking has been unclear.
AI.method: Seven hint generation strategies are built on established marketing frameworks, covering What, Who and When plus a Unified strategy that combines all seven dimensions. Over 1.19 million paired evaluations use embedding-based and LLM-based rankers across five datasets.
AI.result: Individual strategies achieve similar average gains, and Unified offers no consistent advantage. Differences grow under specific generation-ranking configurations, with embedding-based and LLM-based rankers favoring different information dimensions. Larger hint budgets improve rankings with diminishing marginal gains.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes an offline benchmark for ad-side ranking optimization in LLM advertising and points to model-specific hint selection and budget-aware generation and aggregation.

title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
summary: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to 19.86%. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.

AI.tldr: Infrathon is a benchmark of long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks for language agents, with 150 runs of six models under 24-hour budgets. It finds that model rankings change with the evaluation horizon and that agents can beat a human-designed baseline.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons, and short evaluations may miss both optimization gains and shifts in relative model performance.
AI.method: The benchmark spans diverse AI infrastructure optimization tasks at different levels, and six models are evaluated across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Agent trajectories are analyzed for failure modes.
AI.result: Model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, and 135 of the 150 runs improve during the second half of their budgets. Claude Opus 5.5 raises the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% (human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec) to 19.86%. Task violations, unreliable testing and premature completion are identified as barriers to sustained improvement.
AI.conclusion: Shorter evaluations can overlook optimization gains and changes in relative performance, and the framework provides resources for building long-horizon tasks and evaluating frontier agents.

title: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
comment: NeurIPS 2026. 26 pages, 8 figures, 12 tables. Project page: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.

AI.tldr: Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD) is a per-token mixed-policy self-distillation method in which the student generates rollouts and the privileged-context teacher intervenes only where its next-token distribution diverges substantially from the student's. It nearly matches on-policy distillation with 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier.
AI.motivation: Models must internalize absent or updated knowledge and learn new skills, but off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes drifts from test-time behavior, while fully on-policy rollouts drift into low-signal states.
AI.method: The student generates each rollout by default, and the teacher, which is conditioned on the source material, intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's, steering the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction.
AI.result: On three closed-book QA benchmarks for fact recall, knowledge updates and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation with 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently beats off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test it retains the most general capability and achieves the best in-domain accuracy with less supervision than on-policy distillation.
AI.conclusion: SSD gives a better balance of accuracy, supervision cost and forgetting than the compared self-distillation approaches for internalizing knowledge.

title: Translating KV Caches Between Hybrid-Attention Language Models: MLA Latents, Linear-Attention States and Sparse-Attention Indexers
summary: A model that takes over another model's conversation must normally re-read the whole history; a text hand-off shortens the re-read only by dropping content. KV-cache translation instead maps the source's cache into the target's own format, so the target continues from the full context without re-reading it. It works for grouped-query attention (GQA), but open-weights frontier models now cache compressed latents (MLA), sparse-attention indexer keys and fixed-size linear-attention states. We replicate KV-Lingo on a GQA pair and then give, for each of these objects, where to capture and inject it and a mechanism that reaches native quality. We study two hybrid pairs at 16-48B scale in both directions, Kimi-VL-A3B - Kimi-Linear-48B (MLA - MLA + Kimi Delta Attention) and Qwen3.5-27B - Qwen3.8-27B (Gated DeltaNet hybrids), plus a sparse-attention target (Qwen3.8-27B - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). MLA latents translate with token-wise linear maps; recurrent states are copied with a closed-form correction or synthesised by replaying the target's own recurrence. Exact long-range recall needs token identity: decoding token ids from the source's layer-0 MLA latent raises needle recall from 0.09 to 0.99 at 2-32K and to 0.83-1.00 at 64K, eight times the longest training prompt. The hybrid full-MLA direction is within the paired confidence interval of native quality on every task metric, and same-shape GDN hybrids reach the native level in both directions (apart from 6% refusals inherited from the source), with time to first token 18.7 and 46.8 times shorter than a re-read at 64K tokens. Segment-wise multi-turn transfer stays at the re-prefill level; naive re-translation collapses. On the sparse-attention target, predicted indexer keys recall the needle as well as the target's own keys (one seed). We state as a hypothesis how the recipes transfer to 300B+ hybrid flagships.

AI.tldr: The paper extends KV-cache translation to hybrid-attention language models with MLA latents, linear-attention states and sparse-attention indexer keys, so a target model can continue another model's conversation without re-reading the history. Translated caches reach native quality on the full-MLA and same-shape hybrid pairs.
AI.motivation: Handing a conversation to another model normally requires re-reading the whole history, and text hand-offs drop content. KV-Lingo handles grouped-query attention, but newer open models cache compressed latents, sparse indexer keys and fixed-size linear-attention states.
AI.method: For each cache object the paper specifies where to capture and inject it and a mechanism that reaches native quality. MLA latents are translated with token-wise linear maps, recurrent states are copied with a closed-form correction or synthesized by replaying the target's own recurrence, and decoding token ids from the layer-0 MLA latent is used for exact long-range recall. Pairs include Kimi-VL-A3B with Kimi-Linear-48B, Qwen3.5-27B with Qwen3.8-27B, and Qwen3.8-27B with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.
AI.result: Needle recall rises from 0.09 to 0.99 at 2-32K and to 0.83-1.00 at 64K with token identity. The full-MLA direction is within the paired confidence interval of native quality on every task metric. Same-shape GDN hybrids reach native level in both directions, with time to first token 18.7 and 46.8 times shorter than a re-read at 64K tokens. On the sparse-attention target, predicted indexer keys recall the needle as well as native keys (one seed).
AI.conclusion: Cache translation recovers native quality for these hybrid objects with large latency savings, while naive re-translation collapses in multi-turn transfer. Transfer to 300B+ flagship hybrids is stated as a hypothesis, not tested.

title: OGDA: Ontology-Grounded Data Agents for Reliable Analysis over Heterogeneous Data Lakes
summary: Full-pipeline data analysis over real-world data lakes requires LLM agents to locate and integrate information across large collections of tables with different schemas. Existing data agents follow task-specific exploration, which exhausts the context window in massive lakes. As the context fills, the agent's reasoning degrades, leading it to locate and process incorrect data files. These errors propagate into the final answer. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Ontology-Grounded Data Agent (OGDA), which utilizes a compact ontology to reduce exploration overhead and constrain data processing. OGDA constructs the ontology through agentic hypothesis testing. At each step, a proposer agent induces schemas, concepts, and relations from raw sources, and a verifier checks each proposal against the underlying data. During task execution, the ontology serves as a representation of the data lake for the agent to explore. Every data-processing action is constrained by a task graph, which the agent can extend only after observing the semantic meaning of the data. Across KramaBench and DiscoveryBench with three LLM backbones, OGDA outperforms the strongest baselines by up to 10.82 points. These results suggest that explicitly modeling the data lake is a key step toward reliable end-to-end data agents.

AI.tldr: OGDA is an ontology-grounded data agent that builds a compact ontology of a data lake through agentic hypothesis testing and constrains data processing with a task graph. It outperforms the strongest baselines by up to 10.82 points on KramaBench and DiscoveryBench across three LLM backbones.
AI.motivation: Task-specific exploration of large heterogeneous data lakes exhausts the context window, and as context fills the agent's reasoning degrades, so it processes incorrect files and propagates errors into the final answer.
AI.method: A proposer agent induces schemas, concepts and relations from raw sources, and a verifier checks each proposal against the data. During execution the ontology serves as the agent's representation of the data lake, and each processing action is constrained by a task graph that can be extended only after the semantic meaning of the data is observed.
AI.result: OGDA outperforms the strongest baselines by up to 10.82 points on KramaBench and DiscoveryBench with three LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modelling the data lake is a key step toward reliable end-to-end data agents.

title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
summary: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.

AI.tldr: TS-GEAR is a generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery ad search that makes reachability part of the prediction target. Deployed on Taobao Shangou with a 0.1B backbone, it serves over 150 million queries per day and yields 3.8% more ad impressions and 4.2% more ad revenue.
AI.motivation: On-demand delivery requires that merchants beyond the user's range are invalid rather than merely low-ranked. Existing semantic IDs encode geography only softly, aggregated behavior ignores location and query, and autoregressive training has no set-level signal against redundant candidates.
AI.method: Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes. Query-Geo Target Attention uses the real-time query and location as dual targets and encodes each behavior's location into its attention key. GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages within GRPO using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives.
AI.result: The framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on HitRate and geographic validity. Online, it yields 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.
AI.conclusion: Modelling reachability and set-level diversity directly within generative retrieval is effective for on-demand delivery advertising at large scale.

title: A Geometric Invariant of Attention Predicts Head Specialization from Weights Alone
comment: Accepted as an extended abstract at the Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations Workshop (NeurReps), NeurIPS 2026
summary: Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive $\rho$, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. This framework allows us to analyze heads without forward passes, opening a new research direction into data-independent analysis of modern LLMs. Empirically, we find that $\rho$ predicts induction heads, the most-studied circuit type in mechanistic interpretability, with Spearman correlation between $-0.55$ and $-0.74$ across four bias-free RoPE models spanning $135$M to $7$B parameters. As a preliminary proof of concept, we use $\rho$ to apply YaRN to only the top-50% positional heads, which degrades perplexity less than uniform application. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a scalar invariant rho that measures each attention head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings, computed from weights alone. Across four bias-free RoPE models from 135M to 7B parameters, rho predicts induction heads with Spearman correlation between -0.55 and -0.74.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic interpretability identifies circuits such as induction heads only through forward passes, and a data-independent way to analyze attention heads is lacking.
AI.method: The paper exploits continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism to derive rho, which needs no forward pass. As a proof of concept, rho selects the top 50% of positional heads for applying YaRN.
AI.result: rho predicts induction heads with Spearman correlation between -0.55 and -0.74 across four bias-free RoPE models spanning 135M to 7B parameters. Applying YaRN only to the top-50% positional heads degrades perplexity less than uniform application.
AI.conclusion: The invariant opens a data-independent direction for analyzing modern LLMs, and it has a practical use in selective context-extension scaling, although this is only a preliminary proof of concept.

title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Code, data and trained adapters: this https URL
summary: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: On a 2B reasoning model learning two invented rules, training on self-generated worked-solution targets matches sheet-only targets in forward accuracy but loses on composition, where sequential reuse of the same rule is needed. The worked solutions also make trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success.
AI.motivation: Accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules, so the choice of capture context needs testing on composition.
AI.method: The model generates targets either from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution. Targets are filtered for final-answer correctness, the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation, and training uses forward-use questions while the test requires composition across two segments.
AI.result: After six passes, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 points on composition (95% CI 14.6-34.0). On unseen argument values, forward accuracy is identical at 87.5% each, but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). A second target-bank pair repeats the direction at +14.6 points. Ten passes on worked-solution targets narrow the gap to 16.3 and 6.2 points, the latter not significant.
AI.conclusion: Choosing a capture context requires testing how new rules are reused and what each use costs at inference, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.

title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading
comment: Guangyan Gan and Jiahao Li contributed equally to this work
summary: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.

AI.tldr: Agent4Crypto is a multi-agent LLM system for cryptocurrency trading in which three style-specific trader agents propose actions and a PPO-based gating policy learns their weights through dual reflection. It improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional, machine learning, reinforcement learning and LLM-based baselines on BTC, ETH and XRP.
AI.motivation: Crypto markets are non-stationary, and existing methods struggle with opaque decisions and fixed aggregation rules across regimes.
AI.method: Data, analysis, risk, reflection and trading agents synthesize prices, indicators, news and charts. Aggressive, Neutral and Conservative trader agents generate actions and rationales, and a PPO gating policy allocates their weights. One reflection stream distills lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank, and the other estimates counterfactual contribution per trader, feeding the PPO state.
AI.result: Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems on BTC, ETH and XRP. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation add value in volatile crypto markets.

title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation.
