We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.

AI.tldr: WorldFoundry is open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation of generative world models across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action and interactive systems. It catalogues 270 models, 74 benchmarks and 62 metric entries and keeps readiness and execution evidence separate.
AI.motivation: Visual plausibility does not make a successful world model, since outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics or causally consistent responses to interventions. The field needs measurable world intelligence rather than perceptual synthesis alone.
AI.method: The paper defines a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system with a persistent, history-conditioned state that is updated by actions and generates coherent trajectories under interventions. It derives a framework of perceptual grounding, persistent state modelling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction and closed-loop interaction, and builds WorldFoundry with manifests, artifact contracts, modality adapters and evidence-aware scorecards.
AI.result: The catalogue contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. The abstract reports no accuracy numbers.
AI.conclusion: WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems and makes each evaluative claim traceable to its supporting artifacts.

title: Same Measurements, Different Velocity Risk: Complementary Rolling-Shutter Readouts under Clock Uncertainty
comment: 36 pages, including appendices. Lunshuo Tian and Dongheng Liu contributed equally
summary: Camera rigs with identical measurement budgets can have different velocity estimation rates when exposure timing is uncertain. We establish this distinction for rolling-shutter reconstruction with two calibrated moving anchors, unknown scene points, and independently unknown auxiliary poses and clocks. On the same fixed local physical class near a separated lateral rig, repeated readouts have worst-case squared velocity risk at least of order $\sigma\rho_{\mathrm{eff}}$, whereas complementary readouts have minimax risk of order $\sigma^2$, for a fixed admissible clock displacement $\rho_{\mathrm{eff}}>0$ as the noise standard deviation $\sigma$ tends to zero. A finite physical compensation path gives the lower bound; a nonlinear velocity inverse proves complementary stability. All motion, structure, pose, and clock nuisances remain unknown. We identify mounting configurations in which both designs become regular and quantify the risk floor induced by metric uncertainty. We quantify full-parameter domains with independent 6-ms clocks and test in-domain reconstruction under paired noise and a depth-offset intervention. Raster studies examine image formation and calibration sensitivity.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that for rolling-shutter reconstruction with uncertain exposure clocks, complementary readouts give minimax squared velocity risk of order sigma squared, while repeated readouts have worst-case risk at least of order sigma times rho_eff. Identical measurement budgets can therefore yield very different velocity estimation rates.
AI.motivation: Camera rigs with the same measurement budget can differ in velocity estimation rate when exposure timing is uncertain, and this distinction was not established for rolling-shutter reconstruction.
AI.method: The setting has two calibrated moving anchors, unknown scene points, and unknown auxiliary poses and clocks. The authors derive a lower bound through a finite physical compensation path and prove the complementary design's stability with a nonlinear velocity inverse. They identify mounting configurations where both designs are regular and quantify the risk floor from metric uncertainty.
AI.result: Under a fixed admissible clock displacement rho_eff greater than zero, repeated readouts have worst-case squared velocity risk at least of order sigma rho_eff and complementary readouts have minimax risk of order sigma squared as sigma tends to zero. Full-parameter domains with independent 6 ms clocks are quantified, and in-domain reconstruction is tested under paired noise and a depth-offset intervention. The abstract gives no other numbers.
AI.conclusion: Rig design under clock uncertainty matters: complementary readouts remove the first-order risk floor that repeated readouts keep.

title: STAR-VF: Spatio-Temporal Aware Representation Condensation for Data-Efficient Video Fusion
summary: Video fusion aims to integrate complementary cues from heterogeneous sources, producing visually informative videos with coherent spatio-temporal structures. Jointly learning cross-modal complementarity and temporal dependencies typically relies on large-scale, high-quality video datasets, whose storage and repeated use during optimization incur substantial costs, making data-efficient learning highly desirable. To address this challenge, we rethink video fusion from the perspective of dataset condensation and propose STAR-VF, the first framework that condenses spatio-temporal representations for data-efficient video fusion. STAR-VF condenses the original training set into a compact set of learnable spatio-temporal representations, which are decoded into synthetic video clips and optimized using feature-level supervision provided by a frozen proxy model. The resulting condensed data preserves fusion-relevant spatial and temporal cues without requiring ground-truth fused videos as supervision. To adapt fusion learning to condensed representations, we equip the final fusion model with flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation, enabling direct temporal interaction and adaptive selection of fusion-relevant information in representation space. Extensive experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion benchmarks demonstrate that STAR-VF, trained with only approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training set, achieves fusion quality comparable to methods trained on the full data. Further analyses validate the contributions of learned condensation and flow-free temporal modeling, and demonstrate the robustness of the condensed supervision across different proxy encoders and downstream fusion models. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: STAR-VF condenses video fusion training data into a compact set of learnable spatio-temporal representations, reaching fusion quality comparable to full-data training with about 1/16 of the temporal training set. It requires no ground-truth fused videos and is evaluated on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus and medical video fusion.
AI.motivation: Video fusion usually needs large, high-quality datasets whose storage and repeated use during optimization are costly, so data-efficient learning is desirable.
AI.method: The authors apply dataset condensation to video fusion. The training set is condensed into learnable spatio-temporal representations that are decoded into synthetic clips and optimized with feature-level supervision from a frozen proxy model. The fusion model adds flow-free inter-frame temporal modelling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation.
AI.result: Trained with about 1/16 of the original temporal training set, STAR-VF achieves fusion quality comparable to methods trained on the full data across the four benchmark families. Analyses show robustness across proxy encoders and downstream fusion models.
AI.conclusion: Condensed spatio-temporal representations can supervise video fusion without full datasets or fused ground truth, and flow-free temporal modelling is effective.

title: AmodalBox: Automated 3D Bounding Box Annotation under Partial Visibility
summary: Recent progress in vision foundation models (VFMs) has made automated open-vocabulary 3D bounding box annotation increasingly feasible by jointly leveraging LiDAR point clouds and images. However, partial observations remain a major challenge in sparse driving scenes, where visible LiDAR points often cover only a small fraction of the object's surface and provide insufficient cues for estimating its full spatial extent. As a result, existing methods often produce mislocalized boxes or leave objects unlabeled. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{\Ours{}}, an automated annotation framework that leverages image-generated 3D assets as amodal geometric priors for partially observed objects. By establishing correspondences between input images and rendered views of 3D assets, \Ours{} robustly aligns canonical amodal geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR point clouds. To improve temporal consistency and reduce computational cost, \Ours{} generates a single asset per instance, estimates its metric scale once at a single frame and propagates it across frames for dynamic instances, and aggregates multi-frame observations for static instances. 3D object detectors trained on annotations from \Ours{} improve performance over strong baselines by 14.1 mAP on the nuScenes dataset and by 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for the vehicle class on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD). Our project page is available at: \href{this https URL}{this https URL}

AI.tldr: AmodalBox is an automated 3D bounding box annotation framework for sparse driving scenes that uses image-generated 3D assets as amodal geometric priors for partially observed objects. Detectors trained on its annotations gain 14.1 mAP on nuScenes and 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for vehicles on the Waymo Open Dataset.
AI.motivation: In sparse driving scenes, visible LiDAR points cover only a small part of an object's surface, so existing open-vocabulary annotation methods produce mislocalized boxes or leave objects unlabeled.
AI.method: The framework aligns canonical amodal geometry from a generated 3D asset with world-space LiDAR point clouds, using correspondences between input images and rendered asset views. It generates one asset per instance, estimates metric scale once at a single frame and propagates it for dynamic instances, and aggregates multi-frame observations for static instances.
AI.result: Detectors trained on AmodalBox annotations improve over strong baselines by 14.1 mAP on nuScenes and by 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for the vehicle class on the Waymo Open Dataset.
AI.conclusion: Generated amodal 3D assets can serve as geometric priors that make automated 3D annotation of partially observed objects more accurate and temporally consistent.

title: Fine-resolution land-use segmentation and synthetic image-label augmentation in the Kathmandu Valley
summary: Parcel-scale land-use data is missing for most rapidly urbanizing Global South cities, as current segmentation architectures rely on multispectral imagery and planned layouts. We introduce a hand-annotated six-class land-use corpus covering 202 km$^2$ of Kathmandu Valley across 408 fine-resolution RGB scenes. The dataset is uniquely challenging: RGB spectral similarity is high, class imbalance approaches 100:1, and key structural features like rivers measure just two to three pixels wide at a standard hierarchical decoder's prediction stride. Evaluating five architectures reveals that standard random data splitting conceals massive spatial leakage. Switching to a strict sequence-block split drops performance by up to 0.095 mIoU. This penalty exceeds the performance gap between the architectures themselves. We modified the SegFormer baseline by integrating a half-resolution residual detail path, boundary-reliability reweighting, a topology-aware loss, and a presence-balanced sampler. Adding only 1.9% more parameters, the enhanced architecture improves mean IoU across every test fold, with gains concentrated in rare, thin-structure classes. However, both models achieve identical results on the external LoveDA benchmark. Finally, augmenting with diffusion-generated pairs at matched compute degraded accuracy across all architectures, especially harming rare classes it aimed to improve. This demonstrates that blindly incorporating synthetic data can severely damage performance, highlighting a critical need to rigorously evaluate and filter generated samples before training.

AI.tldr: The paper releases a hand-annotated six-class land-use corpus of 408 fine-resolution RGB scenes covering 202 km^2 of Kathmandu Valley. It shows that random splits hide spatial leakage, that a modified SegFormer helps rare thin classes, and that diffusion-generated augmentation degrades accuracy.
AI.motivation: Parcel-scale land-use data is missing for many fast-growing Global South cities, and existing segmentation work relies on multispectral imagery and planned layouts. RGB imagery in such cities is harder, with high spectral similarity, class imbalance near 100:1 and rivers only two to three pixels wide.
AI.method: Five architectures are evaluated under random and strict sequence-block splits. The SegFormer baseline is modified with a half-resolution residual detail path, boundary-reliability reweighting, a topology-aware loss and a presence-balanced sampler, adding 1.9% more parameters. Diffusion-generated image-label pairs are added at matched compute.
AI.result: Random splitting hides spatial leakage, and a strict sequence-block split lowers performance by up to 0.095 mIoU, a larger penalty than the gaps between architectures. The enhanced model improves mean IoU on every test fold, mostly for rare thin-structure classes, but both models match on the external LoveDA benchmark. Diffusion-generated augmentation reduces accuracy for all architectures, especially rare classes.
AI.conclusion: Spatially strict evaluation is essential, and synthetic data must be rigorously evaluated and filtered before training because indiscriminate augmentation can severely damage performance.

title: Beyond Bit Matching: Orthogonal Watermarks for Collusion-Resistant Image Fingerprinting
summary: Image fingerprinting assigns each distributed copy a user-specific watermark for source tracing. Averaging collusion is a central threat: several recipients can average their differently marked copies to suppress each individual mark. Discrete bit-string watermarks are especially vulnerable because averaging drives bit evidence toward ambiguous decisions. We introduce \textbf{VectorMark}, which maps user keys to near-orthogonal high-dimensional unit vectors and identifies colluders by cosine similarity to the extracted watermark direction. Under ideal averaging of $K$ vector keys, the normalized average preserves a cosine signal of order $1/\sqrt{K}$ for each colluder, while unrelated keys remain concentrated near zero. The spherical geometry of random directions gives a shifted-Beta null distribution for cosine similarities, enabling analytic per-key false-positive-rate control after validation on unwatermarked images. VectorMark uses a neural watermark encoder and centered extractor trained with JND masking and a progressive curriculum for photometric, geometric, and collusion robustness. Experiments on MS-COCO, OpenImages, and AI-generated images show that VectorMark maintains robust watermark attribution under photometric and geometric distortions, and achieves the best strict all-colluder detection among evaluated methods, while preserving high visual quality. Our code is publicly available: this https URL

AI.tldr: VectorMark is an image fingerprinting scheme that assigns each user a near-orthogonal unit-vector key and identifies colluders by cosine similarity, which makes per-key false-positive-rate control analytic. It achieves the best strict all-colluder detection among the evaluated methods while keeping high visual quality.
AI.motivation: In image fingerprinting, averaging collusion lets several recipients suppress their individual marks, and discrete bit-string watermarks are especially vulnerable because averaging pushes bit evidence toward ambiguous decisions.
AI.method: User keys are mapped to near-orthogonal high-dimensional unit vectors, and colluders are found by cosine similarity to the extracted watermark direction. A neural watermark encoder and centered extractor are trained with JND masking and a progressive curriculum for photometric, geometric and collusion robustness.
AI.result: Under ideal averaging of K vector keys each colluder keeps a cosine signal of order 1/sqrt(K), and the null distribution is shifted-Beta, enabling analytic per-key false-positive-rate control after validation on unwatermarked images. On MS-COCO, OpenImages and AI-generated images, VectorMark keeps robust attribution under photometric and geometric distortions and gets the best strict all-colluder detection among evaluated methods.
AI.conclusion: Vector-valued keys with cosine-based identification resist averaging collusion better than bit-string watermarks while preserving image quality.

title: Interactive Person Retrieval with On-the-Fly Visual Feedback
summary: Traditional text-based person retrieval (TPR) assumes that a witness provides a complete description at once, whereas interactive person retrieval (Inter-PR) refines a partial description through question-answer exchanges. In this setting, the questioner inspects retrieved candidates to decide what evidence to request next, while the answerer sees only the witness-side memory and cannot report candidate-specific visual differences. Existing methods mainly learn offline question orderings, leaving this visual-feedback loop underexplored. To address this limitation, we introduce visual-feedback interactive person retrieval (VFI-PR), a new interactive retrieval paradigm in which retrieved candidates produce visual feedback that becomes evidence for subsequent questioning and re-ranking. To support training and evaluation in this setting, we construct VFI-PEDES, a dataset and evaluation protocol for visual-feedback interaction, and propose VFI-ReID, a framework that learns to use visual feedback during interactive person retrieval. Through the Dynamic Accumulated-evidence Retriever (DAR) and retrieval-aware question optimization, VFI-ReID adapts retrieval and question generation to evolving evidence states, turning visual feedback into complementary evidence for subsequent retrieval. Experiments show that VFI-ReID consistently improves retrieval across VFI-PR interaction stages, demonstrating the utility of visual feedback for interactive person retrieval and outperforming existing Inter-PR baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces visual-feedback interactive person retrieval (VFI-PR), where retrieved candidates provide visual feedback that guides the next questions and re-ranking. It releases the VFI-PEDES dataset and protocol and proposes VFI-ReID, which outperforms existing interactive retrieval baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing interactive person retrieval learns offline question orderings and ignores the loop in which the questioner sees candidates while the answerer, who sees only witness-side memory, cannot report candidate-specific visual differences.
AI.method: VFI-ReID uses a Dynamic Accumulated-evidence Retriever (DAR) and retrieval-aware question optimization to adapt retrieval and question generation to evolving evidence states, turning visual feedback into complementary evidence for later retrieval.
AI.result: VFI-ReID consistently improves retrieval across the VFI-PR interaction stages and outperforms existing Inter-PR baselines. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Visual feedback is useful evidence for interactive person retrieval, and training on it within the retrieval loop is a promising direction.

title: REDiff-AD: No Training and No Target Masks for Industrial Anomaly Image Generation via Diversity-Driven In-Context MMDiT
summary: Industrial anomaly detection is challenged by the scarcity and diversity of real defects, leaving insufficient anomalous data to effectively train downstream models. Existing anomaly generation methods often require product-specific fine-tuning, target mask annotation, or costly procedures to achieve realistic and diverse defects. We propose REDiff-AD, a framework that requires neither model training nor target masks and introduces Rectified Flow MMDiT into industrial anomaly generation for efficient sampling with fewer generation steps. Given a normal product image and a single masked reference anomaly, REDiff-AD employs in-context learning to transfer the defect appearance from the reference into the normal image. Internal attention signals generated during this process are further reused to localize the synthesized anomaly, while edge and color cues refine the localization into pixel-level pseudo-masks. Two lightweight modules further improve generation quality: adaptive reference conditioning enhances defect fidelity, while diversity guidance promotes varied defect patterns without additional training. Experiments demonstrate that REDiff-AD can well address the tradeoff between realism and diversity for anomaly pattern generation and achieve competitive downstream anomaly classification, detection, and localization performance. These results show that REDiff-AD is a simple, efficient, and effective solution for large-scale anomaly data augmentation and pixel-level data construction. Github code: this https URL

AI.tldr: REDiff-AD generates industrial anomaly images without any training and without target masks, using a Rectified Flow MMDiT with in-context learning to transfer a defect from one masked reference into a normal image. It also produces pixel-level pseudo-masks from attention signals and edge and colour cues.
AI.motivation: Industrial anomaly detection suffers from scarce and diverse real defects, and existing anomaly generation methods need product-specific fine-tuning, target mask annotation or costly procedures.
AI.method: Given a normal product image and a single masked reference anomaly, the model uses in-context learning and Rectified Flow MMDiT for efficient sampling in fewer steps. Internal attention signals localize the synthesized defect and edge and colour cues refine it into pixel-level pseudo-masks. Adaptive reference conditioning improves fidelity and diversity guidance promotes varied defect patterns, both without extra training.
AI.result: The abstract reports competitive downstream anomaly classification, detection and localization performance and a good trade-off between realism and diversity. It gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: REDiff-AD is presented as a simple, efficient and effective way to augment anomaly data and build pixel-level training data at scale.

title: Beyond Real or Fake: A Dual-Channel Authenticity and Reasoning Protocol for Photographic Assessment
summary: Forensic verification has converged on a binary "real vs. fake" label that confates fully synthetic, tampered, and AI-retouched images despite their very different consequences. We argue that GenAI manipulations decompose along two complementary channels: a camera channel of sensor fingerprints (destroyed by neural processing), and a semantic channel of scene-level coherence (disrupted by content edits). Each manipulation type leaves a distinctive two-channel signature. We instantiate this taxonomy in 2CAP (2-Channel Authenticity Protocol), pairing a contrastively-trained camera encoder with a frozen semantic encoder to serve two applications on a shared backbone: (i) four-class authenticity classification via cross-attention fusion with learnable reliability weights; and (ii) evidence generation, where an authentic image serves as a reference for a query and the two encoders produce per-channel alignment scores together with a patch-level saliency map. These signals are supplied as privileged context to a frozen Vision-Language Model (VLM) through an Observe-Generate-Refine loop, yielding explanations with localization without forensic fine-tuning. On a multi-source benchmark, 2CAP attains the best classification performance, including strong retouching detection where existing methods fail, and improves explanation quality.

AI.tldr: 2CAP is a dual-channel authenticity protocol that separates camera-sensor fingerprints from scene-level semantic coherence to classify four authenticity classes and to generate evidence for a frozen vision-language model. It attains the best classification performance on a multi-source benchmark, including strong retouching detection where existing methods fail.
AI.motivation: Forensic verification uses a binary real-versus-fake label that merges fully synthetic, tampered and AI-retouched images, although these have very different consequences.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-channel taxonomy: a camera channel of sensor fingerprints, destroyed by neural processing, and a semantic channel of scene coherence, disrupted by content edits. A contrastive camera encoder and a frozen semantic encoder share a backbone for four-class classification via cross-attention with learnable reliability weights, and for evidence generation via per-channel alignment scores and a patch-level saliency map. These signals feed a frozen VLM through an Observe-Generate-Refine loop.
AI.result: 2CAP attains the best classification performance on a multi-source benchmark, including strong retouching detection where existing methods fail, and it improves explanation quality. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Separating camera and semantic evidence explains different GenAI manipulations more faithfully and yields localized explanations without forensic fine-tuning of the VLM.

title: Remembering to Reason: Structured Memory for Scene and Workflow Understanding in Robot-Assisted Surgery
summary: Surgical video understanding is an important foundation for intelligent assistance in robot-assisted surgery. Similar surgical views can reflect different actions or procedural stages. Interpreting these views requires access to earlier observations, yet frame-centric prompting leaves this history unavailable. We introduce MemSurg, a framework that remembers surgical observations before reasoning over them. Its structured memory graph stores timestamped entity categories, locations, motion cues, and interaction summaries. Chronological links preserve recent context, while entity-associated links connect recurring observations across the procedure. Task-adaptive retrieval then supplies evidence-grounded prompts for scene and workflow reasoning, supporting both frozen inference and memory-conditioned supervised fine-tuning. Evaluation on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two complementary surgical benchmarks shows a 10.43-percentage-point gain over SurgRAW with GPT-4o. Memory conditioning adds 6.52 points under matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and an inference-time plug-in adds 7.04 points to EndoChat. These results support structured memory as a reusable source of procedural evidence for surgical video understanding. Our code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: MemSurg adds a structured memory graph to surgical video understanding so that a model reasons over past observations instead of single frames. It improves scene and workflow reasoning on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two other surgical benchmarks, with gains of 10.43 points over SurgRAW with GPT-4o.
AI.motivation: Similar surgical views can reflect different actions or procedural stages, and frame-centric prompting leaves the earlier observations needed to interpret them unavailable.
AI.method: The framework stores timestamped entity categories, locations, motion cues and interaction summaries in a memory graph. Chronological links keep recent context, entity-associated links connect recurring observations, and task-adaptive retrieval supplies evidence-grounded prompts for frozen inference or memory-conditioned supervised fine-tuning.
AI.result: Relative to SurgRAW with GPT-4o, MemSurg gains 10.43 percentage points. Memory conditioning adds 6.52 points under matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and an inference-time plug-in adds 7.04 points to EndoChat.
AI.conclusion: Structured memory is a reusable source of procedural evidence for surgical video understanding and can be added to both frozen and fine-tuned models.

title: Semantic Synthesis over Brute-Force Search: LLM-Guided Transformation Design for Efficient Learning
summary: Data transformation pipelines shape the training distribution in computer vision, but designing them is a computationally expensive problem. We investigate whether large language models can enable efficient discovery by synthesizing executable transformation programs outside predefined augmentation spaces. We compare nine strategies under a unified training protocol, including standard augmentation policies, brute-force search, direct code generation with two LLMs, and performance-guided generation using LLMs fine-tuned on accuracy-ordered transformation pairs. When the best candidates are retrained for 20 epochs, LLM-generated transformation programs lead on every dataset, reaching 0.8877 accuracy on CIFAR-10, 0.5825 on CIFAR-100, and 0.9588 on SVHN, surpassing brute-force search over 6,000 candidates. The best transform on CIFAR-10 and SVHN comes from a fine-tuned generator using 270 candidates, while the best on CIFAR-100 comes from an off-the-shelf generator using only 10. This needs 22x fewer candidate evaluations in the generation step and 600x fewer for off-the-shelf generations, relative to brute-force search. Beyond transformation discovery, we analyze the reliability of the reduced-budget evaluation commonly used for augmentation search. Correlating one-epoch selection scores with 20-epoch outcomes reveals strong, weak, and absent predictive relationships depending on the dataset and architecture, with correlations ranging from 0.756 to near zero. A positive control indicates that range restriction alone is unlikely to explain the low correlations. Our results indicate that semantic synthesis with code LLMs provides an efficient alternative to search-based transformation discovery and highlight the importance of validating evaluation fidelity when optimizing data transformations.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LLM-synthesized augmentation programs beat brute-force search for image classification, reaching 0.8877 on CIFAR-10, 0.5825 on CIFAR-100 and 0.9588 on SVHN after 20-epoch retraining. It also finds that short-budget evaluation predicts long-run results unreliably and depends on dataset and architecture.
AI.motivation: Data transformation pipelines shape the training distribution, but designing them by search is computationally expensive, and predefined augmentation spaces may miss useful transforms.
AI.method: Nine strategies are compared under one training protocol, including standard augmentation policies, brute-force search, direct code generation with two LLMs, and performance-guided generation by LLMs fine-tuned on accuracy-ordered transformation pairs.
AI.result: With the best candidates retrained for 20 epochs, LLM-generated programs lead on every dataset and beat brute-force search over 6,000 candidates. The best CIFAR-10 and SVHN transforms come from a fine-tuned generator using 270 candidates, and the best CIFAR-100 transform from an off-the-shelf generator using 10. This needs 22x fewer candidate evaluations for the fine-tuned generator and 600x fewer for the off-the-shelf one. One-epoch selection scores correlate with 20-epoch outcomes from 0.756 to near zero.
AI.conclusion: Semantic synthesis with code LLMs is an efficient alternative to search-based augmentation discovery, but reduced-budget evaluation must be validated for each dataset and architecture.

title: Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Pre-training
summary: Medical Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) leverages the semantic richness of radiology reports to learn 3D representations, yet current architectures remain fundamentally anatomy-agnostic. While clinical diagnostics rely on organ-specific context, standard encoders apply a uniform, dense parameterization to all volumetric patches, and existing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers gate on isolated local features without explicit access to the organ composition of the scan or crop. We propose Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts (A$^{2}$MoE), a framework that incorporates anatomical inductive biases within the model's computational path. A$^{2}$MoE introduces two key components: (1) a Histogram Representation Router (HRR) that conditions expert selection on global visual context and a predicted anatomical composition histogram, encouraging anatomy-dependent expert weighting; and (2) an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector (OQMSP) that utilizes learnable queries to extract organ-level embeddings for fine-grained alignment without requiring manual annotations at inference. By routing at the patch level rather than the token level, A$^{2}$MoE reduces routing complexity by orders of magnitude while satisfying load balancing by construction. Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, A$^{2}$MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance across segmentation, classification, and detection benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our anatomically grounded inductive biases support robust generalization to MRI and ultrasound, establishing a scalable foundation for medical representation learning. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: A2MoE is a 3D medical vision-language pre-training framework that routes Mixture-of-Experts by anatomy, using a predicted organ-composition histogram and organ-level queries. Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, it reports state-of-the-art results on segmentation, classification and detection and transfers to MRI and ultrasound.
AI.motivation: Current 3D medical encoders are anatomy-agnostic: they apply uniform dense parameterization to all patches, and existing MoE routers gate on local features without access to the scan's organ composition.
AI.method: The Histogram Representation Router conditions expert selection on global visual context and a predicted anatomical composition histogram. The Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector uses learnable queries to extract organ-level embeddings for fine-grained alignment without manual annotation at inference. Routing is done per patch rather than per token.
AI.result: A2MoE reaches state-of-the-art performance on segmentation, classification and detection benchmarks after pre-training on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, and generalizes to MRI and ultrasound. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Anatomically grounded inductive biases in routing reduce routing complexity by orders of magnitude, balance load by construction and generalize across modalities.

title: Sensitivity-Gated Accumulator Caching for On-Device Learning of Low-Bit Hand Networks
summary: Small hand-tracking networks are deployed as 4- and 8-bit codes, and they should keep adapting to a user's camera after deployment, on the device and within roughly the memory of the model itself. Quantization-aware training cannot do this cheaply, because it keeps a 32-bit master copy of every weight together with its optimizer state, about 96 bits per weight. Training the codes directly with stochastic rounding needs no copy but injects rounding noise at every step, and the methods that remove this noise keep a residual buffer for every weight. We introduce sensitivity-gated accumulator caching (SGAC), which keeps residual state for only a small and changing set of weight groups. A set-associative cache of 8-bit accumulators collects the sub-step updates of the groups with the largest Fisher-weighted squared code step and writes them into the codes as whole steps; an evicted line is flushed by stochastic rounding, and a group without a line does not move until it is admitted. We prove that the write-back is unbiased and show, under a local quadratic model, that rounding a sub-step update costs loss of the same order as the update's own gain, so that rounding pays only where the expected gradient is large relative to the curvature. On a 383k-parameter hand-keypoint network, SGAC trains with 8.1 bits of state per weight. Scored on the 4/8-bit network that the device runs after adaptation, it has the highest mean accuracy of nine deployed low-bit networks on two simulated cameras. On twelve ImageNet-C corruptions it has the highest average of corrupted and clean accuracy of seven deployed methods, ahead of the PEQA-style, ECO-style and direct low-bit baselines with confidence intervals that exclude zero, and it matches an 8-bit accumulator kept for every weight with 56% of that state.

AI.tldr: SGAC trains low-bit hand-tracking networks on the device by caching residual state for only a small, changing set of high-sensitivity weight groups, using about 8.1 bits of state per weight. It has the highest mean accuracy among nine deployed low-bit networks on two simulated cameras and matches an 8-bit accumulator kept for every weight with 56% of its state.
AI.motivation: Hand-tracking networks deployed as 4- and 8-bit codes should adapt to each user's camera on the device within about the model's own memory. Quantization-aware training keeps a 32-bit master copy and optimizer state, about 96 bits per weight, and removing the noise of stochastic rounding usually needs a residual buffer for every weight.
AI.method: A set-associative cache of 8-bit accumulators collects sub-step updates for the weight groups with the largest Fisher-weighted squared code step and writes them into the codes as whole steps. An evicted line is flushed by stochastic rounding, and a group without a line does not move until admitted. The authors prove the write-back is unbiased and give a local quadratic analysis of when rounding pays.
AI.result: On a 383k-parameter hand-keypoint network, SGAC trains with 8.1 bits of state per weight. On twelve ImageNet-C corruptions it has the highest average of corrupted and clean accuracy among seven deployed methods, ahead of PEQA-style, ECO-style and direct low-bit baselines, with confidence intervals excluding zero.
AI.conclusion: Sensitivity-gated residual caching makes on-device low-bit adaptation feasible at a fraction of the state cost of full per-weight accumulators.

title: Efficient 3D plant segmentation through multiscale graph learning and optimized geometric processing
summary: Plant organ segmentation on compact computing platforms requires accurate predictions and affordable geometric preparation. We develop and evaluate a multiscale edge based graph attention model that combines local shape descriptors, two neighborhood scales and a residual stem and leaf correction in approximately 78 thousand parameters. The engineering application is plant point cloud segmentation for precision agriculture, assessed through grouped accuracy experiments and physical Raspberry Pi 5 inference. Broad comparisons with hierarchical, graph and transformer baselines establish PointNeXt as the strongest external accuracy reference among the tested local recipes. A nested four variant ablation on a local maize collection separates geometric information from the combined multiscale configuration across seven outer groups and three seeds. The complete model achieves the highest mean intersection over union, 86.36%, although uncertainty and boundary errors qualify the contribution of each component. We then optimize full cloud principal component analysis, sampling and neighbor queries without changing learned weights or descriptor definitions. All 1,180 paired desktop comparisons on PlantNet and TomatoWUR preserve exact logits and predictions. Multiscale pipeline latency falls from 330.33 to 96.82 milliseconds on PlantNet and from 1,054.52 to 463.10 milliseconds on TomatoWUR. PointNeXt also benefits from optimized sampling and remains faster over the complete pipeline. These results support compact graph learning with reduced geometric overhead, while physical board measurements establish inference feasibility rather than energy efficiency or readiness for autonomous flight.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a compact multiscale graph attention model with about 78 thousand parameters for plant organ segmentation, and speeds up its geometric preprocessing without changing learned weights. The full model reaches 86.36% mean IoU on a local maize collection, and the optimized pipeline runs on a Raspberry Pi 5.
AI.motivation: Plant organ segmentation for precision agriculture must be accurate on compact computing platforms, and the geometric preparation of point clouds has to stay affordable.
AI.method: The model is an edge-based graph attention network with local shape descriptors, two neighbourhood scales and a residual stem and leaf correction. Full cloud PCA, sampling and neighbour queries are optimized without changing weights or descriptor definitions.
AI.result: The complete model gets the highest mean IoU, 86.36%, in a nested four-variant ablation over seven outer groups and three seeds, with uncertainty and boundary errors qualifying each component's contribution. Across 1,180 paired desktop comparisons on PlantNet and TomatoWUR the optimized pipeline keeps exact logits and predictions, and latency falls from 330.33 to 96.82 ms on PlantNet and from 1,054.52 to 463.10 ms on TomatoWUR. PointNeXt is the strongest external accuracy reference among the tested local recipes.
AI.conclusion: Compact graph learning with reduced geometric overhead is feasible on small boards, though the measurements establish inference feasibility rather than energy efficiency or readiness for autonomous flight.

title: Virtual Task Prompting for Multi-Task Scene Understanding
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 24 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables
summary: Multi-task scene understanding models typically rely on modified vision encoders or complex decoders for cross-task interaction, which limits their flexibility and compatibility with off-the-shelf vision foundation models (VFMs). We introduce Virtual Task Prompting (VTP), which frames multi-task prompting as retrieving task-adaptive compositions from a shared virtual state, where both the state and routing process are optimized in an end-to-end manner. Concretely, VTP maintains an expanded set of virtual tasks alongside the backbone. At each layer, learnable routing matrices read task-specific compositions as input to interact with image tokens and write the processed results back, forming explicit pathways that capture the intricacies among tasks outside the encoder. Since VTP keeps the backbone clean, it integrates seamlessly with pretrained VFMs, advancing the state of the art on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2. Stress test on Taskonomy with 13 heterogeneous tasks further shows VTP's robustness in extreme settings. Ablations and analysis indicate that VTP's gains stem from adaptive routing rather than increased capacity. The project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Virtual Task Prompting (VTP) handles multi-task scene understanding by routing task-specific prompt compositions from a shared virtual state through learnable matrices, leaving the backbone clean. It advances the state of the art on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2 and stays robust on a 13-task Taskonomy stress test.
AI.motivation: Multi-task scene models usually need modified vision encoders or complex decoders for cross-task interaction, which limits flexibility and compatibility with off-the-shelf vision foundation models.
AI.method: VTP keeps an expanded set of virtual tasks alongside the backbone. At each layer, learnable routing matrices read task-specific compositions to interact with image tokens and write the results back, forming explicit pathways among tasks. Both the state and the routing are optimized end to end.
AI.result: VTP advances the state of the art on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2 and remains robust in an extreme 13-heterogeneous-task Taskonomy stress test. Ablations indicate the gains come from adaptive routing rather than extra capacity. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Routed virtual task prompts give a clean, backbone-compatible way to model cross-task interaction in multi-task scene understanding.

title: Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning for Adaptive Tokenization in Vision Transformers
summary: Adaptive tokenization aims to reduce the compute spent on uninformative image regions while preserving accuracy. Existing work relies on (i) fixed or frozen scoring rules, which cannot be trained toward the task loss, or (ii) discrete masks trained with straight-through estimators, which yield noisy gradients, while fully differentiable alternatives instead leave the pre-trained regular grid. We revisit adaptive tokenization from a regular-grid perspective and ask: can a two-scale quadtree be learned end-to-end without deleting a single token during training? We show that one coarse token and its four fine children can be made the two endpoints of a single continuous interpolation. We introduce Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning (\dvsp{}), which keeps four \emph{virtual slots} per $2{\times}2$ region and blends their token features and attention mass with a single weight $\alpha$, exactly reproducing the discrete grid at $\alpha \in \{0,1\}$. On COCO detection with EVA-02-B, \dvsp{} retains $97.9\%$ of dense Box AP while removing $64.2\%$ of visual tokens, giving a $1.61\times$ end-to-end speedup, and it outperforms entropy-based APT, DART, and uniform lower-resolution dense adaptation at matched budgets; these gains depend on the conserved attention mass, whose removal costs $1.59$ Box AP. On a frozen Segmenter it also improves Cityscapes mIoU, and on frozen DeiT backbones it exceeds entropy selection at identical per-image token counts.

AI.tldr: Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning (DVSP) learns a two-scale adaptive quadtree end to end inside Vision Transformers, without deleting tokens during training. On COCO detection with EVA-02-B it keeps 97.9% of dense Box AP while removing 64.2% of visual tokens, for a 1.61x end-to-end speedup.
AI.motivation: Adaptive tokenization reduces compute on uninformative regions, but fixed or frozen scoring rules cannot be trained toward the task loss, discrete masks trained with straight-through estimators give noisy gradients, and fully differentiable alternatives leave the pre-trained regular grid.
AI.method: Each 2x2 region keeps four virtual slots, and one coarse token and its four fine children are made the two endpoints of a single continuous interpolation. A single weight alpha blends their token features and attention mass, reproducing the discrete grid exactly at alpha equal to 0 or 1.
AI.result: On COCO detection with EVA-02-B, DVSP keeps 97.9% of dense Box AP while removing 64.2% of visual tokens, a 1.61x end-to-end speedup, and beats entropy-based APT, DART and uniform lower-resolution dense adaptation at matched budgets. Removing the conserved attention mass costs 1.59 Box AP. On a frozen Segmenter it improves Cityscapes mIoU, and on frozen DeiT backbones it beats entropy selection at identical per-image token counts.
AI.conclusion: Learnable, differentiable partitioning can cut ViT token counts substantially while keeping the pre-trained grid, and conserving attention mass is central to its gains.

title: What Does Multiple Choice Actually Measure? Disentangling Video Understanding from Option Exploitation
comment: Accepted to TAE (Trust-AI-Eval) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026 this https URL
summary: Video understanding evaluations are intended to measure a model's proficiency in video perception and task solving. However, current VideoQA benchmarks struggle to isolate these capabilities due to their reliance on multiple-choice (MC) answer guidance, language priors, and fragile scoring pipelines. Disentangling these confounding factors reveals how much of a model's score is supplied by the evaluation context rather than earned through faithful perception. Across six VideoQA benchmarks of varying length, we find that accuracy is significantly above chance without any visual input. This is caused by shortcutting and option-prior reliance. We express these effects in the language of faithfulness: option-exploitation and answer-conditioned reasoning traces are unfaithful even when they are correct. Together, our results show that a VideoQA score is jointly determined by language priors, option timing, and how outputs and labels are converted into correctness. We produce a novel Option-Delayed Replay (ODR) mechanism that discloses options at controlled stages of an open-ended (OE) trajectory, to obtain objective MC scores from faithful option-free inference. Our work demonstrates that agentic methods with ODR and faithful inference can match option-exploiting performance. Finally, we formalize our diagnostic collection and ODR as a reproducible evaluation protocol, and we release a human-relabelled edition of LVBench (correcting $20.5\%$ of keys) to remove annotation noise as a confounding variable.

AI.tldr: Shows that VideoQA multiple-choice scores are inflated by language priors and option exploitation, and proposes Option-Delayed Replay (ODR) to obtain MC scores from option-free open-ended inference. Also releases a human-relabelled edition of LVBench.
AI.motivation: Current VideoQA benchmarks rely on multiple-choice answer guidance, language priors and fragile scoring pipelines, so it is unclear how much of a model's score reflects genuine video perception.
AI.method: Disentangles these confounds across six VideoQA benchmarks, including a no-visual-input condition, and introduces ODR, which discloses options at controlled stages of an open-ended trajectory; the diagnostics and ODR are packaged as a reproducible evaluation protocol.
AI.result: Accuracy is significantly above chance without any visual input, caused by shortcutting and option-prior reliance; option-exploiting and answer-conditioned reasoning traces are unfaithful even when correct; agentic methods with ODR and faithful inference can match option-exploiting performance; the relabelled LVBench corrects 20.5% of keys.
AI.conclusion: A VideoQA score is jointly determined by language priors, option timing and how outputs and labels are converted into correctness, so MC scores need controls such as ODR before they are read as perception.

title: NanoNet: Ultra-Lightweight Network for MRI Brain Tumor Classification toward Edge AI
summary: Automated brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can support accessible medical image analysis, but conventional deep learning models often exceed the resource budgets of highly constrained edge-AI platforms. We present NanoNet, an ultra-lightweight convolutional neural network designed for resourceconstrained MRI classification and motivated by future edge-AI applications. Inspired by MobileNetV2, NanoNet substantially reduces network depth, channel capacity, expansion ratios, and final feature dimensionality, resulting in only five inverted residual blocks and 8,132 parameters. We further investigate dependency-aware structured pruning, knowledge distillation, and INT8 quantization-aware training for additional compression. Experiments on the BRISC 2025 benchmark show that NanoNet achieves 92.80% accuracy and 92.97% macro F1 with 8,132 parameters and 10.498 MFLOPs. Across three compression seeds, it exceeds the mean accuracy of 70%-pruned MobileNetV2 by 5.20 percentage points while using 60.2% fewer parameters and 9.8% less computation. Converted INT8 NanoNet achieves 89.70% accuracy and 90.22% macro F1 across three QAT seeds. Earlier TensorFlow Lite measurements indicate 27.7 KB of baseline model storage, motivating future edge-AI deployment.

AI.tldr: Presents NanoNet, an 8,132-parameter MobileNetV2-inspired CNN for MRI brain tumor classification that reaches 92.80% accuracy on BRISC 2025 and keeps 89.70% accuracy after INT8 quantization-aware training.
AI.motivation: Conventional deep learning models exceed the resource budgets of highly constrained edge-AI platforms for MRI brain tumor classification.
AI.method: Shrinks a MobileNetV2-style design to five inverted residual blocks with reduced depth, channel capacity, expansion ratios and final feature dimensionality, then applies dependency-aware structured pruning, knowledge distillation and INT8 quantization-aware training.
AI.result: NanoNet achieves 92.80% accuracy and 92.97% macro F1 with 8,132 parameters and 10.498 MFLOPs; across three compression seeds it exceeds the mean accuracy of 70%-pruned MobileNetV2 by 5.20 percentage points with 60.2% fewer parameters and 9.8% less computation; converted INT8 NanoNet reaches 89.70% accuracy and 90.22% macro F1; earlier TensorFlow Lite measurements give 27.7 KB of baseline model storage.
AI.conclusion: A very small network can keep competitive accuracy under strong compression, which motivates future edge-AI deployment on constrained hardware.

title: ADC-RANet: Improving Resolution Adaptive Neural Networks with Attention, Distillation and Calibration
summary: Dynamic neural networks are a class of adaptive models in which the computation assigned to each input sample is determined dynamically, potentially reducing computational cost while maintaining similar performance. For image classification, the Resolution Adaptive Network (RANet) is a strong approach that progressively allocates computational resources across input scales based on sample difficulty. In this work, we introduce RANet with Attention, Distillation and Calibration (ADC-RANet), an enhanced version of RANet that improves performance across all computational budgets. Our approach combines three tightly connected components: bottom-up channel attention, top-down cascaded knowledge distillation, and overconfidence correction using MixUp, in a synergistic design that coordinates both pathways. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets show consistent gains while preserving the efficiency of RANet. Our code is available: this https URL

AI.tldr: Proposes ADC-RANet, which strengthens Resolution Adaptive Networks with bottom-up channel attention, top-down cascaded knowledge distillation and MixUp-based overconfidence correction, improving performance across computational budgets on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.
AI.motivation: RANet reduces computation by allocating resources across input scales according to sample difficulty, but its accuracy at each computational budget can be improved while keeping the same efficiency.
AI.method: Combines three tightly connected components: bottom-up channel attention, top-down cascaded knowledge distillation, and overconfidence correction using MixUp, coordinated so that both pathways reinforce each other.
AI.result: Shows consistent gains over RANet on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across all computational budgets while preserving RANet's efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating attention, distillation and calibration in one design yields a more accurate adaptive-resolution network at the same cost.

title: Does Pose Encoding Matter? Analyzing Geometric Representations for Discrete Motion Vocabulary Learning
summary: Compressing continuous human motion into a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens is now the first stage of many motion understanding and generation pipelines. Vector quantization partitions a latent space into Voronoi cells around a finite codebook, but the geometry of that latent space is inherited from the input pose encoding, and it is unclear which encoding admits an efficient discretization. We study four encodings that place skeletal motion in different geometric spaces: Gaussian joint heatmaps on the pixel lattice, which we show to be a morphological dilation of the joint point set by a quadratic structuring function; root-relative joint positions in Euclidean space; local joint rotations on $\SO$ through a continuous 6D embedding; and a redundant full kinematic encoding. For each, we train VQ-VAE tokenizers whose codebooks lie on the unit hypersphere, varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension. Beyond reconstruction, we measure codebook utilization and the effective vocabulary size, i.e., the number of equiprobable spherical Voronoi cells with the same entropy as the observed token distribution. Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty. The smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings, and the effect of temporal stride depends on the encoding. Encodings of the same pose family can thus yield effective vocabularies differing by an order of magnitude, a difference that reconstruction loss alone does not reveal, which points to input geometry as a first-order design choice in motion tokenization.

AI.tldr: Shows that the input pose encoding determines the effective vocabulary of VQ-VAE motion tokenizers, with encodings from the same pose family differing by an order of magnitude in effective vocabulary.
AI.motivation: Vector quantization partitions motion latent space according to the input pose geometry, but it is unclear which encoding discretizes efficiently, and reconstruction loss alone does not reveal the difference.
AI.method: Trains VQ-VAE tokenizers with codebooks on the unit hypersphere for four encodings (Gaussian joint heatmaps, root-relative joint positions, local joint rotations in a 6D embedding, and a redundant full kinematic encoding), varying codebook size, temporal stride and code dimension, and measures codebook utilization and effective vocabulary size.
AI.result: Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty; the smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings; the effect of temporal stride depends on the encoding.
AI.conclusion: Input geometry is a first-order design choice in motion tokenization, because it changes effective vocabulary in ways that reconstruction quality does not show.

title: MySign: A High-Fidelity Motion-Capture Dataset for 3D Sign Generation in Bahasa Isyarat Malaysia
summary: Progress in 3D sign generation is constrained by the scarcity of high-fidelity 3D sign language datasets, a limitation that is particularly severe for under-resourced languages. We introduce MySign, the first motion-capture dataset for isolated signs in Bahasa Isyarat Malaysia (BIM). Its 5,000 samples cover 1,000 lexical items (glosses) and were produced by five Deaf native signers. Prior datasets that rely on SMPL-X parameters regressed from video provide pseudo-labels, which are often affected by depth ambiguity, inaccurate finger poses, and temporal jitter. MySign instead provides ground-truth SMPL-X sequences retargeted from recordings made with a motion-capture setup tailored for sign language; these sequences offer higher-fidelity motion, particularly in fine-grained hand and finger articulation. A controlled comparison on the same glosses and signers indicates that training on these sequences improves generation over training on such pseudo-labels. We establish MySign as a challenging benchmark for gloss-conditioned 3D sign generation: state-of-the-art models produce visually plausible outputs but fall short of the ground truth, most notably in fine-grained articulation, revealing persistent gaps in modeling articulated sign motion. In contrast, recognition baselines consistently achieve high lexical accuracy, indicating that the dataset reliably supports supervised learning. The dataset is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Introduces MySign, a motion-capture dataset of 5,000 isolated sign samples covering 1,000 glosses in Bahasa Isyarat Malaysia, with ground-truth SMPL-X sequences, as a benchmark for 3D sign generation.
AI.motivation: 3D sign generation is limited by scarce high-fidelity data for under-resourced sign languages, and SMPL-X parameters regressed from video carry depth ambiguity, inaccurate finger poses and temporal jitter.
AI.method: Records isolated signs from five Deaf native signers with a motion-capture setup tailored to sign language, and retargets the recordings to ground-truth SMPL-X sequences.
AI.result: In a controlled comparison on the same glosses and signers, training on the motion-capture sequences improves generation over training on pseudo-labels; state-of-the-art generators produce visually plausible outputs but fall short of ground truth, most notably in fine-grained articulation; recognition baselines consistently achieve high lexical accuracy.
AI.conclusion: MySign is a challenging benchmark that reveals persistent gaps in modeling articulated sign motion, and its recognition results show that the dataset reliably supports supervised learning.

title: Query-Only Prompt-Agnostic Attacks on Visual In-Context Learning
summary: Visual In-Context Learning (VICL) enables promptable segmentation by conditioning RGB predictions on visual demonstrations, making it attractive for auto-labeling, but its robustness under query-only access and unknown deployment prompts remains underexplored. We study query-only, prompt-agnostic targeted attacks where the attacker observes only returned RGB outputs, without access to model internals or deployment prompts. Treating prompt-conditioned RGB rendering as a distinct attack surface, we introduce two appearance-space attacks: Color Hijack (CH) drives foreground colors toward the background to suppress visibility, while Task Hijack (TH) collapses instance-distinguishing colors toward a shared color assignment. To transfer across unseen prompts, we propose a Self-Prompt Surrogate (SPS) constructed from the clean query and its output. In a paired, matched-budget SegGPT comparison, SPS outperforms the Random-Prompt Surrogate (RPS), reducing CH instance foreground retention from 0.918 to 0.155 and TH palette-aware tolerance distance from 0.345 to 0.225. Across four VICL models on COCO and HierText, CH suppresses foregrounds across semantic-, instance-, and text-style outputs, while TH collapses instance colors under held-out deployment prompts. After palette-based decoding, TH also reduces the decoded instance count and mask retention while increasing instance merges. Finally, at 30% corruption, CH-corrupted annotations from a publicly accessible VICL-based auto-labeling pipeline reduce downstream YOLO-seg mAP50 from 0.761 to 0.281.

AI.tldr: Studies query-only, prompt-agnostic targeted attacks on Visual In-Context Learning segmentation, introducing Color Hijack and Task Hijack, which transfer to unseen deployment prompts and degrade downstream auto-labeling.
AI.motivation: The robustness of VICL promptable segmentation under query-only access and unknown deployment prompts is underexplored, even though VICL is attractive for auto-labeling.
AI.method: Treats prompt-conditioned RGB rendering as an attack surface and proposes two appearance-space attacks: Color Hijack (CH) drives foreground colors toward the background, and Task Hijack (TH) collapses instance-distinguishing colors toward a shared assignment; attacks transfer through a Self-Prompt Surrogate built from the clean query and its output.
AI.result: In a paired, matched-budget SegGPT comparison, the Self-Prompt Surrogate outperforms the Random-Prompt Surrogate, reducing CH instance foreground retention from 0.918 to 0.155 and TH palette-aware tolerance distance from 0.345 to 0.225; across four VICL models on COCO and HierText, CH suppresses foregrounds and TH collapses instance colors; at 30% corruption, CH-corrupted annotations reduce downstream YOLO-seg mAP50 from 0.761 to 0.281.
AI.conclusion: VICL segmentation can be compromised through its returned RGB outputs alone, and corrupted auto-labels can substantially degrade detectors trained on them.

title: What You Show Is Not What You Get: Rethinking Demonstration Following in Visual In-Context Segmentation
summary: Visual in-context segmentation uses visual demonstrations to guide predictions for a new image. In SegGPT, we identify background color mapping deviation, where non-target regions sharing a background label receive different output colors, and part-to-parent expansion, where predictions extend beyond the requested part into its parent object. These deviations can occur even when the relevant regions remain distinguishable in internal features. Controlled changes to demonstration colors and requested targets support an account in which demonstrations guide role and color assignments over familiar semantic regions, influenced by learned semantic and color preferences. Building on these findings, we introduce Semantic Contrast Prompt Selection (SCPS). Its semantic contrast encoding assigns separate colors to the requested part and the rest of its object while keeping the remaining scene black. SCPS combines existing retrieval scores with quality estimates from labeled development images to select demonstrations and their binary or semantic contrast encodings. Averaged across seven retrieval methods on three benchmarks, SCPS improves target IoU by 0.054 and reduces leakage into the rest of the object by 22.7% relative to the original binary selectors. Our findings offer a new perspective on understanding and improving demonstration following in visual in-context segmentation.

AI.tldr: Identifies background color mapping deviation and part-to-parent expansion in SegGPT, and proposes Semantic Contrast Prompt Selection (SCPS), which improves target IoU and reduces leakage into the rest of the object.
AI.motivation: Visual in-context segmentation can assign inconsistent colors to non-target regions and extend predictions beyond the requested part, even when the relevant regions remain distinguishable in internal features.
AI.method: Controlled changes to demonstration colors and requested targets show that demonstrations guide role and color assignments over familiar semantic regions; SCPS encodes the requested part and the rest of its object with separate colors while keeping the remaining scene black, and selects demonstrations by combining retrieval scores with quality estimates from labeled development images.
AI.result: Averaged across seven retrieval methods on three benchmarks, SCPS improves target IoU by 0.054 and reduces leakage into the rest of the object by 22.7% relative to the original binary selectors.
AI.conclusion: Demonstration following in visual in-context segmentation is shaped by learned semantic and color preferences, and selecting demonstrations with semantic contrast encodings is a practical improvement.

title: CrossLiDAR: Controllable Multi-Sensor LiDAR Sequence Generation
summary: High-fidelity LiDAR simulation remains a bottleneck for scalable development and validation of autonomous systems. Existing generators can synthesize realistic scans, but they are typically constrained to a single sensor configuration, offer limited control over structure and geometry, and drift in long-horizon 4D generation. We present CrossLiDAR, a unified transformer-based framework capable of generating controllable and spatio-temporally consistent multi-sensor LiDAR sequences. Our approach leverages a rectified flow objective with a Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT) backbone, within a compact latent space of range images. To support multiple LiDAR sensors, an Inter-sensor Module enables interaction across sensors, while a ControlNet-style branch provides structural conditioning (e.g., BEV priors or 3D bounding boxes). For modeling the temporal consistency, CrossLiDAR generates short $N$-frame sequences and extends them autoregressively to improve long-horizon coherence. Our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 29.56\% in JSD and 15.36\% in MMD evaluated on nuScenes and the Waymo Dataset. CrossLiDAR bridges the gap to modern autonomous-driving simulation by enabling calibration-consistent multi-sensor LiDAR rollouts over long horizons for controllable, scenario-based testing.

AI.tldr: Presents CrossLiDAR, a transformer-based rectified-flow framework that generates controllable, spatio-temporally consistent multi-sensor LiDAR sequences in a range-image latent space.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR generators are typically limited to a single sensor configuration, offer limited control over structure and geometry, and drift in long-horizon 4D generation.
AI.method: Uses a Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer backbone with a rectified flow objective, an Inter-sensor Module for interaction across sensors, a ControlNet-style branch for structural conditioning such as BEV priors or 3D bounding boxes, and autoregressive extension of short N-frame sequences.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with an average improvement of 29.56% in JSD and 15.36% in MMD on nuScenes and the Waymo Dataset.
AI.conclusion: The framework supports calibration-consistent multi-sensor LiDAR rollouts over long horizons for controllable, scenario-based testing of autonomous driving systems.

title: From Game Generation to Game Playing: Fully Automated Ability Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, Script2Play, by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision.

AI.tldr: Proposes an automated pipeline in which an LLM agent builds game environments and programmatic experts generate demonstrations, used to train Script2Play, a 4B vision-language-action model, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Training VLA models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations.
AI.method: An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and skill-targeted tasks; programmatic experts with privileged simulator state generate aligned instructions, rendered observations and keyboard and mouse actions; a 4B vision-language model is post-trained with behavior cloning.
AI.result: Trained on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay, Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively on multiple public game benchmarks and generalizes across game engines.
AI.conclusion: Targeted synthetic supervision can substitute for human gameplay demonstrations when training game-playing VLA policies.

title: Graphene: A Lightweight Transformer with Ising Mean-Field Refinement for Image Super-Resolution
summary: This paper proposes Graphene, a lightweight image super-resolution architecture with two complementary feature refinement mechanisms: Ising-model-inspired local feature refinement using an Ising Refinement Block (IRB) and stage-history-based feature refinement using a History Attention (HistAttn) module. The IRB reuses attention output features and pre-softmax attention logits to construct signed pairwise token couplings within each local window, applies unrolled mean-field updates, and refines features through a gated residual correction. These signed couplings allow alignment and opposition between latent spins to modulate local feature refinement. HistAttn attends over the current stage output and earlier representations at the same token position and adaptively blends the current stage output with a history-weighted feature aggregate without adding spatial pairwise attention. On Urban100 at $\times4$, Graphene and Graphene-light improve over IET and IET-light by 0.24 dB and 0.38 dB, respectively, with 34.3%/13.7% fewer parameters, 44.8%/44.4% fewer FLOPs, 78.4%/71.5% lower latency, and 76.0%/85.5% lower peak memory. Real-world SR comparisons further show that Graphene recovers fine details and preserves textures across diverse degradations. Code and reference checkpoints are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Presents Graphene, a lightweight image super-resolution transformer with Ising-inspired local feature refinement and history-based attention, which improves on IET on Urban100 at x4 with fewer parameters, FLOPs, latency and peak memory.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to refine features more effectively in a lightweight super-resolution network, using local token coupling and earlier stage representations without adding spatial pairwise attention.
AI.method: The Ising Refinement Block reuses attention outputs and pre-softmax logits to form signed pairwise token couplings within each local window, applies unrolled mean-field updates and a gated residual correction; History Attention blends the current stage output with a history-weighted aggregate of earlier representations at the same token position.
AI.result: On Urban100 at x4, Graphene and Graphene-light improve over IET and IET-light by 0.24 dB and 0.38 dB, with 34.3% and 13.7% fewer parameters, 44.8% and 44.4% fewer FLOPs, 78.4% and 71.5% lower latency, and 76.0% and 85.5% lower peak memory; real-world comparisons show fine details and textures are preserved across diverse degradations.
AI.conclusion: Signed local couplings and stage-history aggregation together yield a lighter super-resolution model with better Urban100 quality than IET.

title: SurgWorld: Learning Surgical Representations Beyond Observation via Latent Prediction
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Surgical procedures are inherently partially observable, requiring surgeons to continuously infer evolving anatomical dynamics and future surgical states beyond the current observation. However, existing self-supervised learning methods primarily learn from observed surgical videos through masked reconstruction or predicting representations within the camera's current field of view, lacking the capability to explicitly model the out-of-sight surgical dynamics. Inspired by latent predictive world models, we introduce SurgWorld, a video-native, self-supervised framework for surgical representation learning, which treats a specified spatial or temporal shift as a pseudo-action and learns to predict the target latent representation from a partial observation. Specifically, we propose Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling (OSDM) as the pretraining objective for predicting representations conditioned on relative spatio-temporal shifts. We further regularize the learned latent dynamics from OSDM with a Geometric Visual Similarity (GVS) objective by aligning patch-level relational structures between predicted and target representations, preserving spatial geometry and local visual coherence for dense perception. These two objectives are integrated through an agglomerative training framework that consolidates complementary supervisory signals from multiple teachers to learn a unified latent representation of surgical dynamics and visual geometry. Extensive transfer learning experiments on 17 surgical benchmarks show that SurgWorld consistently outperforms existing vision foundation models across surgical workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense visual perception. We further conduct tailored qualitative and quantitative analyses, demonstrating that SurgWorld effectively captures surgical dynamics beyond the directly observed context through latent prediction.

AI.tldr: Introduces SurgWorld, a self-supervised surgical representation framework that predicts out-of-sight latent dynamics from pseudo-actions and outperforms existing vision foundation models on 17 surgical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised surgical methods learn from the visible field of view through masked reconstruction or prediction within the current view, so they cannot explicitly model out-of-sight surgical dynamics.
AI.method: Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling (OSDM) predicts target latents conditioned on relative spatio-temporal shifts treated as pseudo-actions; a Geometric Visual Similarity (GVS) objective aligns patch-level relational structure between predicted and target representations; both are integrated in an agglomerative framework that consolidates multiple teachers into one unified latent representation.
AI.result: Transfer experiments on 17 surgical benchmarks show that SurgWorld consistently outperforms existing vision foundation models in surgical workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding and dense visual perception.
AI.conclusion: Latent prediction beyond the directly observed context captures surgical dynamics that visible-context methods miss.

title: Not All Layers Are Equal in Image-to-Video Transfer
summary: Parameter-efficient image-to-video transfer adapts frozen image foundation models to video via lightweight trainable adapters. Existing methods insert the same adapter at every transformer layer, implicitly assuming all layers require equal temporal modeling. A layer-wise sensitivity analysis across four video-native model families and two pretraining paradigms reveals that this assumption is wrong: temporal sensitivity increases with depth, and the pretraining paradigm determines its growth profile. Vision-only models exhibit a gradual rise, while vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery. This finding motivates STRAP, a training-free adapter placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model. Spatial adapters are assigned before this boundary and temporal adapters after it, without modifying the adapter architecture itself. On four fine-grained action recognition benchmarks, STRAP improves accuracy by up to 11.8% over uniform placement, reduces trainable parameters by 29 to 48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%. On standard benchmarks, it matches accuracy with fewer parameters. Code is available at this https URL.
