AI.tldr: Finds that temporal sensitivity grows with depth in image-to-video adapters, and proposes STRAP, a training-free rule that places spatial adapters before a transition boundary and temporal adapters after it, with the boundary derived from a paradigm-matched video model.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient image-to-video transfer inserts the same adapter at every layer, implicitly assuming all layers need equal temporal modeling, which a layer-wise sensitivity analysis shows is wrong.
AI.method: A layer-wise sensitivity analysis across four video-native model families and two pretraining paradigms motivates STRAP, which derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model and assigns adapters accordingly without changing the adapter architecture.
AI.result: On four fine-grained action recognition benchmarks, STRAP improves accuracy by up to 11.8% over uniform placement, reduces trainable parameters by 29 to 48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%; on standard benchmarks it matches accuracy with fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: Adapter placement should follow layer-specific temporal sensitivity, which depends on the pretraining paradigm, and a simple training-free rule can exploit this.

title: Map2SLAM: From Streaming Map Prediction to Real-Time SLAM
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Streaming 3D foundation models (3DFMs) estimate camera poses and dense geometry online, but they fall short of SLAM: their predictions are fixed once emitted, so loop closures cannot correct accumulated drift. With such models already providing strong geometric capability, a central question for SLAM becomes how to schedule their inference and how to keep its results as revisable state. We present Map2SLAM, which keeps LingBot-Map frozen, trains only a lightweight retrieval head, and builds SLAM on the model's inference interface, turning its predictions into observations of an external persistent SLAM state. The front-end tracks every incoming frame with the model's causal streaming inference and decides which frames are written to the persistent state as keyframes. The back-end asynchronously decides when and which past frames to re-observe, re-running the model's joint inference over them with fresh context; verified loop observations correct the trajectory online, and segment observations refine dense geometry after the sequence. All invocations share a single frame encoder pass per image, whose cached features also drive loop retrieval, so frequent re-invocation incurs no additional encoding cost. Map2SLAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by over 40% compared with the best uncalibrated baselines, while maintaining real-time tracking at over 28 FPS at a resolution of $518\times154$ on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Please visit our project page at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents Map2SLAM, which turns a frozen streaming 3D foundation model into a real-time SLAM system by treating its predictions as revisable observations of a persistent state, corrected through loop closures.
AI.motivation: Streaming 3D foundation models estimate camera poses and dense geometry online but fix their predictions once emitted, so loop closures cannot correct accumulated drift.
AI.method: Keeps LingBot-Map frozen and trains only a lightweight retrieval head; a front-end tracks every frame and selects keyframes, and an asynchronous back-end re-runs joint inference over chosen past frames, with a single shared encoder pass per image whose cached features also drive loop retrieval.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by over 40% compared with the best uncalibrated baselines, while tracking in real time at over 28 FPS at 518x154 on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU.
AI.conclusion: Scheduling and revising the inference of streaming 3D models over a persistent state turns them into a practical real-time SLAM system.

title: Source-Anchored Visual Autoregression for Extreme Image Compression
summary: In the extreme-low bitrate range below $0.01$ bpp, image compression becomes a constrained generation problem: the reconstruction depends on inferring plausible missing details while staying close to the input image. Autoregressive token models provide an efficient coarse-to-fine prior for this setting, but the transmitted early-scale tokens often leave object identity and texture underdetermined, which can lead to source-inconsistent reconstructions. We introduce Source-Anchored Visual Autoregression (SAVAR), a generative codec built on Visual Autoregressive (VAR) modeling. SAVAR transmits early-scale tokens and a compact caption. The tokens provide image-specific layout information, while the caption supplies global semantics. SAVAR reconstructs a partial VQ-VAE latent from the retained scales, maps it to the start-of-sequence initialization, and uses the same latent to condition the caption embedding before adaptive layer normalization, separating two roles that are typically driven by a shared condition in VAR-style generation. On the Kodak and CLIC2020 datasets in the extreme-low range, SAVAR reduces perceptual distortion relative to matched ARPC retained-scale operating points, lowering LPIPS by about $8$--$9\%$ and DISTS by up to $22\%$ at a lower bpp. It reconstructs a $512 \times 512$ image in about $218$ ms on one NVIDIA L20X GPU, retaining fast autoregressive decoding in the evaluated setting.

AI.tldr: Proposes SAVAR, a generative codec for extreme low-bitrate image compression below 0.01 bpp that transmits early VAR-scale tokens and a compact caption, lowering perceptual distortion relative to matched ARPC operating points.
AI.motivation: Below 0.01 bpp, the transmitted early-scale tokens leave object identity and texture underdetermined, which can lead to reconstructions inconsistent with the source image.
AI.method: Reconstructs a partial VQ-VAE latent from the retained scales, maps it to the start-of-sequence initialization, and uses the same latent to condition the caption embedding before adaptive layer normalization, separating the layout role and the semantic role that VAR-style generation normally shares in one condition.
AI.result: On Kodak and CLIC2020 in the extreme-low range, relative to matched ARPC retained-scale operating points, SAVAR lowers LPIPS by about 8 to 9% and DISTS by up to 22% at a lower bpp; it reconstructs a 512 x 512 image in about 218 ms on one NVIDIA L20X GPU.
AI.conclusion: Separating token layout from caption semantics in VAR-based generation improves perceptual fidelity at extreme compression while keeping fast autoregressive decoding.

title: Viscot-steer: Disentangling and Transferring Visual Chain-of-Thought via Activation Steering
summary: Visual chain-of-thought (visual-CoT), also known as "thinking with images", equips LVLMs with the ability to locate and use key visual evidence for reasoning. However, acquiring such visual-CoT capabilities requires costly post-training and tightly couples them to a specific backbone, making transfer to other LVLMs difficult. Existing cross-model transfer methods typically treat visual-CoT as a monolithic capability, using a unified representation that ignores the functional distinction between grounding and reasoning and introduces stage-irrelevant interventions. To address this problem, we propose Viscot-steer, a training-free activation steering framework for transferring visual-CoT capabilities across heterogeneous LVLMs. Specifically, Viscot-steer first disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning vectors and extracts them from the source-model layers associated with the corresponding capabilities. It then aligns the vectors with the activation space of the target model and steers the grounding and reasoning layers during bounding-box prediction and reasoning-trace generation, respectively. Across benchmarks covering high-resolution visual understanding, general visual perception and reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning, Viscot-steer transfers capabilities from different visual-CoT models to architecturally diverse LVLMs and outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on the primary evaluation metrics.

AI.tldr: Presents Viscot-steer, a training-free activation steering method that transfers visual chain-of-thought across LVLMs by steering grounding and reasoning layers separately, outperforming the strongest capability-transfer baseline by 1.86 percentage points on average.
AI.motivation: Visual-CoT capabilities need costly post-training and are tied to a specific backbone, and existing cross-model transfer methods treat visual-CoT as a monolithic capability, ignoring the functional difference between grounding and reasoning.
AI.method: Disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning vectors extracted from the corresponding source-model layers, aligns them with the target model's activation space, and steers grounding layers during bounding-box prediction and reasoning layers during reasoning-trace generation.
AI.result: Across benchmarks for high-resolution visual understanding, general visual perception and reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning, Viscot-steer transfers capabilities from different visual-CoT models to architecturally diverse LVLMs and outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on the primary metrics.
AI.conclusion: Separating grounding from reasoning and steering each at its own stage enables training-free transfer of visual reasoning capabilities across heterogeneous LVLMs.

title: DynOLAT: OLAT Video Prediction for Controllable Dynamic Full-Body Relighting
comment: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 (Journal Track). Project page: this https URL
summary: Accurate lighting response is essential for realistic dynamic human relighting, because shadows, highlights, and color changes should follow the target illumination in both direction and relative strength. Current learning-based relighting methods can generate visually plausible videos, but they often exhibit imprecise lighting responses: shadows and highlights may drift away from the target direction, and the output brightness may not faithfully follow the relative intensities in the target environment, making the result closer to appearance harmonization than controllable relighting. To address this issue, we propose DynOLAT, a generalizable OLAT video prediction framework for dynamic full-body humans. Instead of directly synthesizing a single relit appearance, our method predicts temporally consistent One-Light-At-a-Time (OLAT) basis videos from flat-lit inputs, and then linearly combines the predicted bases according to the target environment map. This OLAT-based formulation makes the directional response explicit in the predicted bases, while the relative lighting strength is determined by the linear weights derived from the environment map. We further introduce a dynamic capture pipeline and the first large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset, comprising over 24 million frames from 224 identity-outfit combinations, where different outfits of the same person define separate combinations. Experiments show that DynOLAT responds more faithfully to variations in target lighting direction and relative intensity than the tested baselines, enabling controllable video relighting while preserving fine appearance details and temporal coherence. The dataset and processing tools will be publicly released to foster future research.

AI.tldr: Proposes DynOLAT, which predicts temporally consistent One-Light-At-a-Time (OLAT) basis videos from flat-lit full-body inputs and combines them with environment-map weights for controllable dynamic relighting, and introduces a dataset of over 24 million frames.
AI.motivation: Learning-based dynamic human relighting often behaves like appearance harmonization rather than controllable relighting, with shadows and highlights drifting from the target direction and brightness not following the relative intensities of the target environment.
AI.method: Predicts OLAT basis videos from flat-lit inputs and linearly combines them according to the target environment map, so the directional response is explicit in the bases and the relative strength comes from the linear weights; also introduces a dynamic capture pipeline and the first large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset.
AI.result: The dataset has over 24 million frames from 224 identity-outfit combinations; DynOLAT responds more faithfully than the tested baselines to variations in target lighting direction and relative intensity while preserving fine appearance details and temporal coherence.
AI.conclusion: The OLAT basis formulation enables controllable video relighting, and the dataset and processing tools are to be released to support future research.

title: Disentangling Where and When:Factored Spatio-Temporal Explanations for Video Action Recognition
comment: Accepted at The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Post-hoc explanation methods for video action recognition typically conflate spatial appearance and temporal dynamics into a single saliency or importance map. We propose a perturbation-based framework that disentangles these contributions into a spatial appearance mask ($M_a$) and a temporal motion mask ($M_m$). The two masks are jointly optimized against a frozen action recognition model through factored perturbation architecture, with nearest frame replacement to identify important temporal dynamics. A separation penalty discourages the appearance mask from spending budget on frames that the motion mask has already discarded. A ReLU-based area constraint penalizes explanations larger than an assigned budget. To evaluate these explanations, we introduce a separation protocol that sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames independently, backed by proofs characterizing the proposed method. Across EPIC-Kitchens-55, EGTEA Gaze+, and Something-Something V2, our method attains the lowest deletion AUC against leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.

AI.tldr: Proposes a perturbation-based explainer for video action recognition that separates spatial appearance and temporal motion into two jointly optimized masks, attaining the lowest deletion AUC among leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc explanations for video action recognition merge spatial appearance and temporal dynamics into a single saliency or importance map, which obscures which of the two drives the prediction.
AI.method: A spatial appearance mask and a temporal motion mask are jointly optimized against a frozen recognition model through factored perturbations with nearest-frame replacement; a separation penalty and a ReLU-based area constraint regularize the masks, and a separation protocol sweeps pixels and frames independently, backed by proofs.
AI.result: Across EPIC-Kitchens-55, EGTEA Gaze+ and Something-Something V2, the method attains the lowest deletion AUC against leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.
AI.conclusion: Factoring explanations into where and when components yields sparser explanations with lower deletion AUC than single-map baselines.

title: Auto-GlaKG: Automated Biomarker Reasoning for Explainable Glaucoma Detection
summary: Interpretable glaucoma detection requires a transparent connection between fundus images, clinically meaningful biomarkers, and diagnostic predictions. Knowledge graph (KG) reasoning provides this structure, but performance measured using annotated biomarkers does not establish performance when only images are available. We present Auto-GlaKG, an automated framework that combines image-based biomarker prediction with fixed clinical-prior rules. A ResNet50 network predicts the cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) and six morphological signs using biomarker supervision, and a KG reasoner aggregates their signed rule contributions into a glaucoma score. On 689 fundus images evaluated using stratified, group-aware five-fold cross-validation, Auto-GlaKG achieves a pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.951 (95\% confidence interval: 0.931--0.969), with sensitivity of 0.970 and specificity of 0.779. The matched image classifier also achieves an AUC of 0.951, while the rule stage adds 0.2~ms per image. Replacing predicted CDR with its annotation increases fold-mean AUC from 0.953 to 0.995. The framework provides an explicit rule-level account of image-based predictions and identifies CDR estimation as a priority for validation using independently measured biomarkers.

AI.tldr: Presents Auto-GlaKG, which predicts the cup-to-disc ratio (CDR) and six morphological signs from fundus images and aggregates signed rule contributions in a knowledge graph to score glaucoma, reaching a pooled AUC of 0.951 on 689 images.
AI.motivation: Knowledge-graph reasoning gives interpretable glaucoma detection, but its performance has been measured with annotated biomarkers, which does not establish performance when only images are available.
AI.method: A ResNet50 predicts CDR and six morphological signs with biomarker supervision, and a KG reasoner aggregates their signed rule contributions into a glaucoma score; evaluated with stratified, group-aware five-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: Pooled AUC of 0.951 (95% CI 0.931 to 0.969) with sensitivity 0.970 and specificity 0.779; the matched image classifier also achieves an AUC of 0.951; the rule stage adds 0.2 ms per image; replacing predicted CDR with its annotation raises fold-mean AUC from 0.953 to 0.995.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives an explicit rule-level account of image-based predictions and identifies CDR estimation as the priority for validation with independently measured biomarkers.

title: DuSS-PET: Self-Supervised Low-Dose PET Reconstruction Using Pseudo-Dual-Domain Consistency Without Paired Data
comment: Author accepted manuscript. Published in IEEE Transactions on Radiation and Plasma Medical Sciences (Early Access, 2026)
summary: Positron emission tomography (PET) is pivotal in medicine and healthcare, but requires high radiation doses for quality imaging. Although deep learning has shown promise for low-dose PET reconstruction/enhancement, existing methods primarily rely on fully supervised learning, which requires paired low- and full-dose scans that are clinically impractical to obtain. To overcome this fundamental limitation, we propose DuSS-PET, a novel self-supervised PET reconstruction framework that operates without any paired low- and full-dose data. Our method is built upon a computational Noisier2Noise (Nr2N) paradigm, featuring a Bernoulli corruption strategy that serves as an image-space approximation to emulate low-count noise patterns in image-derived pseudo-sinogram representations. The DuSS-PET framework integrates three core components: an adaptive Swin transformer for pseudo-sinogram restoration, a plug-and-play module for image enhancement, and a consistency-constrained SSL strategy that enforces agreement between the pseudo-sinogram and image representations. Extensive experiments on multi-center datasets demonstrate that DuSS-PET achieves superior reconstruction performance, outperforming state-of-the-art SSL methods and achieving comparable or even better results than fully supervised approaches across various dose levels. In particular, it exhibits exceptional generalization across different scanner vendors. This work is among the first self-supervised low-dose PET reconstruction framework that enforces consistency between reconstructed images and pseudo-sinograms, where the pseudo-sinogram generated in the image space serves as a solid computational consistency constraint for enhanced imaging without full-dose training scans. The source code will be publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes DuSS-PET, a self-supervised low-dose PET reconstruction framework that needs no paired low- and full-dose scans, built on a Bernoulli-corrupted Noisier2Noise paradigm with consistency between pseudo-sinogram and image representations.
AI.motivation: Deep learning methods for low-dose PET are mostly fully supervised and require paired low- and full-dose scans, which are clinically impractical to obtain.
AI.method: Builds on a computational Noisier2Noise paradigm with a Bernoulli corruption strategy that approximates low-count noise in image-derived pseudo-sinograms, an adaptive Swin transformer for pseudo-sinogram restoration, a plug-and-play image enhancement module, and a consistency-constrained self-supervised strategy.
AI.result: On multi-center datasets, DuSS-PET outperforms state-of-the-art self-supervised methods and achieves comparable or better results than fully supervised approaches across dose levels, with strong generalization across scanner vendors.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing consistency between reconstructed images and image-space pseudo-sinograms provides a computational constraint that enables enhanced low-dose PET without full-dose training scans.

title: BiRefNet-V2: Rethinking Bilateral Reference for High-Resolution Dichotomous Image Segmentation
summary: Dichotomous image segmentation requires pixel-accurate foreground-background separation while preserving fine structures such as thin filaments, sharp edges, and intricate textures. BiRefNet addressed this challenge through bilateral references, combining image patches and gradient information, but its inward reference loses local spatial structure and lacks semantic guidance, while its outward reference relies on single-channel gradient attention. We recast this paradigm as controlled information recovery - locality determines what spatial information survives, semantic selectivity what information enters, and focused boundary supervision where refinement occurs - and propose BiRefNet-V2 to implement it: (1) locality-preserving and semantically guided detail injection through space-to-depth transformation, overlapping patches, and a Semantically Guided Gate; (2) a learned boundary stream with focused supervision that generates full-channel residual attention without requiring boundary annotations; and (3) a dual-branch decoder integrating depth-wise boundary convolutions with large-kernel attention. A modernized framework - LayerNorm, GELU, the Lion optimizer, and a DINOv3 backbone - cuts training from 600 to 50 epochs. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on DIS5K, camouflaged object detection, and high-resolution salient object detection across all 13 evaluation sets. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents BiRefNet-V2, which recasts bilateral reference as controlled information recovery through locality-preserving detail injection, a learned boundary stream and a dual-branch decoder, reporting state-of-the-art performance across all 13 evaluation sets.
AI.motivation: BiRefNet's inward reference loses local spatial structure and lacks semantic guidance, while its outward reference relies on single-channel gradient attention, which limits recovery of thin and fine structures in dichotomous segmentation.
AI.method: Uses space-to-depth transformation, overlapping patches and a Semantically Guided Gate for detail injection; a boundary stream with focused supervision that produces full-channel residual attention without boundary annotations; a dual-branch decoder with depth-wise boundary convolutions and large-kernel attention; and a modernized framework with LayerNorm, GELU, the Lion optimizer and a DINOv3 backbone.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on DIS5K, camouflaged object detection and high-resolution salient object detection across all 13 evaluation sets, and reduces training from 600 to 50 epochs.
AI.conclusion: Framing bilateral reference as controlled information recovery, with locality, semantic selectivity and focused boundary supervision, yields strong dichotomous segmentation with much shorter training.

title: TransArt3D: From Two States to Articulated 3D Reconstruction with Video Transition Priors
summary: Reconstructing interactable articulated assets from a few images is key to robotics and simulation, yet highly underconstrained. Existing optimization-based methods fit an articulated asset under a static 3D prior that scores each state independently, so per-state reconstruction errors leak into the estimated moving part and joint as false motion. Video diffusion models capture how objects move between states, but only implicitly in 2D. To this end, we present TransArt3D, an optimization-based framework that reconstructs an articulated 3D asset from two endpoint images by translating this video transition prior into explicit part structure and joint kinematics. It first lifts frames generated between the endpoints with a transition-coupled 3D consensus that applies the static 3D prior jointly across frames, stabilizing unchanging regions and initializing the parts and joint. A rectified-flow kinematic refinement then lets the video prior supervise a 3D motion field over the whole transition, while part assignment and a shared joint constrain the field throughout optimization, keeping per-state errors out of the articulation. Finally, a motion-aware canonical appearance fusion uses the recovered articulation to map both endpoint images onto one canonical surface, texturing regions that only one state reveals. On PartNet-Mobility, TransArt3D outperforms methods given the same two endpoints in geometry and joint accuracy, and surpasses methods given six observed states in articulated-state geometry, joint localization and appearance.

AI.tldr: TransArt3D reconstructs an articulated 3D asset from only two endpoint images by using a video diffusion model's transition prior to recover part structure and joint kinematics. It outperforms methods given the same two endpoints and surpasses methods given six observed states on PartNet-Mobility.
AI.motivation: Optimization-based articulated reconstruction scores each state independently under a static 3D prior, so per-state errors leak into the estimated moving part and joint as false motion. Video diffusion models capture how objects move between states, but only implicitly in 2D.
AI.method: A transition-coupled 3D consensus applies the static 3D prior jointly across frames generated between the endpoints to stabilize unchanging regions and initialize parts and the joint. A rectified-flow kinematic refinement lets the video prior supervise a 3D motion field, with part assignment and a shared joint constraining it. A motion-aware canonical appearance fusion maps both endpoint images onto one canonical surface.
AI.result: On PartNet-Mobility, TransArt3D beats methods given the same two endpoints in geometry and joint accuracy. It also surpasses methods given six observed states in articulated-state geometry, joint localization and appearance.
AI.conclusion: Translating a video transition prior into explicit part structure and joint kinematics makes articulated reconstruction feasible from two images, reducing the dependence on many observed states.

title: Beyond Similarity Entropy: A Rank-Guided Data-Free Quantization Framework for Vision Transformers
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, yet their computational and memory demands pose significant challenges for deployment on mobile devices. Data-free quantization (DFQ) enables the compression of ViTs without access to their original training data. Existing DFQ methods often synthesize calibration samples by maximizing the entropy of patch similarity. However, similarity entropy describes the dispersion of similarity values without ensuring that the generated samples cover diverse feature directions, potentially limiting their effectiveness for quantization calibration. To address this limitation, we propose RankQ-ViT, a rank-guided DFQ framework for ViTs. We first observe that patch similarity matrices derived from Gaussian noise tend to have lower ranks than those derived from real images. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a block-aware self-contrastive objective that promotes feature diversity during synthetic data generation without explicitly computing matrix rank at each optimization step. We then select calibration samples based on their rank and semantic consistency and use them for block-wise reconstruction of the quantized model. Experiments on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet demonstrate the effectiveness of RankQ-ViT across multiple architectures and tasks, particularly under low-bit quantization. The code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: RankQ-ViT is a data-free quantization framework for Vision Transformers that synthesizes calibration samples by promoting feature diversity measured through patch-similarity rank rather than similarity entropy. It is reported to be effective across multiple architectures and tasks, particularly under low-bit quantization.
AI.motivation: Existing data-free quantization methods maximize the entropy of patch similarity to synthesize calibration samples, but similarity entropy does not guarantee that samples cover diverse feature directions.
AI.method: The authors observe that patch similarity matrices from Gaussian noise have lower rank than those from real images. They add a block-aware self-contrastive objective that promotes feature diversity during synthesis without computing matrix rank at each step. Calibration samples are then selected by rank and semantic consistency and used for block-wise reconstruction of the quantized model.
AI.result: Experiments on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40 and ShapeNet show the method is effective across multiple architectures and tasks, with particular gains under low-bit quantization. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Rank-guided sample synthesis and selection gives better calibration data for data-free ViT quantization than similarity entropy alone.

title: Conditional Diffusion-Based Proxy Representation Recovery for BCVA Prediction with Missing SLO Modality
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at IEEE BIBM 2026
summary: Preoperative prediction of postoperative best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) can support prognosis assessment and individualized decision-making in cataract surgery. Multimodal learning can integrate preoperative optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (SLO) images, and clinical text to characterize patient status. However, SLO images are often missing in real-world clinical data due to acquisition or data-management issues, resulting in incomplete multimodal inputs. To address this problem, this paper proposes a conditional diffusion-based method for SLO proxy representation recovery and fusion prediction. Instead of reconstructing raw SLO images, the proposed method formulates SLO missingness as proxy representation recovery in the latent feature space. Specifically, OCT image features and clinical text features are first fused to construct an OCT-text conditional representation, which guides the reverse denoising process of the diffusion model to estimate sample-specific SLO proxy representations. The recovered SLO proxy representation is then used as a substitute for the unavailable SLO modality and incorporated into the downstream multimodal fusion prediction network for postoperative BCVA prediction. Experiments were conducted on 2,141 preoperative multimodal cataract samples, with an SLO missing rate of 58.80%. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 0.9714 under the criterion of an absolute prediction error within 0.1 LogMAR and a mean absolute error of 0.0423, outperforming representative postoperative visual acuity prediction and missing-modality learning methods. These results indicate that representation-level proxy recovery can alleviate the impact of SLO modality missingness on postoperative BCVA prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a conditional diffusion model that recovers missing SLO image features as latent proxy representations for predicting postoperative BCVA after cataract surgery. On 2,141 samples with 58.80% SLO missingness, it reports an accuracy of 0.9714 within 0.1 LogMAR and an MAE of 0.0423.
AI.motivation: SLO images are often missing in real clinical data, leaving multimodal BCVA prediction with incomplete inputs.
AI.method: Instead of reconstructing raw SLO images, the method recovers SLO proxy representations in the latent feature space. OCT and clinical text features are fused into a conditional representation that guides the reverse denoising of a diffusion model. The recovered proxy is fed into a downstream multimodal fusion prediction network.
AI.result: On 2,141 preoperative cataract samples with an SLO missing rate of 58.80%, the method achieves an accuracy of 0.9714 at an absolute error within 0.1 LogMAR and an MAE of 0.0423. It outperforms representative postoperative visual acuity prediction and missing-modality learning methods.
AI.conclusion: Representation-level proxy recovery can reduce the impact of SLO missingness on postoperative BCVA prediction.

title: MoT3DVG: A Benchmark for Outdoor 3D Visual Grounding with Motion-Aware Descriptions and Temporal Cues
summary: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MoT3DVG, a benchmark for outdoor 3D visual grounding with motion-aware descriptions and temporal cues, built on nuScenes. It also proposes DynaVG, which adds a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding module and reports state-of-the-art results on the benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D visual grounding research focuses on static indoor objects, which limits its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving, where motion descriptions can capture temporal dynamics.
AI.method: The MoT3DVG dataset contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes and 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. DynaVG adds a SLIDE module before language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models local motion cues with short-term window encoding and global temporal context with long-term window shifting.
AI.result: DynaVG achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Motion-aware encoding is effective for outdoor 3D visual grounding, and the work points to open challenges for future research in this setting.

title: NuJEV: Structured Visual Judgments for Consistent Nuclei Quantification
summary: Nuclear quantification requires locating and typing nuclei, beyond generating a count. Inspired by Jev's structured decisions in place of free-form generation, we introduce NuJEV for nuclear perception in Qwen3-VL-2B. We jointly train visual LoRA and a parallel head to predict nuclear presence, centers, and types. One image encoding feeds both the nuclear head and original language decoder. The decoder interprets region and type requests, with counts computed from the predicted nuclei. On 2,732 PanNuke test images, NuJEV achieves a five-query mean absolute error ($\mathrm{MAE}_5$) of 1.844 overall and 5.268 on dense images, with localization/typed F1 of 0.816/0.682. A matched encoder ablation shows 41.0\% lower dense error with visual adaptation. For language requests, NuJEV reduces request MAE by 76.2\% relative to direct generation. Our code will be released as open source.

AI.tldr: NuJEV trains a Qwen3-VL-2B model with a visual LoRA and a parallel head that predicts nuclear presence, centers and types, so that counts are computed from structured predictions rather than free-form generation. It reports an MAE of 1.844 on 2,732 PanNuke test images.
AI.motivation: Nuclear quantification requires locating and typing nuclei, not only producing a count, and free-form language generation is an unreliable way to do this.
AI.method: A visual LoRA and a parallel head are trained jointly to predict nuclear presence, centers and types. One image encoding feeds both the nuclear head and the original language decoder. The decoder interprets region and type requests, and counts are computed from the predicted nuclei.
AI.result: On 2,732 PanNuke test images, NuJEV reaches a five-query MAE of 1.844 overall and 5.268 on dense images, with localization and typed F1 of 0.816 and 0.682. A matched encoder ablation shows 41.0% lower dense error with visual adaptation. For language requests, request MAE drops by 76.2% relative to direct generation.
AI.conclusion: Structured visual judgments are more consistent than free-form generation for nuclear quantification, and visual adaptation helps most on dense images. The code is promised as open source.

title: SegDis: Foreground Segmentation Followed by Type Discrimination for Salient and Camouflaged Object Detection
summary: Salient and camouflaged object detection (SOD and COD) both recover foreground support, yet most joint methods output only a binary mask and therefore cannot distinguish the type. USC12K distinguishes the two types, but its baseline USCNet still binds foreground existence to the type within a single normalization, so the failure source cannot be attributed. Our cross-task study shows that foreground localization transfers between SOD and COD, whereas type discrimination does not: a COD-only model recovers foreground on SOD images but its type judgement follows the training distribution rather than the foreground-background relation, so the two decisions require separate mechanisms. SegDis factorizes the output into an explicit foreground probability and a conditional type probability given foreground: FLR provides high-quality task-agnostic support, and RTA refines the SOD/COD assignment from the foreground-background relation without a task identifier. Because support is explicit, each ground-truth foreground pixel is classified as correct-type, type-swapped, or missed, so foreground-recovery and type-assignment errors are diagnosed separately. With PVT-v2-B2, SegDis attains 68.98% FG-mIoU and 78.35% mIoU on USC12K at about one-eighth of USCNet's parameters; CSCS is 5.75.

AI.tldr: SegDis factorizes salient and camouflaged object detection into an explicit foreground probability followed by a type probability conditioned on foreground, which lets foreground recovery and type assignment be diagnosed separately. With PVT-v2-B2 it reports 68.98% FG-mIoU and 78.35% mIoU on USC12K at about one-eighth of USCNet's parameters.
AI.motivation: Most joint salient and camouflaged object detection methods output only a binary mask and cannot distinguish the type. The USCNet baseline binds foreground existence to the type within one normalization, so failure sources cannot be attributed.
AI.method: The output is split into a foreground probability and a conditional type probability given foreground. FLR provides task-agnostic foreground support, and RTA refines the SOD/COD assignment from the foreground-background relation without a task identifier. Each ground-truth foreground pixel is labeled as correct-type, type-swapped or missed.
AI.result: With PVT-v2-B2, SegDis attains 68.98% FG-mIoU and 78.35% mIoU on USC12K at about one-eighth of USCNet's parameters. The CSCS score is 5.75. A cross-task study shows foreground localization transfers between SOD and COD while type discrimination does not.
AI.conclusion: Separating foreground localization from type discrimination with separate mechanisms gives a more accurate and more diagnosable joint detector.

title: Let the Gallery Learn Itself: Training-Free Iterative Side-View Face Recognition
summary: What if a face recognition system could learn from every encounter without a single gradient update? We present Gallery Self-Evolution (GSE), a training-free framework where the gallery itself adapts at test time. The core mechanism---dedup-FIFO curation---archives novel appearance samples after successful recognition while permanently locking the enrollment template, bounded at 30 embeddings per identity. On CFP-FP and IJB-C benchmarks, GSE closes the side-view gap by +23 points at 45° yaw and boosts TAR@FAR=0.001 by +9.4 points, all at CPU-level cost. No retraining. No GPU. Just a gallery that grows smarter every time it meets you.

AI.tldr: Gallery Self-Evolution (GSE) is a training-free face recognition framework in which the gallery adapts at test time through dedup-FIFO curation, keeping at most 30 embeddings per identity. On CFP-FP and IJB-C it closes the side-view gap by 23 points at 45 degrees yaw and raises TAR@FAR=0.001 by 9.4 points.
AI.motivation: Side-view face recognition performs poorly, and existing approaches typically require retraining or GPU compute to adapt.
AI.method: After successful recognition, novel appearance samples are archived into the gallery with dedup-FIFO curation, while the enrollment template is permanently locked. The gallery is bounded at 30 embeddings per identity.
AI.result: On CFP-FP and IJB-C, GSE closes the side-view gap by +23 points at 45 degrees yaw and boosts TAR@FAR=0.001 by +9.4 points, at CPU-level cost.
AI.conclusion: Test-time gallery curation can substantially improve recognition across viewpoints without any gradient updates or GPUs.

title: GenRM-Flow: Generators are Process-aware Reward Models in Flow Matching
summary: Aligning video generation models with human preference depends critically on the quality of the reward model that scores generated videos. Current video reward models, however, source their reward signal from a model's representational rather than generative capacity: they either repurpose vision-language models as pixel-space scorers, or train auxiliary scoring heads on top of frozen generator features. The generator's actual ability to predict velocities, denoise latents, and produce videos plays no role in scoring its own generations. We argue that this overlooks a structural property of offline preference learning. Any preference optimization objective that approximates an offline preference dataset mathematically targets a strictly defined KL-constrained optimal policy. By isolating the reward term from this analytical solution and mapping the exact generation log-likelihood to its flow-matching surrogate, the empirical reward emerges deterministically as the relative difference in continuous-time velocity-prediction errors. We formalize this equivalence into GenRM-Flow, a framework where a preference-tuned video generator inherently operates as a process-aware reward model directly in the noisy latent space. We further show theoretically that distinct fine-tuning objectives, whether contrastive like DPO and IPO or non-contrastive like RWR, are alternative optimization pathways toward the same optimal policy, each inducing a reward readout from the generator's velocity-prediction errors. Furthermore, the extracted process reward seamlessly substitutes external VLM scorers in FlowAWR. Operating purely on native latent outputs without auxiliary reward networks, this generative reward drives measurable improvements in downstream video generation.

AI.tldr: GenRM-Flow shows that a preference-tuned flow-matching video generator can serve as its own process-aware reward model, with the reward given by the relative difference in velocity-prediction errors in latent space. It replaces external VLM scorers in FlowAWR and yields measurable gains in downstream video generation.
AI.motivation: Current video reward models take their signal from a model's representational capacity, either repurposing VLMs or training heads on frozen generator features, and ignore the generator's own generative ability to predict velocities and denoise.
AI.method: Starting from the KL-constrained optimal policy that offline preference objectives target, the reward term is isolated and the exact generation log-likelihood is mapped to a flow-matching surrogate. The empirical reward then equals the relative difference in continuous-time velocity-prediction errors. The authors also argue that DPO, IPO and RWR are alternative routes to the same optimal policy, each inducing such a readout.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. It states that the extracted process reward substitutes external VLM scorers in FlowAWR and that the generative reward drives measurable improvements in downstream video generation.
AI.conclusion: A generator can provide its reward in latent space without auxiliary reward networks, making reward modeling for video alignment simpler.

title: Flex-DDCM: Zero-Shot Task-Oriented Image Compression via Diffusion Trajectory Guidance
summary: Recent zero-shot image compression methods exploit the powerful priors of pretrained diffusion models to produce perceptually pleasing reconstructions without compression-specific training. However, image compression serves not only human viewing but also machine analysis, while existing zero-shot codecs have limited flexibility in meeting the diverse reconstruction requirements of these applications. In this paper, we propose Flex-DDCM, a framework for zero-shot task-oriented image compression via diffusion trajectory guidance. Building on Turbo-DDCM, we adapt the coded diffusion trajectory through task-guided noise selection, embedding the effects of task guidance into the compressed representation. Guidance terms can be applied individually or combined, with timestep-dependent strengths controlling their influence throughout denoising. This design enables task adaptation without introducing additional decoding complexity. Experiments demonstrate flexible trade-offs among pixel fidelity, perceptual quality, and downstream task performance, with competitive performance against trained task-oriented codecs and faster decoding than Diff-ICMH.

AI.tldr: Flex-DDCM is a zero-shot task-oriented image compression method built on Turbo-DDCM that adapts the coded diffusion trajectory through task-guided noise selection. It offers flexible trade-offs among pixel fidelity, perceptual quality and downstream task performance, with faster decoding than Diff-ICMH.
AI.motivation: Existing zero-shot diffusion codecs have limited flexibility for the varied reconstruction needs of human viewing and machine analysis.
AI.method: Task-guided noise selection embeds the effects of task guidance into the compressed representation. Guidance terms can be applied individually or combined, with timestep-dependent strengths that control their influence during denoising. Decoding complexity is not increased.
AI.result: The abstract reports competitive performance against trained task-oriented codecs and faster decoding than Diff-ICMH. It describes flexible trade-offs among fidelity, perceptual quality and task performance without specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Task adaptation can be achieved in zero-shot diffusion compression by guiding the coded trajectory, without extra decoding cost.

title: Unlearning at Speed: Rapid Activation Dampening for Efficient Machine Unlearning in Real-World Face Recognition
summary: Machine unlearning has become increasingly important in face recognition, where regulations like the GDPR empower users to request the removal of their personal data from deployed models. However, most existing unlearning methods are designed for closed-set classification with small-scale models and training data, and therefore do not generalize to real-world face recognition systems, which operate in an open-set setting with large-scale models and data. In this work, we propose Rapid Activation Dampening (RAD), a fast and targeted unlearning method tailored specifically for large-scale open-set face recognition. RAD approximates differences in average neuron activations between forget and retain identities, identifying and selectively suppressing neurons that are most associated with the targeted identity through a sensitivity-controlled dampening mechanism. We further propose the Forget Score (FS), which addresses the mismatch between existing unlearning metrics and open-set problems by providing a probabilistic interpretation of forgetting directly in the representation space. Experiments across several recent large-scale face recognition architectures and datasets show that RAD achieves strong forgetting while preserving overall model utility and substantially improving unlearning speed. These findings establish RAD as a scalable and practical approach to machine unlearning in face recognition systems.

AI.tldr: Rapid Activation Dampening (RAD) is a fast, targeted unlearning method for large-scale open-set face recognition that suppresses neurons associated with the forget identity. The paper also proposes the Forget Score, a probabilistic metric of forgetting in representation space, and reports strong forgetting with preserved utility and much faster unlearning.
AI.motivation: Existing unlearning methods target closed-set classification with small models and data, and do not transfer to open-set face recognition with large models and data, where regulations such as GDPR require removal of personal data.
AI.method: RAD approximates differences in average neuron activations between forget and retain identities. It then selectively suppresses the neurons most associated with the target identity through a sensitivity-controlled dampening mechanism. The Forget Score addresses the mismatch between existing metrics and open-set problems.
AI.result: Across several recent large-scale face recognition architectures and datasets, RAD achieves strong forgetting while preserving overall utility and substantially improving unlearning speed. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: RAD is presented as a scalable and practical approach to machine unlearning in real-world face recognition.

title: How to "train" a surgeon? Benchmarking generalist agents in surgical scene understanding
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. 64 pages including appendices. Project page: this https URL
summary: Evaluating general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for surgical scene understanding remains limited due to scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols. We address these challenges through a two-stage evaluation framework for surgical scene understanding. In Stage I, we introduce SurgKnowBench, a diagnostic benchmark that harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks and evaluates proprietary and open-source MLLMs to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgKnowBench reveals that current models retain partial visual priors but remain weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Building on this failure frontier and motivated by the scaffolded nature of surgical training, we introduce SurgAgentGym, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks. SurgAgentGym evaluates whether generalist agents can improve surgical understanding at inference time through tool-mediated evidence use, without additional surgical training. Our results show that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. This opens a path toward future studies of agentic surgical understanding.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage evaluation of general-purpose multimodal LLMs for surgical scene understanding: SurgKnowBench as a diagnostic benchmark, and SurgAgentGym as an agentic environment with bounded knowledge search and visual grounding. It finds agentic inference helps mainly on perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Evaluating general-purpose MLLMs for surgical scene understanding is limited by scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols.
AI.method: SurgKnowBench harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgAgentGym lets general-purpose MLLM agents use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general visual grounding at inference time, without additional surgical training.
AI.result: SurgKnowBench shows that current models retain partial visual priors but are weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Tool-mediated agentic inference helps generalist models on some surgical tasks, and the paper opens a path toward agentic surgical understanding research.

title: Semantically Aligned KV Cache Compression for Efficient Agentic Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: Agentic autoregressive video generation combines semantic planning, sequential generation, and visual verification for controllable synthesis. Growing visual histories enlarge the key-value (KV) cache, increasing memory use and attention costs across candidate rollouts. Existing compression methods primarily optimize individual generators without the planner's semantic constraints, risking low priority for states supporting requested attributes or actions. We introduce SemanticKV, a training-free method for semantically aligned KV cache compression. To our knowledge, SemanticKV is the first KV cache compression method for agentic autoregressive video generation that explicitly uses planner-extracted semantic constraints to guide retention. Text cross-attention identifies constraint-related video positions, whose self-attention queries are collected into separate groups. Attention weights are averaged within each group and maximized across groups, giving each cached entry a high score when strongly used by any represented constraint. A single top-k selection retains high-scoring entries under the memory budget, leaving their keys, values, and positions unchanged. For fixed query groups and equal entry costs, this selection minimizes an additive upper bound on worst-group discarded attention. The method operates independently within each candidate without retraining or additional video generations. We evaluate four AR video backbones on three benchmarks for 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation. On Causal Forcing at a compression ratio of 0.7, SemanticKV obtains a VBench Total Score of 84.10, compared with 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV. It achieves a 1.22x speedup over Full KV and reduces KV-cache memory from 6.04 GB to 1.81 GB, a 3.35x reduction.

AI.tldr: SemanticKV is a training-free KV cache compression method for agentic autoregressive video generation that uses planner-extracted semantic constraints to decide which cached entries to keep. At a compression ratio of 0.7 on Causal Forcing it reaches a VBench Total Score of 84.10 with a 1.22x speedup and a reduction of KV-cache memory from 6.04 GB to 1.81 GB.
AI.motivation: Growing visual histories enlarge the KV cache and attention costs, and existing compression methods optimize individual generators without the planner's semantic constraints, which can drop states that support requested attributes or actions.
AI.method: Text cross-attention identifies constraint-related video positions, whose self-attention queries are collected into groups. Attention weights are averaged within each group and maximized across groups, and a single top-k selection retains high-scoring entries under the memory budget. Retained entries keep their keys, values and positions unchanged, and the method runs per candidate without retraining.
AI.result: On Causal Forcing at a compression ratio of 0.7, SemanticKV obtains a VBench Total Score of 84.10, versus 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV. It gives a 1.22x speedup over Full KV and cuts KV-cache memory from 6.04 GB to 1.81 GB, a 3.35x reduction. Four AR video backbones are evaluated on three benchmarks for 5, 30 and 60 second generation.
AI.conclusion: Using planner semantics to guide KV retention preserves or slightly improves quality while substantially reducing memory and time for agentic video generation.

title: ForeAct: Geometry-Guided Action Learning from World Representations
summary: Robotic manipulation requires representations that capture both scene geometry and its evolution during interaction. Existing approaches have largely treated these two aspects separately. World action models capture such dynamics by coupling action prediction with future video generation, but their reliance on iterative diffusion or rectified-flow inference leads to high computational cost, while their representations lack explicit spatial structure. Explicitly modeling scene geometry typically requires auxiliary modules that increase both parameter count and computational cost. Conversely, geometry-centric policies primarily recover observed spatial structure and often lack explicit supervision for anticipating future geometric changes during interaction. To address these limitations, we introduce ForeAct, which repurposes a pretrained video world model as a single-pass representation backbone for low-latency control. ForeAct directly processes the clean latent of the current observation in one forward pass, eliminating future-frame synthesis and iterative denoising while retaining the backbone's pretrained spatiotemporal priors. Rather than introducing a separate geometry backbone, ForeAct uses learnable tokens supervised by next-frame relative depth to shape the shared video representation through bidirectional self-attention. This compact interface turns the spatial knowledge already encoded in the backbone into a future-aware representation for action generation, with little parameter overhead. The lightweight geometry readout is used only during training and removed at deployment, enabling low-latency, geometry-aware control without depth input or an external geometry backbone. Without additional large-scale pretraining, ForeAct achieves 96.6% average success on LIBERO, 63.5% on SimplerEnv-Bridge, and a 74.4% success rate across 90 real-world rollouts.

AI.tldr: ForeAct repurposes a pretrained video world model as a single-pass representation backbone for low-latency robotic action learning, with learnable tokens supervised by next-frame relative depth. It reaches 96.6% average success on LIBERO, 63.5% on SimplerEnv-Bridge and 74.4% over 90 real-world rollouts, without depth input at deployment.
AI.motivation: World action models couple action prediction with future video generation, which requires costly iterative denoising and gives representations without explicit spatial structure. Geometry-centric policies recover observed structure but lack supervision for anticipating future geometric change.
AI.method: ForeAct processes the clean latent of the current observation in one forward pass, avoiding future-frame synthesis and iterative denoising. Learnable tokens supervised by next-frame relative depth shape the shared video representation through bidirectional self-attention. The depth readout is used only during training and removed at deployment.
AI.result: ForeAct achieves 96.6% average success on LIBERO, 63.5% on SimplerEnv-Bridge and a 74.4% success rate across 90 real-world rollouts, without large-scale additional pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware, future-aware control can be obtained at low latency with little parameter overhead by reusing the spatial knowledge already in a video world model.

title: AgentCT: A Vision-Language Agent for Universal CT Imaging
summary: Computed tomography (CT) restoration methods often use a single network for low-dose CT (LDCT), sparse-view CT (SVCT), and metal artifact reduction (MAR), despite the distinct physics of these degradations. We propose AgentCT, a vision-language agent that identifies the degradation and routes images to task-specific restoration models. A LoRA-adapted Qwen3-VL-4B controller predicts degradation type and severity, selects a specialist, and reassesses the restored image. The LDCT specialist uses an image-domain diffusion model, whereas the SVCT and MAR specialists combine projection-domain correction, data consistency, differentiable filtered back-projection, and image refinement. We evaluated the controller and specialists separately on patient-disjoint Mayo 2020 abdominal CT data across three severity levels for each degradation. The controller achieved 95.7% accuracy for degradation type and 93.9% for severity, with a 100% JSON parse rate. Using ground-truth degradation labels for routing, AgentCT achieved an overall PSNR/SSIM of 46.18 dB/0.984, compared with 44.93 dB/0.976 for AMIR and 44.29 dB/0.979 for TAMP, and attained the highest PSNR in all nine settings. For SVCT, its dual-domain specialist achieved 46.04 dB with 4.2 million parameters, compared with 44.43 dB for single-task AMIR and 43.57 dB for all-in-one AMIR with 23.5 million parameters. These results support degradation-specific CT restoration with controller-based model selection; evaluation under automatic routing and on independent clinical data remains necessary. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: AgentCT is a vision-language agent that identifies the CT degradation type and severity with a LoRA-adapted Qwen3-VL-4B controller and routes images to task-specific restoration specialists. With ground-truth routing it reaches 46.18 dB PSNR and 0.984 SSIM overall, the highest PSNR in all nine settings.
AI.motivation: CT restoration often uses one network for low-dose CT, sparse-view CT and metal artifact reduction, although these degradations have distinct physics.
AI.method: A LoRA-adapted Qwen3-VL-4B controller predicts degradation type and severity, selects a specialist, and reassesses the restored image. The LDCT specialist uses an image-domain diffusion model. The SVCT and MAR specialists combine projection-domain correction, data consistency, differentiable filtered back-projection and image refinement.
AI.result: The controller reaches 95.7% accuracy for degradation type and 93.9% for severity, with a 100% JSON parse rate. With ground-truth routing, AgentCT achieves 46.18 dB/0.984 overall, versus 44.93 dB/0.976 for AMIR and 44.29 dB/0.979 for TAMP. For SVCT its dual-domain specialist reaches 46.04 dB with 4.2 million parameters, versus 44.43 dB for single-task AMIR and 43.57 dB for all-in-one AMIR with 23.5 million parameters.
AI.conclusion: Degradation-specific restoration with controller-based model selection is supported on patient-disjoint Mayo 2020 data, though evaluation under automatic routing and on independent clinical data is still needed.

title: Reaching Is Not Finding: Map-Anchored Visual Prompting for the Last Mile of Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) asks a drone to find an object described in natural language. The description usually locates the object relative to named landmarks, such as streets and buildings. We observe that current navigators often bring the drone close to the target and then stop at the wrong place: they reach the target without finding it. This gap is shared by navigators of very different designs, from imitation learners to a fine-tuned 7B vision-language model. A simple test reveals the cause. When we replace the target object in the instruction with another one next to the same landmarks, no navigator goes to it, and most stop where they did before. Navigators learn to reach the landmarks, not to identify the described object. We therefore propose MAP-VP, a plug-and-play module for the last step. After any navigator stops, MAP-VP draws the landmarks named in the instruction onto the drone's current view, using the landmark outlines that the benchmark provides on a map. A fine-tuned 4B vision-language model then locates the target relative to these landmarks. The training data are generated automatically from the benchmark annotations. Neither drawing the landmarks nor fine-tuning helps much alone, but together they are highly effective. Without retraining any navigator, MAP-VP significantly improves all six navigators we test on CityNav. It roughly doubles the success rate of the two strongest trained navigators, raising HETT from 25.9% to 54.6% and FlightGPT from 24.2% to 48.9%, whereas CityNav's official detector-based last step adds less than two points to HETT.

AI.tldr: MAP-VP is a plug-and-play last-step module for aerial vision-language navigation that draws the landmarks named in the instruction onto the drone's view and uses a fine-tuned 4B VLM to locate the target relative to them. It roughly doubles the success rate of the two strongest trained navigators on CityNav, raising HETT from 25.9% to 54.6% and FlightGPT from 24.2% to 48.9%.
AI.motivation: Current aerial navigators often reach the vicinity of the target and stop at the wrong place, because they learn to reach landmarks rather than to identify the described object. Replacing the target object with another next to the same landmarks leaves navigator behavior unchanged.
AI.method: After any navigator stops, MAP-VP draws the instruction's landmarks onto the current view using the landmark outlines provided by the benchmark's map. A fine-tuned 4B VLM then locates the target relative to these landmarks. Training data are generated automatically from benchmark annotations.
AI.result: Without retraining any navigator, MAP-VP significantly improves all six navigators tested on CityNav. HETT rises from 25.9% to 54.6% and FlightGPT from 24.2% to 48.9%, while CityNav's official detector-based last step adds less than two points to HETT. Neither landmark drawing nor fine-tuning helps much alone.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly grounding the target relative to drawn landmarks fixes the last-mile failure of aerial VLN, and the two components are only effective together.

title: InfCoiL: Coordinated Planner-Controller Learning for Closed-Loop Physics-Based Human-Object Interaction
summary: Text- and goal-conditioned human-object interaction (HOI) provides an intuitive interface for specifying high-level intents in physics-based character animation. Mapping such intents to physically plausible, contact-rich behaviors naturally calls for a generative planner and a physics-based controller, yet existing planner-controller systems either execute plans open-loop or close the loop while keeping the planner fixed, so execution feedback never reshapes what is planned. We present InfCoiL, a closed-loop framework for physics-based HOI from coordinated planner-controller learning. InfCoiL couples a morphology-aware flow-matching planner with a unified multi-morphology controller through a shared morphology interface in an autoregressive plan-and-execute loop, and alternately fine-tunes both components with reinforcement learning from the same physical rollouts. To optimize the flow-matching planner online, we introduce Semantic Flow Policy Optimization (SFPO), which stochasticizes selected denoising transitions with channel-wise semantic covariance over heterogeneous HOI features and assigns group-relative, sequence-level rewards from complete closed-loop executions. On held-out OMOMO sequences, InfCoiL outperforms open-loop hierarchical baselines in goal-reaching task success and physical tracking accuracy. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: InfCoiL is a closed-loop physics-based human-object interaction framework that couples a flow-matching planner with a multi-morphology controller and fine-tunes both with reinforcement learning from the same physical rollouts. On held-out OMOMO sequences it outperforms open-loop hierarchical baselines in goal-reaching success and physical tracking accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing planner-controller systems either execute plans open-loop or close the loop while keeping the planner fixed, so execution feedback never changes what is planned.
AI.method: A morphology-aware flow-matching planner is coupled with a unified multi-morphology controller through a shared morphology interface in an autoregressive plan-and-execute loop. The two are alternately fine-tuned with RL. The planner is optimized online by Semantic Flow Policy Optimization (SFPO), which adds channel-wise semantic covariance noise at selected denoising transitions and assigns group-relative, sequence-level rewards from complete closed-loop executions.
AI.result: On held-out OMOMO sequences, InfCoiL outperforms open-loop hierarchical baselines in goal-reaching task success and physical tracking accuracy. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Coordinated planner-controller learning with feedback from physical execution yields more reliable closed-loop physics-based HOI.

title: Dropping Tokens Without Dropping Them: Causal Attribution for Diabetic Retinopathy
summary: In this work, we investigate whether attention-based attribution maps in a vision transformer provide causal explanations for diabetic retinopathy (DR) classification. We introduce a principled decomposition of attention into two attribution maps: the contribution ($c_t$), which satisfies the completeness axiom in explainable artificial intelligence (xAI), and the pull ($p_t$), which quantifies causal explanations. We define an identity relating $c_t$ and $p_t$ that characterizes when $c_t$ fails to capture causality. We test whether each map is causally faithful on the MAPLES-DR dataset by dropping/inserting tokens, and report Necessity ($N$), Sufficiency ($Su$), and Faithfulness Correlation ($FC$). The pull $p_t$ achieves the highest causal alignment ($FC = 0.53$, $N = 0.71\%$, $Su = 3.0\%$), outperforming Attention Rollout, Grad-CAM, and AttnLRP. Occlusion retains better sufficiency ($Su = 1.6\%$) but is about 800 times slower. Furthermore, on MAPLES-DR, $p_t$ achieves $70\%$ of the average precision (AP) of HRDecoder, a state-of-the-art supervised lesion segmentation model, despite the absence of pixel-level supervision. Together, these findings show that the pull $p_t$ and the contribution $c_t$ form computationally efficient attribution maps for reliable causal interpretation in safety-critical medical diagnostics. The code and demo are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes ViT attention into a contribution map and a pull map, and finds that the pull map gives the most causal attribution for diabetic retinopathy classification on MAPLES-DR. Pull achieves FC of 0.53, Necessity of 0.71% and Sufficiency of 3.0%, and reaches 70% of HRDecoder's average precision without pixel-level supervision.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether attention-based attribution maps in vision transformers provide causal explanations for diabetic retinopathy classification, and completeness-based contribution maps may fail to capture causality.
AI.method: Attention is decomposed into a contribution map c_t, which satisfies the completeness axiom, and a pull map p_t, which quantifies causal explanation. An identity relating the two characterizes when the contribution map fails to capture causality. Faithfulness is tested by dropping and inserting tokens and measuring Necessity, Sufficiency and Faithfulness Correlation.
AI.result: The pull map achieves the highest causal alignment with FC of 0.53, N of 0.71% and Su of 3.0%, outperforming Attention Rollout, Grad-CAM and AttnLRP. Occlusion has better sufficiency at 1.6% but is about 800 times slower. The pull map reaches 70% of HRDecoder's average precision on lesion segmentation.
AI.conclusion: The pull and contribution maps form computationally efficient attribution maps for causal interpretation in safety-critical medical diagnosis.

title: NightSteps: A Night-Time Dataset and Benchmark for Pedestrian Crossing Intention Prediction
summary: Autonomous vehicles use pedestrian crossing intention prediction (PCIP) to participate safely in traffic. Existing models are largely trained under favourable daytime conditions with sufficient daylight. Little is known about the robustness of these models under night-time and low-light conditions, due to the lack of datasets containing night-time footage. This paper investigates how a dataset, named NightSteps, can be constructed and evaluated as a baseline benchmark. The dataset is based on nighttime dashcam footage collected from six different cities around the world, capturing a wide variety of road conditions. The dataset consists of dashcam-recorded point-of-view footage, raw data of pedestrians' locations with corresponding 'track ids' and ground-truth labels containing accurate information about pedestrian crossing behaviour, resulting in a diverse dataset. Gemini, ChatGPT, and human assessment are used to demonstrate the usability of the dataset by predicting crossings in clips from the dataset and comparing the results with the initial ground-truth labels. These results show that human input achieves an accuracy of 88.17% and an F1-score of 80.21%. Predictions from Gemini and ChatGPT perform lower, with accuracies of 60% and 79.13% respectively, and F1-scores of 42.50% and 63.64%. The evaluation demonstrates that the NightSteps dataset can be used for future model evaluation to test the performance of PCIP, with the aim of improving road safety at night.

AI.tldr: NightSteps is a night-time dashcam dataset with pedestrian location tracks and crossing labels from six cities, used to benchmark pedestrian crossing intention prediction under low light. Human assessment reaches 88.17% accuracy and 80.21% F1, while Gemini and ChatGPT reach 60% and 79.13% accuracy respectively.
AI.motivation: Pedestrian crossing intention prediction models are largely trained on daytime footage, and their robustness at night is unknown because night-time datasets are lacking.
AI.method: The dataset is built from night-time dashcam footage from six cities, with point-of-view video, pedestrian locations with track IDs and ground-truth crossing labels. Gemini, ChatGPT and human assessors predict crossings on clips and are compared with the ground-truth labels.
AI.result: Human input achieves 88.17% accuracy and 80.21% F1. Gemini achieves 60% accuracy and 42.50% F1, and ChatGPT achieves 79.13% accuracy and 63.64% F1.
AI.conclusion: NightSteps can serve as a baseline benchmark for evaluating crossing prediction models at night, with the aim of improving road safety.

title: FastGRT: Accelerating Training of 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing
summary: Ray Tracing enables rendering capabilities that are difficult to achieve with rasterization-based approaches such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). However, the training cost of Gaussian-based ray tracing (GRT) is much higher than that of 3DGS. In this paper, we study how ray tracing using Gaussians executes on GPUs and show that a considerable fraction of the training cost arises from how the computation is organized. We develop FastGRT, which decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses work done in the forward pass for the backward pass. FastGRT further incorporates optimizations such as fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to tackle other major bottlenecks in the training pipeline. We implement FastGRT in Vulkan. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first Vulkan-based GRT implementation that supports both training and rendering. Compared to 3DGRT, FastGRT improves training time by 1.9$\times$ to 4.97$\times$, while preserving the original rendering formulation. Our code is open source.

AI.tldr: FastGRT is a Vulkan-based implementation of Gaussian ray tracing that speeds up 3DGRT training by 1.9x to 4.97x while keeping the original rendering formulation. It is described as the first Vulkan-based GRT implementation supporting both training and rendering.
AI.motivation: Gaussian-based ray tracing is much more expensive to train than 3D Gaussian Splatting, and a considerable part of that cost comes from how the computation is organized on GPUs.
AI.method: FastGRT decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses forward-pass work in the backward pass. It adds fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to address other bottlenecks in the training pipeline.
AI.result: Compared with 3DGRT, FastGRT improves training time by 1.9x to 4.97x while preserving the original rendering formulation. The abstract gives no other numbers.
AI.conclusion: Restructuring the computation of Gaussian ray tracing gives large training speedups without changing what is rendered, and the code is open source.

title: Martine: Benchmarking Multi-View 3D Surface Reconstruction Across Viewpoint Coverage, Resolution, and Lighting
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 23 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Controlled acquisition setups are widely used for high-accuracy multi-view 3D surface reconstruction, as they allow sensor configuration, image resolution, viewpoint distribution, and illumination to be specified. Yet benchmarking remains difficult, since reconstruction accuracy depends jointly on the reconstruction paradigm, object properties, and acquisition regime. Existing benchmarks often restrict viewpoint coverage, resolution, or illumination, which can bias comparisons towards methods suited to the chosen setting. Others lack accurate 3D ground truth or quantified image-to-geometry alignment, limiting their use for metric surface evaluation. We introduce Martine, a benchmark for controlled 3D object surface reconstruction. Martine comprises 28 objects, including transparent materials and fine structures, captured at 9568 x 6376 pixels from 84 views over a spherical cap under both single-light and multi-light regimes. It provides object-independent camera calibration, accurate 3D ground-truth scans, calibration and image-to-geometry accuracy quantified on test images, and 3D property masks for analysing errors by material properties, visibility, curvature and fine structures.
