Building on these formulations, SBA replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised depth learning, providing more reliable relative poses for view synthesis. In turn, depth estimates from the well-trained depth estimation network provide scale references for SBA, improving scale consistency while allowing individual 3-D landmark positions to be refined. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, as well as two newly collected large-scale datasets, demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms representative existing approaches in both depth and trajectory estimation accuracy and is applicable to different camera models.

AI.tldr: S2D-FVO is a monocular fisheye visual odometry framework that couples spherical bundle adjustment with unsupervised depth learning to improve scale consistency and depth accuracy. It outperforms representative approaches in depth and trajectory estimation on multiple public datasets and two newly collected datasets.
AI.motivation: Monocular fisheye VO is attractive for robotics, but scale drift over long trajectories remains a major challenge, and the strong distortion of fisheye images makes accurate unsupervised depth estimation difficult.
AI.method: Spherical bundle adjustment (SBA) uses tangent-space angular reprojection residuals derived from the spherical logarithmic map, which keep sensitivity along both tangent directions, and adds a median depth-based scale regularization term. SBA replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised depth learning, and depth estimates from the trained depth network provide scale references for SBA.
AI.result: The framework outperforms representative existing approaches in both depth and trajectory estimation accuracy on multiple public datasets and two newly collected large-scale datasets. It is also applicable to different camera models.
AI.conclusion: Coupling spherical bundle adjustment with unsupervised depth learning in both directions improves scale consistency and allows individual 3-D landmark positions to be refined, giving a practical fisheye VO system.

title: Watching Itself Watch: Self-Auditing Visual Reliance for Video Reasoning
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Video reasoning hinges on a small number of visually decisive tokens embedded in otherwise largely language-driven chains of thought. Yet prevailing post-training methods such as GRPO overlook this structure, assigning coarse trajectory-level rewards while requiring multiple rollouts and often costly external judges. We introduce Visually-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (VIOS), a post-training framework that identifies where a model under-utilizes visual evidence and concentrates learning at those positions. Our key insight is that a model can audit its own visual reliance: the divergence between its next-token distributions with and without the video reveals how strongly each prediction depends on the visual input. Measuring this reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged teacher exposes a per-token reliance gap, identifying positions where the teacher exploits visual evidence that the student overlooks. VIOS translates this signal into dense, targeted supervision through three complementary components: an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher that co-evolves with the student, a contrastive objective that encourages predictions to depend on the video, and a reliance-gap gate that focuses learning on visually under-utilized tokens. Crucially, VIOS requires only a single on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers. Across 12 benchmarks spanning general, temporal, spatial, knowledge-intensive, and long-video understanding, VIOS consistently improves three model backbones and outperforms contemporary video-reasoning systems, while training in over 9x fewer steps, 60x fewer FLOPs, and 111x fewer generated tokens. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: VIOS is a post-training method for video reasoning that uses a model's own visual reliance to find the tokens where it under-uses visual evidence and concentrates learning there. It needs only a single on-policy rollout and no external rewards or judges, and it improves three backbones across 12 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Video reasoning depends on a few visually decisive tokens inside mostly language-driven chains of thought, but GRPO-style post-training assigns coarse trajectory-level rewards, needs multiple rollouts and often uses costly external judges.
AI.method: The divergence between next-token distributions with and without the video measures per-token visual reliance for a student and an answer-privileged teacher, giving a reliance gap. VIOS combines an EMA teacher that co-evolves with the student, a contrastive objective that encourages predictions to depend on the video, and a reliance-gap gate that focuses learning on visually under-utilized tokens.
AI.result: Across 12 benchmarks spanning general, temporal, spatial, knowledge-intensive and long-video understanding, VIOS consistently improves three model backbones and outperforms contemporary video-reasoning systems. It trains in over 9x fewer steps, with 60x fewer FLOPs and 111x fewer generated tokens.
AI.conclusion: A model can audit its own visual reliance to supply dense, targeted supervision, so visual reasoning can be improved with a single rollout and without external rewards, judges or larger teachers.

title: UltraVoxelGS: Voxel-First Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for 3D Ultrasound Reconstruction
summary: We present UltraVoxelGS, a 3D ultrasound reconstruction method that achieves both fast reconstruction and physically faithful rendering for the first time, bringing live spatial feedback during 2D ultrasound scanning within reach. This is made possible by a feed-forward design that predicts a complete Gaussian scene representation from posed ultrasound images directly, entirely bypassing the per-scene optimization bottleneck that has confined prior methods to offline use. Realising such feed-forward prediction in this setting is non-trivial: unlike natural images, ultrasound slices share at most one-dimensional intersections and exhibit view-dependent appearance due to acoustic propagation and attenuation, violating the dense overlap and photometric consistency assumed by existing feed-forward Gaussian methods. Hence, to achieve fast reconstruction, we introduce a feed-forward voxel-to-Gaussian pass that decouples representation size from input count by lifting all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support and predicting Gaussian parameters directly. For faithful rendering, we propose ultrasound-aware appearance rendering strategy factorize reflection from cumulative attenuation during training and exploit appearance continuity among spatially adjacent slices for efficient Render-time Appearance Adaptation. On both real-world and simulated datasets, UltraVoxelGS achieves best PSNR/SSIM compared with per-scene optimization baselines while reducing inference from 10-20 minutes to approximately 10 seconds (over 35 times faster) and scales to sequences exceeding 1,000 frames. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: UltraVoxelGS is a feed-forward method that predicts a complete Gaussian scene representation from posed 2D ultrasound images for 3D reconstruction, enabling live spatial feedback. It achieves the best PSNR and SSIM among compared per-scene optimization baselines and runs in about 10 seconds instead of 10 to 20 minutes.
AI.motivation: Prior 3D ultrasound reconstruction methods rely on per-scene optimization, which confines them to offline use. Ultrasound slices share at most one-dimensional intersections and have view-dependent appearance, which violates the dense overlap and photometric consistency assumed by existing feed-forward Gaussian methods.
AI.method: A feed-forward voxel-to-Gaussian pass lifts all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support and predicts Gaussian parameters directly, decoupling representation size from input count. An ultrasound-aware rendering strategy factorizes reflection from cumulative attenuation during training, and Render-time Appearance Adaptation exploits appearance continuity among adjacent slices.
AI.result: On real-world and simulated datasets UltraVoxelGS achieves the best PSNR and SSIM compared with per-scene optimization baselines. Inference drops from 10 to 20 minutes to about 10 seconds, over 35 times faster, and the method scales to sequences exceeding 1,000 frames.
AI.conclusion: Feed-forward voxel-based Gaussian prediction with ultrasound-aware rendering makes fast, physically faithful 3D ultrasound reconstruction practical for live use during scanning.

title: 3R-Adapter: Retrieval, Rewiring, and Refinement for Efficient Adaptation of 3D Reconstruction Model
summary: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models have demonstrated strong generalization under large-scale pre-training, yet they struggle in long-tail scenarios such as low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation. We observe relational attention structure collapse, manifested as the failure of cross-view correspondences, as a primary cause of these limitations. While adaptation offers a practical way to bridge this gap, existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches mainly perform channel-wise feature adjustment and lack mechanisms to explicitly adapt relational structures, leaving correspondence failures unresolved. In this work, we formulate adaptation of 3D reconstruction models as a problem of correspondence recovery under domain shift and propose 3R-Adapter, a PEFT paradigm for long-tail 3D reconstruction scenarios. Our method consists of three components: Deformable Retrieval for task-adaptive relation candidate retrieval, Relational Rewiring for reconstructing cross-view relational structures, and Consistency Refinement for injecting the rewired relations into stable predictions. Extensive experiments on low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation demonstrate that our approach significantly improves robustness over existing PEFT methods while maintaining efficient lightweight adaptation. Our code is released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: 3R-Adapter is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that adapts feed-forward 3D reconstruction models to long-tail scenarios by recovering cross-view correspondences. It improves robustness on low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction and test-time adaptation over existing PEFT methods.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models generalize well but fail in long-tail scenarios, and the paper traces this to relational attention structure collapse, which breaks cross-view correspondences. Existing PEFT methods mainly adjust features channel-wise and do not adapt relational structure.
AI.method: Adaptation is formulated as correspondence recovery under domain shift, with three components: Deformable Retrieval for task-adaptive relation candidate retrieval, Relational Rewiring for reconstructing cross-view relational structures, and Consistency Refinement for injecting the rewired relations into stable predictions.
AI.result: The approach significantly improves robustness over existing PEFT methods on low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction and test-time adaptation while keeping adaptation lightweight and efficient.
AI.conclusion: Adapting relational attention structure, rather than only channel-wise features, is an effective and lightweight way to recover correspondences for 3D reconstruction under domain shift.

title: AnyBreak: Towards Jailbreaking Any T2I Model for Any Concept
comment: Accepted for poster presentation at ICME 2026
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in image generation and editing, yet this progress has also introduced significant security risks. Prior work has shown that adversarial prompt can induce the generation of Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) content, including pornographic, violent, and graphic imagery. However, such attacks are typically mitigated by prompt filters and often rely on white-box assumptions. In this paper, we propose AnyBreak, a novel jailbreak framework that constructs adversarial images via multi-scale progressive semantic alignment. During the generation process, these adversarial images steer the generation trajectory in latent space towards unsafe data manifolds, enabling cross-modal transfer of malicious concepts from the text modality to the image modality. AnyBreak operates using only clean textual prompts and adversarial images at inference time, and can jailbreak any T2I models towards any malicious concepts in a fully black-box setting. We further introduce AnyBreak-V, an enhanced variant that incorporates a compensation term to bypass post-hoc safety checkers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AnyBreak achieves high attack success rates while preserving visual fidelity and semantic consistency with the input prompts under black-box and clean-text constraints. Our findings reveal that existing T2I defense leave critical cross-modal attack surfaces insufficiently addressed. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: AnyBreak is a black-box jailbreak framework that builds adversarial images to steer any text-to-image model toward any malicious concept using only clean text prompts at inference time. AnyBreak-V adds a compensation term to bypass post-hoc safety checkers.
AI.motivation: Prior adversarial prompt attacks that induce NSFW generation are typically mitigated by prompt filters and often assume white-box access, and existing T2I defenses leave cross-modal attack surfaces insufficiently addressed.
AI.method: AnyBreak constructs adversarial images via multi-scale progressive semantic alignment. During generation these images steer the latent trajectory toward unsafe data manifolds, transferring malicious concepts from the text modality to the image modality. AnyBreak-V incorporates a compensation term to bypass post-hoc safety checkers.
AI.result: Experiments show that AnyBreak achieves high attack success rates while preserving visual fidelity and semantic consistency with the input prompts under black-box and clean-text constraints.
AI.conclusion: Existing T2I defenses do not adequately cover cross-modal attack surfaces, so image-based inputs require protection beyond prompt filtering.

title: HIST3R: Decomposing and Rectifying State Updates with History for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Streaming 3D reconstruction with recurrent states enables long-video scene understanding under bounded memory, but turns reconstruction into a state-evolution problem: each incoming frame updates a compact scene memory on which all subsequent predictions depend, so unreliable updates overwrite historical context and accumulate into long-horizon geometric drift. We analyze CUT3R-style recurrent updates through a direction--magnitude decomposition, in which the magnitude sets the update gain, i.e., how strongly an observation is written into the state, and the direction encodes the geometric intent, i.e., where the update drives the state. This decomposition provides a unified view of CUT3R and its variants, revealing that existing training-free extensions perform magnitude-only control: they can attenuate an unreliable update but cannot correct its direction. We propose HIST3R, a training-free framework built on CUT3R that controls both components using history. HIST3R rectifies the update direction using locally consistent historical states, and modulates the update magnitude according to the visual discrepancy between the current observation and its history, suppressing redundant updates while preserving complementary evidence. Across camera pose estimation, 3D reconstruction, and video depth estimation, HIST3R consistently improves long-horizon performance while retaining the memory footprint and inference speed of CUT3R. With 1000 input frames, it reduces ATE by 23.87% on ScanNet and 33.65% on TUM-Dynamics relative to the strongest competing method; with 500 frames, it improves median reconstruction accuracy over the strongest CUT3R-based variant by 56.52% on 7-Scenes and 33.96% on NRGBD.

AI.tldr: HIST3R is a training-free framework for streaming 3D reconstruction that corrects both the direction and the magnitude of CUT3R's recurrent state updates using history. It reduces long-horizon error and keeps CUT3R's memory footprint and inference speed.
AI.motivation: Streaming reconstruction with recurrent states is a state-evolution problem in which unreliable updates overwrite historical context and accumulate into long-horizon geometric drift. Existing training-free extensions of CUT3R only control the update magnitude and cannot correct its direction.
AI.method: CUT3R-style updates are decomposed into a magnitude, which sets the update gain, and a direction, which encodes the geometric intent. HIST3R rectifies the direction using locally consistent historical states and modulates the magnitude by the visual discrepancy between the current observation and its history, suppressing redundant updates while keeping complementary evidence.
AI.result: Across camera pose estimation, 3D reconstruction and video depth estimation, HIST3R consistently improves long-horizon performance. With 1000 input frames it reduces ATE by 23.87% on ScanNet and 33.65% on TUM-Dynamics relative to the strongest competing method. With 500 frames it improves median reconstruction accuracy over the strongest CUT3R-based variant by 56.52% on 7-Scenes and 33.96% on NRGBD.
AI.conclusion: Controlling both components of the recurrent update, rather than the magnitude alone, reduces drift in long-horizon streaming reconstruction without training or extra memory.

title: TIRAD: Text-guided Image Residual Learning for Generalist Anomaly Detection
summary: Recent anomaly detection studies have shown that residual features, which model the discrepancy between normal and abnormal patterns, provide strong generalization to anomalies unseen during training. However, existing residual-based approaches mainly rely on visual discrepancies derived from image representations, while semantic discrepancies that can be explicitly expressed through language remain largely underexplored. To address this problem, we propose TIRAD, Text-guided Image Residual Learning for Generalist Anomaly Detection, a multimodal residual learning framework that defines the discrepancy between textual representations of normal and abnormal states as a Text Residual Feature and uses it to guide the Image Residual Feature. Specifically, a Text Fusion Module converts patch-level text residuals into a gate that modulates the image residual of each patch. The gate retains the visual discrepancies that the text residual identifies as defect-related and attenuates the others, leading to more discriminative anomaly representations. Extensive experiments on industrial benchmarks and industrial-to-medical transfer demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing image-centric residual learning methods.

AI.tldr: TIRAD is a multimodal residual learning framework for generalist anomaly detection that uses a text residual, the difference between textual representations of normal and abnormal states, to gate image residual features. It outperforms image-centric residual methods on industrial benchmarks and industrial-to-medical transfer.
AI.motivation: Residual-based anomaly detection generalizes to unseen anomalies, but existing methods rely on visual discrepancies only, leaving semantic discrepancies that language can express largely unexplored.
AI.method: A Text Fusion Module converts patch-level text residuals into a gate that modulates the image residual of each patch. The gate keeps visual discrepancies that the text residual identifies as defect-related and attenuates the rest.
AI.result: The method outperforms existing image-centric residual learning methods on industrial benchmarks and on industrial-to-medical transfer.
AI.conclusion: Using language-derived residuals to guide image residuals yields more discriminative anomaly representations than visual residuals alone.

title: Single Image Super-Resolution via Semantic Prompt and Cross-Modal Training on Content Area
summary: Enhancing image quality through super-resolution is crucial in image and video processing. While contemporary deep learning models, such as CNNs and Transformers, excel in pixel-level enhancements, they often overlook the rich semantic context within images. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that synergizes pixel intensity with semantic information for superior detail recovery. Our method involves extracting semantic data, including textual descriptors and spatial positioning, and encoding this information. We also present a Cross-Modal Feature Fusion module for generating semantic feature maps via multimodal training, and a Prompt Traction Head to augment the backbone network with semantic insights, thereby refining image details. Our empirical results across various datasets validate the superiority of our approach.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a single-image super-resolution method that combines pixel information with semantic information from textual descriptors and spatial positioning. It uses a Cross-Modal Feature Fusion module and a Prompt Traction Head to inject semantic insights into the backbone and refine image details.
AI.motivation: CNN and Transformer super-resolution models excel at pixel-level enhancement but often overlook the semantic context within images.
AI.method: Semantic data, including textual descriptors and spatial positioning, is extracted and encoded. A Cross-Modal Feature Fusion module generates semantic feature maps through multimodal training, and a Prompt Traction Head augments the backbone with these semantic features.
AI.result: The abstract reports that empirical results across various datasets validate the superiority of the approach, without giving specific numbers or baselines.
AI.conclusion: Combining semantic prompts and cross-modal training with pixel-level super-resolution is presented as superior for detail recovery, though the abstract provides no quantitative evidence.

title: SAFE-Hair: Scalp-Anchored Fields for Exportable Single-View Hair Reconstruction
summary: Single-view 3D hair reconstruction has progressed rapidly, but many methods optimize for visual plausibility rather than producing strand assets that can be directly used in grooming, editing, or simulation pipelines. We propose SAFE-Hair, a framework that reconstructs explicit strand grooms from a single portrait by decoding hair from persistent follicles in a canonical scalp-UV domain. Given a fitted template head, SAFE-Hair projects self-supervised image features onto the scalp, uses a conditional Rectified Flow model to generate latent scalp fields, and decodes occupancy, segment directions, length allocation, and total length at a fixed set of scalp follicles. This representation enforces scalp-rooted strand identities by construction and enables direct export with follicle IDs and guide-family metadata. We further introduce attachment, collision, and bending priors to improve geometric validity without per-subject test-time optimization. To evaluate both reconstruction fidelity and asset usability, we introduce HairBench-3D, a benchmark built from public 3D hair assets with standardized alignment, rendering, resampling, and metrics for geometry, direction consistency, invisible-region completion, silhouette agreement, and collision. SAFE-Hair improves Chamfer distance from 3.74 mm to 3.28 mm, F-score from 77.9 to 81.7, invisible-region F-score from 66.1 to 69.8, and penetration ratio from 4.8% to 3.9% over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: SAFE-Hair reconstructs explicit strand grooms from a single portrait by decoding hair from persistent follicles in a canonical scalp-UV domain, so the output can be exported directly as strand assets. It improves Chamfer distance, F-score and penetration ratio over the strongest baseline on the new HairBench-3D benchmark.
AI.motivation: Single-view hair reconstruction methods optimize visual plausibility rather than producing strand assets usable in grooming, editing or simulation pipelines.
AI.method: Self-supervised image features are projected onto the scalp of a fitted template head, and a conditional Rectified Flow model generates latent scalp fields. The model decodes occupancy, segment directions, length allocation and total length at fixed scalp follicles, enforcing scalp-rooted strand identities by construction. Attachment, collision and bending priors improve geometric validity without per-subject test-time optimization.
AI.result: SAFE-Hair improves Chamfer distance from 3.74 mm to 3.28 mm, F-score from 77.9 to 81.7, invisible-region F-score from 66.1 to 69.8, and penetration ratio from 4.8% to 3.9% over the strongest baseline. These are evaluated on HairBench-3D, a benchmark the paper introduces.
AI.conclusion: Representing hair through persistent follicles yields exportable strand assets with follicle IDs and guide-family metadata, and the method improves both reconstruction fidelity and asset usability.

title: Leveraging Complementary Event Frame and Voxel Representations for RGB-Guided Multimodal Pre-training
summary: In this paper, we propose CM3AE 2.0, a unified RGB Frame and Event-Voxel/-Frame pre-training framework. By jointly learning multimodal spatiotemporal representations and exploiting latent cross-modal dependencies through cross-modal generation, the framework enhances multimodal information interaction and collaborative modeling capabilities. Specifically, we first propose an Event-aware Spatiotemporal Masked Reconstruction (ESMR) strategy to learn unified multimodal spatiotemporal representations. It leverages event responses to guide masking toward dynamically salient regions. Through spatiotemporal masked reconstruction, it learns spatial structures and their temporal variations from continuous RGB-Event observations. In addition, it incorporates multimodal fusion reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive learning to facilitate the modeling of cross-modal complementary information and the learning of shared representations. Building upon this, we further propose a Hierarchical Cross-modal Generation (HCG) strategy to learn latent cross-modal dependencies through visual and language generation. At the visual level, Event-conditioned RGB generation is performed using a pre-trained diffusion model to capture visual associations between the two modalities. At the language level, video-level text description generation based on joint RGB-Event representations establishes connections between multimodal visual features and linguistic semantics, further enriching the learning of cross-modal dependencies. Extensive experiments on four diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that CM3AE 2.0 consistently improves performance, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability of the proposed pre-training framework.

AI.tldr: CM3AE 2.0 is a unified pre-training framework for RGB frames and event data in both voxel and frame forms, using event-guided masking and hierarchical cross-modal generation. The paper reports consistent gains on four downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Learning joint multimodal spatiotemporal representations and modeling latent dependencies between RGB and event modalities remain open for pre-training, and the paper aims to strengthen multimodal interaction.
AI.method: Event-aware Spatiotemporal Masked Reconstruction (ESMR) uses event responses to guide masking toward dynamically salient regions and adds multimodal fusion reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive learning. Hierarchical Cross-modal Generation (HCG) adds event-conditioned RGB generation with a pre-trained diffusion model and video-level text description generation from joint RGB-Event representations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four diverse downstream tasks show that CM3AE 2.0 consistently improves performance over the baselines. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The framework's visual and language generation objectives improve cross-modal dependency learning, and the authors present its effectiveness and generalization as validated.

title: Four-Step Text-Bearing Image Generation via Distillation with Local Response Regularization and Teacher-Guided Training
summary: Generating text-bearing images requires coherent scenes and accurate characters. Large text-to-image models improve both capabilities through repeated denoising, at substantial sampling cost. Few-step distillation reduces this cost but requires the student to organize scenes and refine glyphs within a short trajectory. We present a four-step distillation framework combining local response regularization with teacher-guided text training. Built on distribution matching, the framework distills the GLM-Image DiT while retaining its autoregressive visual prior, glyph encoder, and VAE. A path-length penalty promotes consistent local responses of the conditional denoising field. Progressive training combines synthetic strings with teacher-generated imagery to preserve character accuracy and scene-integrated typography. The student achieves GenEval Overall 0.84 and CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.5045, compared with 0.81 and 0.1690 for four-step TDM. A coefficient study favors $10^{-5}$, and Qwen-Image experiments show additional gains from response regularization and text supervision. Single-image inference takes 1.742 s, compared with 5.818 s for the teacher, yielding a $3.34\times$ speedup at the same 40 GB GPU memory requirement.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a four-step distillation framework for text-bearing image generation that combines local response regularization with teacher-guided text training. The student reaches GenEval 0.84 and CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.5045 and runs 3.34 times faster than the teacher at the same 40 GB memory.
AI.motivation: Text-bearing image generation needs coherent scenes and accurate glyphs, and large text-to-image models do this only with repeated denoising, which is costly. Few-step distillation reduces cost but forces the student to organize scenes and refine glyphs within a short trajectory.
AI.method: Built on distribution matching, the framework distills the GLM-Image DiT while keeping its autoregressive visual prior, glyph encoder and VAE. A path-length penalty promotes consistent local responses of the conditional denoising field, and progressive training mixes synthetic strings with teacher-generated imagery. A coefficient study favors 10^-5.
AI.result: The student achieves GenEval Overall 0.84 and CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.5045, versus 0.81 and 0.1690 for four-step TDM. Single-image inference takes 1.742 s compared with 5.818 s for the teacher, a 3.34x speedup at the same 40 GB GPU memory. Qwen-Image experiments show further gains from response regularization and text supervision.
AI.conclusion: Local response regularization and teacher-guided text training make four-step distillation effective for text-bearing images, with a substantial speedup over the teacher at no extra memory.

title: Attention-Guided Sequence Feature Fusion and Mixed-Space Metric Learning for Cross-View Image Sequence Geo-Localization
summary: Cross-view image sequence geo-localization aims to determine the geographic location of a sequence of ground images by matching it against geo-tagged satellite imagery. Although sequential observations provide complementary scene information, substantial overlap between adjacent images introduces feature redundancy, while conventional fusion strategies may weaken spatial relationships essential for cross-view matching. Therefore, we propose a cross-view image sequence geo-localization method via Attention-guided Sequence fusion and Metric Learning (ASML). Specifically, a Sequential Content Fusion (SCF) module models cross-image feature correlations to suppress redundant content and adaptively preserve geographically informative non-overlapping regions. Next, a Spatial Feature Aggregation (SFA) module is used to capture and aggregate the spatial and semantic information of local features, so as to maintain the spatial layout of the image sequence. Finally, a Geo-InfoNCE loss function is proposed, which comprehensively considers the feature distance and geographic distance for mixed-space metric learning, thus improving the ability of the model to distinguish hard negative samples. A new cross-view image sequence dataset CrossRoad-66K is established to provide more complex scenarios. Extensive experiments and visualizations on the SeqGeo and CrossRoad-66K datasets demonstrate that compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, the proposed method ASML achieves an improvement of 3.37% and 2.10% at R@1, respectively.

AI.tldr: ASML is a cross-view image sequence geo-localization method that fuses ground-image sequences with attention while suppressing redundant overlap, and uses a mixed-space Geo-InfoNCE loss. It improves R@1 by 3.37% on SeqGeo and 2.10% on the new CrossRoad-66K dataset.
AI.motivation: Sequential ground images carry complementary scene information, but overlap between adjacent images causes feature redundancy, and conventional fusion can weaken the spatial relationships needed for cross-view matching.
AI.method: A Sequential Content Fusion (SCF) module models cross-image feature correlations to suppress redundant content and keep non-overlapping regions. A Spatial Feature Aggregation (SFA) module aggregates spatial and semantic local features to maintain sequence layout. Geo-InfoNCE combines feature distance and geographic distance for mixed-space metric learning to improve hard-negative discrimination.
AI.result: Compared with state-of-the-art methods, ASML improves R@1 by 3.37% on SeqGeo and 2.10% on CrossRoad-66K. The new CrossRoad-66K dataset is introduced to cover more complex scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Attention-guided sequence fusion combined with mixed-space metric learning improves cross-view image sequence geo-localization, especially in harder scenes.

title: Weight-Space Programming for Medical Imaging: Do We Still Need Training Data?
summary: Can a large language model (LLM) write the parameters of a medical image classifier from medical knowledge alone, without any training data? Such classifiers normally require labelled images, which are costly and often unavailable. We investigate this question through weight-space programming (WSP), in which an LLM writes or adapts the weights and biases of a neural network directly, without optimisation on training data. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra each generate the parameters of a small LeNet-style CNN in a single reply, without tool use and without access to any image. We compare these networks against zero-shot MedSigLIP and against the same architecture trained on labels using the Adam optimiser, across 7 classification tasks in four modalities: chest X-ray, breast ultrasound and abdominal CT (all from MedMNIST), and pelvic MRI (SynthUterus). The LLM-written networks perform above chance on all six MedMNIST tasks, with a mean test AUC of 0.719 for Opus and 0.711 for Astra. Both models outperform MedSigLIP on 5 of 6 tasks while using more than 10,000 times fewer parameters. However, the same network trained with Adam on only 256 labelled images achieves a higher AUC on every MedMNIST task (mean AUC 0.828). On SynthUterus, Opus attains an AUC of 0.764, whereas Astra falls below chance (AUC 0.136) owing to a systematic error. These results show that LLMs can write functional medical classifiers, but that they do not yet replace training data. We release the protocol, logs and all generated weights at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether LLMs can write the weights of a medical image classifier without any training data, using weight-space programming. LLM-written LeNet-style networks reach mean test AUC 0.719 (Opus) and 0.711 (Astra), but Adam training on only 256 labelled images does better.
AI.motivation: Medical image classifiers normally need labelled images, which are costly and often unavailable, so the paper asks whether medical knowledge alone can produce a working classifier.
AI.method: Weight-space programming (WSP) has an LLM write or adapt the weights and biases of a small LeNet-style CNN in a single reply, without tool use or image access. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra generate the networks, which are compared with zero-shot MedSigLIP and with the same architecture trained with Adam, across 7 classification tasks in four modalities.
AI.result: The LLM-written networks perform above chance on all six MedMNIST tasks, with mean test AUC 0.719 for Opus and 0.711 for Astra. Both outperform MedSigLIP on 5 of 6 tasks while using more than 10,000 times fewer parameters. The Adam-trained network on 256 labelled images achieves higher AUC on every MedMNIST task, with mean AUC 0.828. On SynthUterus, Opus reaches AUC 0.764 while Astra falls below chance at 0.136 because of a systematic error.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can write functional medical classifiers, but they do not yet replace training data.

title: MPEG-Diffusion: Mixed-Resolution Video Generation
summary: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) generate realistic videos, but their heavy computational cost limits broader real-world applications. Mixed-resolution generation reduces this cost by generating the visually important region at high resolution (HR) and the rest at low resolution (LR), yet existing methods suffer a severe quality drop on videos and require knowing the HR region in advance. We show that these failures are not inherent to mixed resolution, and propose $\textbf{MPEG-Diffusion}$ to address their three root causes: (1) dual-resolution attention to mitigate the curse of mixed resolution, where each query reads the K/V of its own resolution, (2) a mixed-resolution decoder to blend the HR and LR latents before decoding and resolve distortion, and (3) a self-selected HR region using the DiT's knowledge to find the visually important region without requiring it in advance. Processing only $30\%$ of full-resolution tokens, MPEG-Diffusion speeds up denoising by $4.8\times$ on Wan2.1 14B ($3.8\times$ on 1.3B), outperforming prior methods on nearly every metric. In the user study, we demonstrate the high quality of MPEG-Diffusion, with raters preferring it over prior mixed-resolution methods in over $90\%$ of pairs and rating it close to full resolution.

AI.tldr: MPEG-Diffusion is a mixed-resolution video diffusion transformer that generates the salient region at high resolution and the rest at low resolution, while avoiding the quality drop of prior methods. It speeds up denoising by 4.8x on Wan2.1 14B and 3.8x on 1.3B while processing only 30% of full-resolution tokens.
AI.motivation: Video diffusion transformers are computationally expensive. Existing mixed-resolution methods suffer a severe quality drop on videos and require the high-resolution region to be known in advance.
AI.method: The method uses dual-resolution attention, in which each query reads the keys and values of its own resolution, to address the curse of mixed resolution. It adds a mixed-resolution decoder that blends high- and low-resolution latents before decoding, and a self-selected high-resolution region that uses the DiT's own knowledge to find the visually important area.
AI.result: On Wan2.1 14B, denoising is 4.8x faster, and on 1.3B it is 3.8x faster, while using 30% of full-resolution tokens. The method outperforms prior methods on nearly every metric. In a user study, raters preferred it over prior mixed-resolution methods in over 90% of pairs and rated its quality close to full resolution.
AI.conclusion: The abstract argues that the failures of prior mixed-resolution video generation are not inherent to mixed resolution, and that the three proposed components address their root causes to make it a practical speedup for video DiTs.

title: Color wave: A systematic evaluation of active screen illumination for injection attack detection in remote face authentication
summary: Remote face authentication requires protection against both presentation attacks and biometric data injection attacks prior to face matching. Methods based on active screen illumination appear promising for both by introducing randomized visual stimuli through the user's device screen and evaluating the corresponding facial responses. Although such methods have been more studied for presentation attack detection (PAD), their systematic evaluation for injection attack detection (IAD) remains limited. To address this gap, we first classify injected content into static images, prerecorded videos, and real-time deepfakes based on their expected responses to the challenge. We then adapt an active screen-illumination approach into an implementation we term color wave and develop a systematic, injection-specific evaluation protocol. The protocol examines detection effectiveness, generalization across operating conditions, robustness to signal degradation, and susceptibility to selected evasion strategies. The findings demonstrate a strong discriminative signal under controlled conditions but also reveal performance limitations under overexposure, low screen brightness, and subject motion, as well as vulnerabilities to selected evasion strategies. By relating detection outcomes to attack types and operating conditions, this study provides an interpretable assessment of when and why active screen illumination succeeds or fails as an IAD mechanism.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically evaluates "color wave", an active screen-illumination method, for detecting biometric injection attacks in remote face authentication. It finds strong discrimination under controlled conditions but clear limits under overexposure, low screen brightness, subject motion and some evasion strategies.
AI.motivation: Active screen illumination has been studied mainly for presentation attack detection, while its systematic evaluation for injection attack detection remains limited.
AI.method: The authors classify injected content into static images, prerecorded videos and real-time deepfakes according to their expected responses to the challenge. They adapt an active screen-illumination approach into a method called color wave and design an injection-specific evaluation protocol covering detection effectiveness, generalization across operating conditions, robustness to signal degradation and susceptibility to selected evasion strategies.
AI.result: Color wave shows a strong discriminative signal under controlled conditions. Performance is limited under overexposure, low screen brightness and subject motion, and the method is vulnerable to selected evasion strategies.
AI.conclusion: The study gives an interpretable assessment of when and why active screen illumination succeeds or fails as an injection attack detection mechanism, by relating detection outcomes to attack types and operating conditions.

title: How a Model's Architecture and Performance Influences Explainability: A Study of Grad-CAM and CRAFT in CNN-Based Image Classification
comment: Accepted at the 4th World Conference on eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (xAI 2026), Fortaleza, Brazil, July 1-3, 2026. To appear in Springer CCIS. 12 pages, 5 figures
summary: Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), are widely adopted in computer vision, yet their opaque decision-making raises concerns in high-risk applications like healthcare and autonomous systems, where trust and accountability are critical. Therefore, robust explainable AI (XAI) methods are desirable to provide transparent insights into model decisions. To ensure these methods are reliable and effective across diverse scenarios, it is important to understand how model performance and architectural complexity influence explanation quality. Our study takes an initial step toward systematically investigating the impact of these two factors on key XAI evaluation metrics. We constructed a pipeline using 10 subsets of ImageNet-1K, each containing 80 unique classes, on each of which we trained three CNN architectures of increasing structural complexity: VGG16, ResNet50, and ConvNeXt-Tiny. For each individual model, we analyzed 10 training checkpoints representing increasing levels of model accuracy using two XAI methods: Grad-CAM (feature-attribution-based) and CRAFT (concept-based). We assessed these methods across four evaluation categories: Faithfulness, Correctness, Sensitivity, and Simplicity. Our findings reveal that as training progresses, the complex architectures (ResNet50 and ConvNeXt-Tiny) exhibit improved Faithfulness and lower Sensitivity, indicating more robust explanations. In contrast, VGG16's simpler architecture yields simpler but less faithful and correct explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how CNN architecture and training progress affect the quality of two explainability methods, Grad-CAM and CRAFT, on ImageNet-1K subsets. Deeper architectures (ResNet50, ConvNeXt-Tiny) yield more faithful and less sensitive explanations as training proceeds, whereas VGG16 yields simpler but less faithful ones.
AI.motivation: Explainable AI methods must be reliable across models, but how model performance and architectural complexity influence explanation quality had not been systematically studied.
AI.method: The authors build a pipeline on 10 subsets of ImageNet-1K with 80 classes each, train VGG16, ResNet50 and ConvNeXt-Tiny on each, and analyze 10 checkpoints per model with two XAI methods: Grad-CAM (feature-attribution-based) and CRAFT (concept-based). Explanations are assessed on Faithfulness, Correctness, Sensitivity and Simplicity.
AI.result: As training progresses, ResNet50 and ConvNeXt-Tiny show improved Faithfulness and lower Sensitivity. VGG16 produces simpler but less faithful and less correct explanations.
AI.conclusion: The study is presented as an initial step toward understanding how model performance and architecture shape XAI evaluation outcomes, indicating that explanation quality depends on architectural complexity.

title: Compass 1: Towards Open-World and Persistent Embodied Navigation from Monocular RGB Videos
comment: Technical Report. Project Page: this https URL
summary: Embodied navigation requires agents to achieve persistent spatial awareness and long-horizon execution stability in open-world environments. However, existing navigation architectures struggle to sustain both capabilities, remaining effective only over a handful of recent frames. We present Compass 1, the first embodied navigation foundation model to unify language understanding and video generation while enabling memory backtracking through nearly 2mins of visual history. Without altering the underlying architecture, we introduce History Representation, which integrates sparse visual keyframes with an explicit History Representation Map to preserve long-term spatiotemporal context. To effectively leverage this history, we further introduce History Utilization, a structured VQA supervision protocol comprising three categories: task-stage grounding, exploration consistency, and spatiotemporal target retrieval, enabling map-grounded reasoning and stable persistent long-horizon navigation. To fuel this system, we establish a complete annotation pipeline for monocular RGB videos and open-source a massive dataset featuring over 500 hours of high-quality real-world interactions and over 2,000 hours of annotated web videos. Trained mainly on the distribution of 1m height camera, Compass 1 generalizes seamlessly across diverse embodiments and scenarios, ranging from indoor environments to pedestrian-dense streets, spanning wheeled robot at 0.35m, quadruped dog at 0.5m, humanoid at 0.85m, and aerial drone at 1.5m. Compass 1achieves a dominant overall success rate of 79.4% across open-world evaluations, compared to 17.8% for the strongest baseline. It demonstrates exceptional zero-shot execution exceeding 90% on foundational tasks, a 250% boost in exploration, and an unparalleled leap from 0% to 58% in challenging persistent history backtracking.

AI.tldr: Compass 1 is an embodied navigation foundation model that unifies language understanding and video generation and keeps memory over nearly 2 minutes of visual history. It reports a 79.4% success rate on open-world evaluations versus 17.8% for the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing navigation architectures remain effective only over a handful of recent frames and cannot sustain persistent spatial awareness and long-horizon execution in open-world environments.
AI.method: The model adds History Representation, which combines sparse visual keyframes with an explicit History Representation Map, without changing the underlying architecture. History Utilization is a structured VQA supervision protocol with three categories: task-stage grounding, exploration consistency and spatiotemporal target retrieval. The authors also build an annotation pipeline for monocular RGB videos and release a dataset of over 500 hours of real-world interactions and over 2,000 hours of annotated web videos.
AI.result: Compass 1 achieves a 79.4% overall success rate in open-world evaluations, against 17.8% for the strongest baseline. It exceeds 90% zero-shot on foundational tasks, gives a 250% boost in exploration, and rises from 0% to 58% on challenging persistent history backtracking. It generalizes across wheeled robots at 0.35m, quadrupeds at 0.5m, humanoids at 0.85m and aerial drones at 1.5m, although it is trained mainly on a 1m camera height.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that long-horizon persistent memory, supplied by keyframe history and structured VQA supervision, enables navigation that generalizes across embodiments and environments.

title: RAPA: Ray-Aware Physics Augmentation for Robust Camera-LiDAR Calibration
summary: Camera-LiDAR calibration is essential for reliable perception in robotic and autonomous systems. Most target-based calibration methods rely on checkerboard observations, but accurate checkerboard feature extraction from LiDAR point clouds remains challenging due to measurement sparsity. Existing approaches either require manual annotation of 3D corners or depend on geometric feature extraction methods, both of which can become unreliable when checkerboard features are insufficiently observed. In this paper, we formulate checkerboard localization as a 2D detection problem using cylindrical LiDAR reflectivity images. To overcome the limited availability of labeled training data, we propose ray-aware physics augmentation (RAPA), which generates diverse synthetic samples from a single checkerboard observation. The generated data are used to improve detector robustness and generalization under varying sensing conditions. Across four independently captured indoor and outdoor locations, the proposed synthetic augmentation exceeds the strongest evaluated image-space augmentation baseline by 16.1-43.1 percentage points in mAP@0.5. Compared with training-free target-based methods on 242 observations, RAPA yields the largest number of valid target localizations, with 96.4% of its returned detections yielding valid target poses. These reliable localizations support downstream camera-LiDAR calibration across all four evaluated locations. Overall, RAPA addresses a key bottleneck in target-based calibration by enabling automated LiDAR-side target localization with only a single annotated target observation.

AI.tldr: RAPA formulates checkerboard localization in LiDAR as 2D detection on cylindrical reflectivity images and uses ray-aware physics augmentation to create training samples from a single annotated observation. It yields reliable target localizations for camera-LiDAR calibration across four indoor and outdoor locations.
AI.motivation: Target-based camera-LiDAR calibration relies on checkerboard features that are hard to extract from sparse LiDAR point clouds. Existing approaches need manual 3D corner annotation or depend on geometric feature extraction, both of which become unreliable when features are poorly observed.
AI.method: The checkerboard is localized as a 2D detection problem on cylindrical LiDAR reflectivity images. Ray-aware physics augmentation (RAPA) generates diverse synthetic samples from a single checkerboard observation to improve detector robustness and generalization under varying sensing conditions.
AI.result: Across four independently captured indoor and outdoor locations, the synthetic augmentation exceeds the strongest evaluated image-space augmentation baseline by 16.1 to 43.1 percentage points in mAP@0.5. On 242 observations, RAPA returns the largest number of valid target localizations among training-free target-based methods, with 96.4% of its detections yielding valid target poses.
AI.conclusion: RAPA automates LiDAR-side target localization with only one annotated target observation, and its reliable localizations support downstream calibration at all four evaluated locations.

title: DisasterVL: Evidence-Based Visual Reasoning Dataset and Model for Disaster Scene Understanding
summary: We introduce DisasterVL, a dataset and benchmark for evidence-grounded reasoning about disaster imagery. It contains approximately 1.2 million images from 142 countries, paired with 25 million structured annotations covering scene captions, incident and location assessments, spatial relationships, and visual question answering (VQA). The VQA annotations link answers to visible evidence and include questions about both present and absent cues, multiple answer formats, and difficulty labels. Region-level annotations link caption phrases to bounding boxes and spatial relationships to the regions they connect. The test set contains 38,254 images spanning 75 countries and 28 hazard types. Gemini 3.1 Pro audited the test annotations, and human reviewers validated a stratified subset. On this benchmark, the 9B DisasterVLM model outperforms the evaluated general-purpose baselines on captioning, open-ended VQA, incident reasoning, and region-level grounding. Gains in text overlap are larger than gains in evidence scores. We plan to publicly release the dataset, trained models, and code.

AI.tldr: DisasterVL is a dataset and benchmark for evidence-grounded visual reasoning on disaster imagery, with about 1.2 million images from 142 countries and 25 million structured annotations. The 9B DisasterVLM model outperforms the evaluated general-purpose baselines on captioning, open-ended VQA, incident reasoning and region-level grounding.
AI.motivation: Existing resources do not provide evidence-grounded annotations for reasoning about disaster scenes, including answers linked to visible evidence and questions about absent cues.
AI.method: The dataset includes scene captions, incident and location assessments, spatial relationships and VQA. VQA answers are linked to visible evidence, and questions cover present and absent cues, multiple answer formats and difficulty labels. Region-level annotations link caption phrases to bounding boxes and spatial relationships to regions. The test set has 38,254 images across 75 countries and 28 hazard types.
AI.result: The 9B DisasterVLM model outperforms the evaluated general-purpose baselines on captioning, open-ended VQA, incident reasoning and region-level grounding. Gains in text overlap are larger than gains in evidence scores. Gemini 3.1 Pro audited the test annotations, and human reviewers validated a stratified subset.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark offers a resource for evidence-based disaster scene understanding, and the authors plan to release the dataset, trained models and code publicly.

title: EgoLabel: Zero-Shot Egocentric Auto-Labeling with Cross-Modal Consistency
summary: Egocentric auto-labeling requires depth, camera pose, object, and human-pose estimates to agree across independently developed models. Differences in units, coordinate conventions, and scale can make individually plausible predictions geometrically inconsistent. We present \textbf{EgoLabel}, a zero-shot pipeline that combines off-the-shelf models without target-domain labeled training and provides explicit cross-modal registration and consistency diagnostics. The pipeline integrates MonST3R for geometry, LocateAnything with GMC-BoT-SORT and SAM~2 for objects, and V-HPOT for hands; FisheyeViT provides a separate whole-body compatibility demonstration. Our main hand evaluation uses H2O sensor depth. Across 20 sequences, per-hand depth anchoring reduces the mean of per-sequence median hand--depth residuals by $23\%$ relative to a single global scale, yielding a pooled median of $84.6\,\mathrm{mm}$ against a $20.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ ground-truth reference. Hand PA-MPJPE is $14.53\pm1.29\,\mathrm{mm}$, whereas absolute MPJPE is $119.1\pm31.3\,\mathrm{mm}$, revealing a substantial gap between aligned and metric accuracy. On three RGB-only sequences, camera ATE is $1.40\pm0.29\,\mathrm{cm}$ after $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ alignment. We also identify a sliding-window implementation issue that allows sensor-initialized depth to change during optimization. Because hand anchoring and its residual share the same depth map, the residual measures internal consistency rather than independent accuracy. These results characterize both the utility and the current limits of the registration pipeline.

AI.tldr: EgoLabel is a zero-shot pipeline that combines off-the-shelf models for egocentric auto-labeling and adds explicit cross-modal registration and consistency diagnostics. Its hand depth anchoring reduces residuals by 23%, but the paper shows a large gap between aligned and metric accuracy.
AI.motivation: Egocentric auto-labeling needs depth, camera pose, object and human-pose estimates to agree, yet independently developed models differ in units, coordinate conventions and scale, making predictions geometrically inconsistent.
AI.method: The pipeline integrates MonST3R for geometry, LocateAnything with GMC-BoT-SORT and SAM 2 for objects, and V-HPOT for hands, with no target-domain labeled training. Per-hand depth anchoring is compared with a single global scale. FisheyeViT is a separate whole-body compatibility demonstration.
AI.result: Across 20 sequences, per-hand depth anchoring reduces the mean per-sequence median hand-depth residual by 23% relative to a global scale, giving a pooled median of 84.6 mm against a 20.5 mm ground-truth reference. Hand PA-MPJPE is 14.53 plus or minus 1.29 mm, while absolute MPJPE is 119.1 plus or minus 31.3 mm. On three RGB-only sequences, camera ATE is 1.40 plus or minus 0.29 cm after Sim(3) alignment.
AI.conclusion: The results show the utility and current limits of the registration pipeline. The residual measures internal consistency rather than independent accuracy because hand anchoring and the residual share one depth map, and a sliding-window issue lets sensor-initialized depth change during optimization.

title: CADMA: Capacity-Aware Coverage Decomposition for Generative Model Assessment
summary: Evaluating generative models requires measuring not only sample fidelity but also how well a generated set covers the real data distribution. Recent work has therefore introduced recall-oriented metrics for distribution-level evaluation. However, existing recall metrics often reduce distributional coverage to geometry-based coverage. This simplifying assumption weakens their diagnostic value and interpretability in two ways: these metrics provide only a single aggregate score that cannot distinguish essential diversity failures such as mode dropping and mode collapse, and geometry-based coverage can provide unreliable estimates by assigning high scores to poorly covered generative distributions. We therefore introduce CADMA, a capacity-aware framework for recall-oriented evaluation and diagnosis. CADMA evaluates distributional coverage through local capacity matching between real and generated samples, separating geometry-based coverage from effective coverage. This yields multi-dimensional coverage diagnostics that quantify mode dropping and mode collapse while reducing the overly optimistic estimates produced by geometry-based metrics. Through extensive experiments on toy data, real-world datasets, and generative models, we show that CADMA provides more reliable coverage estimates and more fine-grained, interpretable diagnostic signals of diversity failures than existing metrics. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CADMA is a capacity-aware framework for recall-oriented evaluation of generative models. It separates geometry-based coverage from effective coverage, giving multi-dimensional diagnostics for mode dropping and mode collapse and more conservative coverage estimates.
AI.motivation: Existing recall metrics reduce distributional coverage to geometry-based coverage, which yields only a single aggregate score that cannot separate mode dropping from mode collapse, and can overestimate coverage of poorly covered distributions.
AI.method: CADMA evaluates coverage through local capacity matching between real and generated samples. This separates geometry-based coverage from effective coverage and produces multi-dimensional coverage diagnostics.
AI.result: On toy data, real-world datasets and generative models, CADMA gives more reliable coverage estimates and more fine-grained, interpretable signals of diversity failures than existing metrics, and it reduces the optimistic estimates of geometry-based metrics.
AI.conclusion: Capacity-aware coverage offers a more reliable and interpretable basis for diagnosing diversity failures in generative models than single-score recall metrics.

title: A forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models: an EFM3D case study for crime scene reconstruction
summary: Foundation models increasingly combine geometry, semantics, and spatial context for three-dimensional scene understanding, but their suitability for forensic crime scene reconstruction remains unclear. This study presents a structured forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models and demonstrates it using the Egocentric Foundation Model for 3D (EFM3D). Four simulated indoor crime scenes were recorded with Meta Project Aria Gen~1 at Robert Gordon University's East Lodge House forensic training facility. The framework evaluates room-scale reconstruction, semantic scene understanding, computational performance, and forensic suitability. Across the four scenes, EFM3D generated meshes averaging $12{,}668\pm2{,}430$ vertices and $24{,}838\pm4{,}903$ faces, with 39,529 recorded semantic predictions spanning 21--24 categories at a mean confidence of 0.40. Because reference meshes and expert-labelled 3D ground truth were unavailable, these statistics are treated as descriptive outputs rather than measures of geometric or detection accuracy. Final inference runs processed $1{,}388\pm203$ snippets per scene at $0.69\pm0.01$ samples/s and required $50.77\pm6.12$ minutes per recording. A seven-criterion capability profile indicated stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context, and spatial relationships than for fine-scale forensic evidence. The results position EFM3D as a complementary tool for contextual documentation and scene review rather than a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture. The framework provides a reproducible basis for evaluating future egocentric foundation models in specialised forensic settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models and applies it to EFM3D on four simulated indoor crime scenes recorded with Meta Project Aria. EFM3D is judged a complementary tool for contextual documentation and scene review, not a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture.
AI.motivation: Foundation models combine geometry, semantics and spatial context for 3D scene understanding, but their suitability for forensic crime scene reconstruction was unclear.
AI.method: The framework evaluates room-scale reconstruction, semantic scene understanding, computational performance and forensic suitability. It is demonstrated on EFM3D using recordings from four simulated indoor crime scenes at a forensic training facility. A seven-criterion capability profile summarizes support for each aspect.
AI.result: EFM3D produced meshes averaging 12,668 plus or minus 2,430 vertices and 24,838 plus or minus 4,903 faces, with 39,529 semantic predictions across 21 to 24 categories at a mean confidence of 0.40. Inference took 50.77 plus or minus 6.12 minutes per recording. The capability profile indicated stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context and spatial relationships than for fine-scale forensic evidence. The statistics are descriptive, since no reference meshes or expert 3D ground truth were available.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a reproducible basis for evaluating future egocentric foundation models in forensic settings, and EFM3D is positioned as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for high-fidelity capture.

title: TMT: Adapting CLIP to Infrared Imagery via Text-Derived Modality Knowledge Transfer
summary: Vision-language models such as CLIP achieve strong performance across computer vision tasks, yet their image-text alignment is less reliable for infrared (IR) imagery because large-scale pre-training is dominated by visible-spectrum data. Due to the high cost of the infrared-text labeling, we investigate adapting CLIP to IR through only paired infrared-visible images, which requires considering modality-specific knowledge while preserving scene content and CLIP's image-text alignment. To achieve this, we propose TMT (Text-Derived Modality Knowledge Transfer), which adapts CLIP's image encoder through a text-defined infrared-to-visible direction and supervision from paired IR-visible images. First, we found that modality discrepancy can be described by corresponding text embeddings, thus using the direction of text embedding differences to guide the knowledge transfer between visible and infrared modalities without erasing infrared-specific information. To enhance the representation of semantics and details of infrared images, we introduce Generative-Perceptual Co-Supervision that combines semantic alignment from CLIP visible image encoder with diffusion noise-prediction feedbacks. On four source-disjoint IR classification benchmarks, TMT achieves the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among the compared methods (48.92%). It also achieves the best IR-text retrieval results among the compared methods without infrared-text supervision during adaptation and the highest open-vocabulary segmentation mIoU on both CART and SemanticRT among the CLIP-like methods.

AI.tldr: TMT adapts CLIP's image encoder to infrared imagery using only paired infrared-visible images, with no infrared-text supervision. It reaches 48.92% mean zero-shot accuracy on four source-disjoint IR classification benchmarks and gives the best IR-text retrieval and open-vocabulary segmentation mIoU among CLIP-like methods.
AI.motivation: CLIP's image-text alignment is less reliable for infrared imagery because pre-training is dominated by visible-spectrum data, and infrared-text labeling is expensive.
AI.method: TMT, or Text-Derived Modality Knowledge Transfer, uses the direction of text-embedding differences between visible and infrared descriptions to guide transfer from visible to infrared without erasing infrared-specific information. Generative-Perceptual Co-Supervision combines CLIP visible-image semantic alignment with diffusion noise-prediction feedback to strengthen semantic and detail representation of infrared images.
AI.result: On four source-disjoint IR classification benchmarks, TMT achieves the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among the compared methods, at 48.92%. It also gives the best IR-text retrieval results among the compared methods and the highest open-vocabulary segmentation mIoU on both CART and SemanticRT among CLIP-like methods.
AI.conclusion: Text-derived modality directions and generative-perceptual supervision allow CLIP to be adapted to infrared without infrared-text labels, improving infrared image-text alignment.

title: ReVMap: Vectorized Global Mapping via Connectivity-Aware Local Map Fusion
summary: Large-scale annotation of vectorized high-definition (HD) maps is labor-intensive and costly, motivating local-to-global auto-labeling approaches that incrementally construct global maps from local vectorized predictions. However, existing approaches often overlook prediction uncertainty and rely on heuristic map integration, potentially propagating errors and introducing topological inconsistencies. To address these limitations, we propose ReVMap, a reliable local-to-global framework that iteratively refines local map predictions and global map construction through uncertainty-guided prior utilization and connectivity-guided global map revision. Specifically, ReVMap leverages point-wise localization uncertainty to incorporate global map priors into local map prediction, improving robustness against inaccurate prior information. It then predicts local-to-global connectivity and selectively updates the global map through uncertainty-aware fusion based on the reliability of local predictions. By iteratively coupling local prediction and global revision, ReVMap progressively improves both local map accuracy and global map consistency. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 benchmarks demonstrate that ReVMap achieves state-of-the-art performance in both local map prediction and global map construction.

AI.tldr: ReVMap is a local-to-global framework for vectorized HD map construction that iteratively refines local predictions and the global map using uncertainty-guided prior utilization and connectivity-guided revision. It reports state-of-the-art local map prediction and global map construction on nuScenes and Argoverse 2.
AI.motivation: Annotating vectorized HD maps is costly. Existing local-to-global auto-labeling methods often ignore prediction uncertainty and rely on heuristic map integration, which can propagate errors and create topological inconsistencies.
AI.method: Point-wise localization uncertainty is used to incorporate global map priors into local map prediction. The method predicts local-to-global connectivity and updates the global map by uncertainty-aware fusion weighted by the reliability of local predictions. These steps are iterated so that local prediction and global revision refine each other.
AI.result: The abstract reports that ReVMap achieves state-of-the-art performance in both local map prediction and global map construction on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Coupling local prediction with connectivity-aware global revision progressively improves local map accuracy and global map consistency.

title: QCC-WM: Linking Macro-State Dynamics and Visual Generation via Quotient Causal Construction
summary: A key challenge in action-conditioned world modeling is to construct macro-states from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction under actions, while keeping their predicted evolution consistent with visual changes in generated observations. We propose QCC-WM, a visual world model based on Quotient-based Causal Construction. QCC-WM uses action responses to guide macro-variable construction for recursive action-conditioned prediction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains the consistency between predicted states and observed changes, allowing macro-level predictions to provide structured constraints for future visual generation. Using translational and rotational actions and their predicted responses, the model aggregates local visual features into macro-nodes with spatial correspondence through causal abstraction, and recursively predicts node content and motion under a shared reference measurement. Macro-level predictions guide future observation generation, while predicted motion transports historical appearance information. Node-level errors between generated observations and macro-level targets are then mapped back to the corresponding spatial regions for correction, improving consistency between visual generation and macro-level predictions. On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each prediction horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68%, and 30.23% for four-step prediction and eight- and sixteen-step recursive extrapolation, respectively. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses show that motion-guided reference transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, while node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency between generated observations and macro-level predictions.

AI.tldr: QCC-WM is an action-conditioned visual world model that builds macro-states through quotient-based causal construction and links their predicted evolution to generated visual observations. On the US-VLA dataset it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68% and 30.23% against the best baseline at each horizon.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned world models need macro-states built from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction, and their predicted evolution must stay consistent with the visual changes in generated frames.
AI.method: Action responses guide macro-variable construction, and local visual features are aggregated into spatially corresponding macro-nodes through causal abstraction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains predicted states against observed changes. Motion-guided reference transport carries historical appearance information, and node-level errors between generated frames and macro-level targets are mapped back to spatial regions for correction.
AI.result: On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59% for four-step prediction, 41.68% for eight-step and 30.23% for sixteen-step recursive extrapolation. Ablations show that motion-guided transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, and node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency.
AI.conclusion: Linking macro-state dynamics to visual generation through quotient-based causal construction improves the consistency and perceptual quality of long-horizon action-conditioned predictions.

title: TRIAD: Multimodal Retrieval across Abstraction, Constraints, and State
summary: Multimodal retrieval increasingly supports agentic systems, where user requests can involve cross-level relations, combine multiple constraints, and evolve across dialogue turns. In these settings, a highly similar result may still violate the user's requirements, while retrieved content may directly inform downstream actions without human screening. We introduce TRIAD, a multimodal retrieval benchmark for evaluating how well retrieval systems satisfy these complex, evolving requests. TRIAD comprises three tracks: abstraction, testing bidirectional retrieval between visual instances and concepts at different hierarchical levels; constraints, testing the joint satisfaction of positive and negative conditions; and state, testing the integration of requirements across dialogue turns and the updating of earlier conditions when users revise their requests. The benchmark contains six subsets, each with 1,000 queries and a fixed pool of 1,000 candidates per query, evaluated using a common multi-positive mean average precision (mAP) protocol. Simpler reference tasks and hard negatives grouped by the requirements they violate help characterize specific retrieval difficulties. We evaluate 20 configurations of 17 systems and find that no system leads across all six subsets. Performance declines with hierarchical distance, and negative-only queries generally underperform positive-only queries with the same number of constraints. Across paired tasks expressing the same final intent, multi-turn retrieval yields lower mAP in 39 of 40 configuration-domain comparisons. The benefits of explicit reasoning also vary across models and tasks. These findings highlight the gap between retrieving similar content and satisfying a complete request.

AI.tldr: TRIAD is a multimodal retrieval benchmark that tests how well systems satisfy complex, evolving requests across abstraction, constraints and dialogue state. Across 20 configurations of 17 systems, no system leads on all six subsets, and multi-turn retrieval yields lower mAP in 39 of 40 comparisons.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems increasingly rely on multimodal retrieval where a highly similar result can still violate the user's requirements, so retrieving similar content is not the same as satisfying a complete request.
AI.method: The benchmark has three tracks. Abstraction tests bidirectional retrieval between visual instances and concepts at different hierarchy levels. Constraints tests joint satisfaction of positive and negative conditions. State tests integration of requirements across dialogue turns and revision of earlier conditions. It contains six subsets, each with 1,000 queries and a fixed pool of 1,000 candidates per query, scored with multi-positive mean average precision (mAP), and hard negatives are grouped by the requirements they violate.
AI.result: No system leads across all six subsets. Performance declines with hierarchical distance, and negative-only queries generally underperform positive-only queries with the same number of constraints. Multi-turn retrieval yields lower mAP in 39 of 40 configuration-domain comparisons on paired tasks with the same final intent. The benefits of explicit reasoning vary across models and tasks.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight a gap between retrieving similar content and satisfying a complete, evolving request, which current retrieval systems do not close.

title: PTC-IoU: CPU-Friendly Detection Quality Estimation for Edge Video Analytics
summary: An edge video analytics system must estimate the quality of local detections since there are no ground-truth labels available during runtime. Detectors usually provide confidence scores for their results, but these scores can not reveal every missed object or misplaced bounding box. So a quality estimator is necessary to provide a decision signal indicating which frame has potential detection failures that need to be escalated to a more powerful model in the cloud. Neural network based estimators add workload to the GPU already running detection, while CPU capacity may remain available. We present Predictive Temporal Consistency IoU (PTC-IoU), which moves this workload to CPU by compacting detection boxes histories to support deterministic result scoring. Comparing to neural counterparts, experiments on representative edge hardware, Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, show that our method reduced per-frame estimator latency from 10.3 ms for neural counterparts to 2.2 ms (4.7x faster), increased pipelined throughput by 13.6%, and cuts estimator energy consumption by up to 95%, while maintaining competitive final detection quality verified on multiple datasets.
