AI.motivation: Real-time cooperative perception among connected vehicles is resource-intensive, so it should run selectively in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects.
AI.method: A mixed-model architecture combines conventional object detection, vision-language reasoning to find impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module that checks visibility, with chain-of-thought prompting for interpretable, intent-aware decisions.
AI.result: On real-world data from connected vehicles in urban traffic, the method exceeds 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing, and the authors compare four state-of-the-art VLMs.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a scalable, interpretable and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional cooperative perception pipelines for future connected traffic systems.

title: Elastic Representations via Hyperbolic Geometry
summary: Learned representations (or embeddings) are the foundation of modern machine learning systems, yet they are typically trained as fixed-size embeddings, without accounting for varying downstream resource or task constraints. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) addresses this limitation by learning nested representations, but requires costly end-to-end retraining and does not support post hoc expansion, while Contrastive Sparse Representations (CSR) reduce training overhead via lightweight adaptors but operate at a 4x larger dimensionality. Additionally, all prior works restrict their framework towards compression only. In this work, we introduce Hyperbolic Elastic Representation Learning (HERL), a framework for learning dimension-adaptive embeddings (compression and expansion) through a lightweight adaptor without retraining the base encoder. Our key idea is to exploit the exponential capacity of hyperbolic geometry by learning a non-linear mapping from the encoder space to hyperbolic space. We train a simple MLP to downsample the representations before projecting them onto a Lorentzian and learn adaptive representations that respect the Lorentzian geometry. Our approach is model-agnostic and effective in both supervised and unsupervised settings. Through extensive experiments across image and text modalities, we show that HERL preserves downstream performance across a wide range of embedding sizes, exhibits smooth interpolation between dimensions, and achieves these benefits at a fraction of the computational cost. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: HERL is a hyperbolic elastic representation learning framework that adapts embedding dimension for both compression and expansion through a lightweight adaptor, without retraining the base encoder.
AI.motivation: Matryoshka Representation Learning needs costly end-to-end retraining and does not support post hoc expansion, CSR uses lightweight adaptors but works at a 4x larger dimensionality, and prior work targets compression only.
AI.method: A simple MLP downsamples the encoder representations, which are then projected onto a Lorentzian hyperboloid, exploiting hyperbolic geometry's exponential capacity so that adaptive embeddings respect Lorentzian geometry; the method is model-agnostic.
AI.result: Across image and text modalities in supervised and unsupervised settings, HERL preserves downstream performance over a wide range of embedding sizes, interpolates smoothly between dimensions, and does so at a fraction of the computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic adaptors offer an efficient way to make fixed encoders dimension-elastic in both directions.

title: HARP-Bench: Benchmarking Robot Manipulation Around Active Humans
summary: Recent robot manipulation benchmarks have enabled systematic evaluation of general-purpose robot policies across diverse objects, scenes, instructions, and embodiments. However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on HARP-Bench. Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HARP-Bench is a benchmark for robot manipulation in workspaces shared with active humans, organized into four human-present conditions, with a demonstration-generation pipeline and evaluations of VLA, imitation learning and heuristic policies.
AI.motivation: Existing manipulation benchmarks assume the robot is the only active agent, which ignores humans who reveal goals, complete part of the task, change object availability or constrain robot motion.
AI.method: The benchmark defines Cueing, Contribution, Interruption and Co-presence conditions using everyday tasks with paired human-present and standard variants, and provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings.
AI.result: Human presence challenges current policies, higher task success does not consistently mean better safety, and manipulation and recovery are the dominant failure modes; training on HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation, and a real-world study shows gains under human contribution but not under interruption.
AI.conclusion: Human-aware evaluation exposes safety and transfer limits that success rates alone hide, and the benchmark's data is useful but limited in real-world transfer.

title: Confidence-driven adaptive semantic transmission for task-oriented communication
summary: Image-based remote monitoring over wireless networks faces a trade-off between communication cost and classification reliability. Transmitting complete images is communication-intensive, whereas relying solely on lightweight edge classifiers may compromise accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose Confidence-Driven Adaptation (CDA) for image transmission and classification. An edge device (ED) captures images and applies a lightweight classifier before transmission to a remote server. Based on its classification confidence, the ED selects among three transmission modes with varying levels of information: a short text string reporting its predicted class when confidence is high, a compressed Region of Interest (ROI) at intermediate confidence levels, or an uncompressed ROI when confidence is low. The server accepts the predicted class directly in the first case and performs classification using a more powerful classifier in the other two cases. Numerical evaluations under bandwidth-limited, lossy links and latency-constrained settings demonstrate that CDA achieves high task accuracy at the receiver compared with non-adaptive baselines that transmit only the edge-classifier outcome or the uncompressed ROI.

AI.tldr: Confidence-Driven Adaptation (CDA) lets an edge device choose among three transmission modes for image-based remote monitoring, based on the confidence of a lightweight local classifier, to trade off communication cost against classification accuracy.
AI.motivation: Transmitting full images is communication-heavy, while relying on a lightweight edge classifier alone can reduce accuracy over wireless links.
AI.method: The edge device sends a short text string with the predicted class when confidence is high, a compressed Region of Interest at intermediate confidence, or an uncompressed Region of Interest at low confidence, and the server classifies with a more powerful model except in the first mode.
AI.result: Under bandwidth-limited, lossy and latency-constrained links, CDA achieves high task accuracy at the receiver compared with non-adaptive baselines that send only the edge-classifier outcome or the uncompressed Region of Interest.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-driven selection of the information sent gives a practical balance between communication cost and classification reliability for wireless remote monitoring.

title: Full Fine-Tuning is not the Problem: Why Adam Fails and SGD Succeeds in Few-Shot CLIP Adaptation
summary: Few-shot CLIP adaptation is often treated as a parameterization problem. Full fine-tuning is assumed to overfit, so parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are preferred. In this paper, we show that this conclusion conflates parameterization with optimization. Across 11 datasets, 3 CLIP backbones, and 5 shot levels, dense full fine-tuning with plain SGD outperforms representative PEFT methods under the reported evaluation protocol, whereas Adam/AdamW collapses. We trace this collapse to unreliable support-set preconditioning. The few-shot second moment systematically underestimates the corresponding full-data statistic, already at initialization. Adam's inverse-square-root normalization converts this error into an oversized adaptive update. Matching Adam's first-step update budget to SGD resolves most of the collapse, whereas numerator-side alignment does not explain the failure. Shampoo and SOAP also fail, so richer preconditioning alone does not resolve the problem. Theory formalizes how few-shot estimation error is amplified into unsafe updates. SGD succeeds because it avoids unreliable preconditioners and stays close to pretrained CLIP. Interpolation probes show low-loss connections along tested directions, and curvature probes show favorable directional curvature. These results identify optimizer-induced preconditioning, not dense full fine-tuning itself, as the main source of failure in few-shot CLIP adaptation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that few-shot CLIP adaptation fails under Adam and AdamW because of unreliable second-moment estimates from small support sets, while dense full fine-tuning with plain SGD outperforms parameter-efficient methods.
AI.motivation: Few-shot CLIP adaptation is usually framed as a parameterization problem in which full fine-tuning is assumed to overfit, but the authors suspect the conclusion conflates parameterization with optimization.
AI.method: Across 11 datasets, 3 CLIP backbones and 5 shot levels, the authors compare dense full fine-tuning with SGD against PEFT methods and Adam, AdamW, Shampoo and SOAP, and analyze the second-moment estimate, the first-step update budget, and theory on how estimation error is amplified into unsafe updates, with interpolation and curvature probes.
AI.result: Dense full fine-tuning with plain SGD outperforms representative PEFT methods, whereas Adam and AdamW collapse; the few-shot second moment underestimates the full-data statistic already at initialization, and matching Adam's first-step budget to SGD resolves most of the collapse, while Shampoo and SOAP also fail.
AI.conclusion: Optimizer-induced preconditioning, rather than dense full fine-tuning itself, is the main source of failure in few-shot CLIP adaptation, and SGD succeeds by avoiding unreliable preconditioners and staying close to pretrained CLIP.

title: Edge Computing for Computer Vision in IoT: Feasibility and Directions
summary: The convergence of decentralized architectures integrating Machine Learning, Computer Vision and Low Power Wide Area Networks is increasingly becoming an integral part of our daily existence. Internet of Things serves as a real-time data conduit enhancing decision making via embedded technology and continuous data exchange. This paper explores the feasibility of Edge Computing as a foundational pillar in this evolving landscape. We experiment under real world, dynamic conditions, evaluate the technological aspects, strategies, process flows and key observations under the broad Edge Computing domain. Research pathways include Multi-access Edge topologies in future 6G networks, model quantization, and satellite-enhanced communication platforms. Additionally, a discussion is added supporting the advanced AI functionalities, including zero-shot learning, multi modal perception, and decentralized generative AI, thereby broadening the scope of intelligent applications across various domains. The significance and research objective of this study are threefold: (1) evaluation of LoRaWAN and satellite IoT communication strategies, (2) analysis of CV workloads on edge hardware and (3) future research directions where Edge Computing can support low-latency, energy-efficient and socially impactful IoT applications. By explicitly addressing these aspects, we aim to establish a clear link between the technological feasibility, ultimately with a practical and socioeconomic relevance.

AI.tldr: The paper examines the feasibility of edge computing for computer vision in IoT, evaluating LoRaWAN and satellite communication, CV workloads on edge hardware, and future directions such as 6G multi-access edge, quantization and decentralized generative AI.
AI.motivation: Integrating machine learning, computer vision and low-power wide-area networks into IoT needs practical evidence on edge feasibility under real-world dynamic conditions.
AI.method: The authors run experiments under real-world conditions and evaluate technologies, strategies and process flows, covering LoRaWAN and satellite IoT strategies, CV workloads on edge hardware, and a discussion of future research pathways.
AI.result: The abstract reports observations rather than specific quantitative findings for the three stated objectives.
AI.conclusion: The study aims to link technological feasibility to practical and socioeconomic relevance for low-latency, energy-efficient and socially impactful IoT applications.

title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
summary: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

AI.tldr: Chatter Attack is a resource consumption attack that optimizes adversarial prompts to induce short doubt-inducing target phrases, sustaining self-doubt during generation so the LLM produces very long outputs, with a Bayesian prompt optimization method for black-box settings.
AI.motivation: Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token, and the search space of sampling-based generation grows exponentially with length, so optimization is unstable.
AI.method: The attack optimizes prompts toward short target phrases using inference attention loss and global entropy loss to sustain the induced state, and extends to black-box settings with Bayesian Prompt Optimization that models the objective with a discrete token kernel.
AI.result: Across multiple models and datasets the method outperforms baselines, increasing maximum response length by up to 31.5 times and revealing resource-depletion risks for LLM inference services.
AI.conclusion: Targeting short phrases avoids search-space explosion and exposes practical cost and latency risks for deployed LLM services.

title: A Unified Framework for License Plate Identification and Character-Recognition
summary: This paper presents a unified framework for license plate detection and character recognition on low-power edge hardware. The proposed network uses a shared CSP-Darknet and PANet feature encoder with an anchor-free localization head and a RoIAlign-based sequence-recognition branch. Character decoding is performed directly on aligned feature maps, avoiding image-space plate cropping and a second recognition backbone. The model is trained on an AI-assisted dataset of approximately 37,000 manually verified images covering license plate layouts from all 50 United States. The dataset includes variations in illumination, viewpoint, weather, blur, occlusion, and plate design. The framework is converted to an INT8 TensorRT engine and evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB memory. The INT8 model shows an mAP50 of 97.8% and a full-sequence accuracy of 90.7%. It records 147 FPS at 6.8 ms end-to-end latency, with 315 MB inference memory and 9.4 W average power consumption. Relative to the YOLOv8s+CRNN baseline, the proposed deployment provides a 7.1x throughput increase and a 77.8% reduction in allocated inference memory

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified network for license plate detection and character recognition that runs on low-power edge hardware, decoding characters directly from aligned feature maps and reaching 147 FPS on a Jetson Orin Nano in INT8.
AI.motivation: Conventional plate recognition crops plates from the image and uses a second recognition backbone, which costs computation and memory on edge devices.
AI.method: A shared CSP-Darknet and PANet encoder feeds an anchor-free localization head and a RoIAlign-based sequence-recognition branch, trained on an AI-assisted dataset of about 37,000 verified images covering plates from all 50 United States, then converted to an INT8 TensorRT engine.
AI.result: The INT8 model reaches 97.8% mAP50 and 90.7% full-sequence accuracy, runs at 147 FPS with 6.8 ms end-to-end latency, uses 315 MB inference memory and 9.4 W average power, and gives 7.1x throughput and a 77.8% reduction in allocated inference memory relative to a YOLOv8s+CRNN baseline.
AI.conclusion: Sharing features and avoiding image-space cropping make accurate plate recognition practical on low-power edge hardware.

title: Multi-Node Transformers for Object Detection and Captioning Across Distributed Edge Networks
summary: This paper presents a unified transformer-based framework for object detection and dense region captioning across distributed edge networks. The architecture uses a shared visual encoder followed by detection, region extraction, and autoregressive language-decoding stages, allowing localization and region description to reuse the same image features. This design removes the second image-encoding path required by decoupled detection and captioning pipelines. To support execution on resource-limited devices, a workload-allocation formulation assigns model stages and input streams across connected edge nodes while accounting for execution time, memory capacity, processor utilization, power limits, and intermediate tensor transfer cost. The framework is evaluated on a six-device edge testbed comprising four NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and Orin NX inference nodes and two Raspberry Pi 5 auxiliary CPU nodes, with TensorRT FP16 and INT8 execution on the NVIDIA devices. On a Jetson Orin Nano, the unified INT8 model achieves 38.1 FPS with 3.5 GB peak memory use and 11.8 W measured power. Under four concurrent streams, the proposed allocation achieves 35.2 FPS and 28.4 ms mean end-to-end latency with an internode transfer rate of 6.8 MB/s.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified transformer that performs object detection and dense region captioning on a shared visual encoder, with a workload-allocation formulation that distributes its stages across a heterogeneous edge testbed.
AI.motivation: Decoupled detection and captioning pipelines encode the image twice, which is wasteful on resource-limited devices distributed across edge networks.
AI.method: One shared visual encoder feeds detection, region extraction and autoregressive language decoding, and a workload-allocation formulation assigns model stages and input streams across connected nodes while accounting for execution time, memory, utilization, power and intermediate tensor transfer cost.
AI.result: On a six-device testbed of Jetson Orin Nano and Orin NX nodes plus Raspberry Pi 5 nodes, the unified INT8 model reaches 38.1 FPS on an Orin Nano with 3.5 GB peak memory and 11.8 W, and under four concurrent streams the allocation achieves 35.2 FPS and 28.4 ms mean end-to-end latency at 6.8 MB/s internode transfer.
AI.conclusion: Sharing the visual encoder and allocating stages by cost-aware scheduling makes joint detection and captioning feasible across distributed edge devices.

title: Single-Radar Bilateral 3D Near-Field Imaging for Mobile Robots
summary: Mobile robots operating in homes need reliable 3D perception of nearby furniture and surrounding structures, yet recovering this information on both sides of the robot's path with a single forward-mounted millimeter-wave radar remains challenging because of near-field wavefront curvature, viewpoint-dependent target visibility, and limited elevation diversity. This paper presents a motion-assisted framework for reconstructing structures on both sides of a robot's trajectory. Our near-field model relates scene reflectivity to stepped-frequency multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) observations across frequencies and robot positions using spherical paths from transmitter (Tx) to scatterer to receiver (Rx). Bilateral Tx combining provides wideband directional weighting, while sliding-aperture back-projection coherently focuses the measurements using near-field propagation distances. Top-K power fusion combines local images with different visibility. The reconstruction provides lateral-forward support for multi-layer height extraction, followed by guarded adaptive height refinement using the original MIMO channels. Experiments in controlled, office/study, and corridor environments produce mean lateral-forward localization errors of 4.65, 5.63, and 5.98 cm, respectively, with peak-to-background ratios (PBRs) exceeding 13 dB. The framework recovers bilateral 3D scattering structure from one forward pass using a single radar, without relying on learned representations of the scene.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a motion-assisted framework that reconstructs 3D structures on both sides of a robot's path from one forward-mounted millimeter-wave radar, using near-field stepped-frequency MIMO processing.
AI.motivation: Home robots need 3D perception of furniture on both sides of their path, but a single forward radar faces near-field wavefront curvature, viewpoint-dependent visibility and limited elevation diversity.
AI.method: The near-field model relates scene reflectivity to stepped-frequency MIMO observations over frequencies and robot positions using spherical propagation paths, with bilateral transmit combining, sliding-aperture back-projection for coherent focusing, top-K power fusion of local images, and guarded adaptive height refinement.
AI.result: In controlled, office and corridor environments the mean lateral-forward localization errors are 4.65, 5.63 and 5.98 cm, with peak-to-background ratios above 13 dB, and the framework recovers bilateral 3D structure in one forward pass without learned scene representations.
AI.conclusion: Physics-based near-field processing with robot motion can recover bilateral 3D scene structure from a single radar without learning.

title: Decomposing Earth Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Earth observation foundation models produce global metre-resolution embeddings that underpin work across agriculture, ecology, hydrology, and beyond. Yet these embeddings are opaque: each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, which makes them difficult to interpret and their robustness hard to assess. Here, we propose sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as a principled way to decompose Earth embeddings into sparse, approximately monosemantic features over an overcomplete dictionary. Because LLM judges of interpretations do not transfer to satellite pixels, and spatial autocorrelation matters, we introduce a tailored evaluation protocol. It scores any SAE on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concepts, and spatial scale, each against baselines that include an SAE whose decoder is a frozen random dictionary. On this protocol, SAEs reconstruct AlphaEarth and Tessera embeddings better than every baseline at matched sparsity. Their features align with far fewer reference concepts than raw embedding dimensions (on AlphaEarth, 88% align with at most one of 20 concept groups, most with none, against a median of 12 per raw dimension). They also carry more of their variance at fine spatial scales (23 to 32% within a 640 m patch for BatchTopK and Matryoshka, against 9%). An SAE with a frozen random decoder shares both properties, which therefore follow from sparsity, whereas only a learned dictionary reconstructs the embedding accurately: on AlphaEarth, trained SAEs leave eight times less variance unexplained. We test the sparse code on two applications, discovering land-cover sub-concepts and detecting out-of-distribution pixels by area-of-applicability estimation. Both indicate how sparse features could be used, but neither is yet reliable enough for practical use. Together, these results are a step toward Earth observation models whose features can be inspected.

AI.tldr: The paper uses sparse autoencoders to decompose Earth observation foundation model embeddings into sparse, approximately monosemantic features and introduces an evaluation protocol for reconstruction, concept alignment and spatial scale.
AI.motivation: Earth embeddings underpin agriculture, ecology and hydrology work, but each dimension entangles unrelated physical concepts, and LLM-based interpretation judges do not transfer to satellite pixels while spatial autocorrelation matters.
AI.method: The authors train SAEs over an overcomplete dictionary and score them on reconstruction at matched sparsity, alignment with reference concept groups, and spatial scale, against baselines including an SAE with a frozen random decoder; they also test land-cover sub-concept discovery and out-of-distribution detection by area-of-applicability estimation.
AI.result: On AlphaEarth and Tessera embeddings, SAEs reconstruct better than every baseline at matched sparsity, 88% of AlphaEarth SAE features align with at most one of 20 concept groups against a median of 12 per raw dimension, and 23 to 32% of variance sits at fine 640 m scale against 9%, with the random-decoder SAE sharing the interpretability properties but not the reconstruction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Sparsity drives the interpretability properties while learned dictionaries are needed for accurate reconstruction, a step toward inspectable Earth observation features, though the two applications are not yet reliable enough for practical use.

title: Off-Policy RL with Online Inference Tuning: My Solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval Challenge
comment: Technical report for the RoboEval Challenge at CoRL 2026. Code: this https URL ; checkpoint: this https URL ; project page: this https URL
summary: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $\pi_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.

AI.tldr: The author's solution to the CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge combines off-policy RL on a pi0.5-based policy with competition-specific data, reaching 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.
AI.motivation: The challenge ranks bimanual policies on how well they perform every stage of eight tasks, scored safely, efficiently and in arm coordination, against human demonstrations, which needs targeted data beyond local exploration.
AI.method: The generic part is off-policy RL on a pi0.5-based policy that also serves as its own value function, trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the official score, where each rollout doubles as a Thompson-sampling trial over about 20 inference parameters; the competition part adds generated demonstrations reaching full reward and recovery episodes from the policy's own failures.
AI.result: The generic method reaches 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days and is still far from convergence, and the submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.
AI.conclusion: Combining generic off-policy RL with generated demonstrations and recovery data that exploration cannot find gives strong performance on the challenge's score.

title: Kimodo-Policy: Learning Kinematic Action Models for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.

AI.tldr: Kimodo-Policy uses a pretrained kinematic motion generator as the action backbone for humanoid loco-manipulation, introducing Kinematic Action Models that treat whole-body motion as the pretraining target.
AI.motivation: Vision-language-action and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors, which do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion needed for whole-body humanoid coordination.
AI.method: A frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone is combined with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning, a root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, and motion-history conditioning with repeated action-chunk prediction links motion synthesis to closed-loop control.
AI.result: After large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters of which 92M are trainable, and ablations confirm the value of the pretrained motion backbone.
AI.conclusion: Motion generation is a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning, with initial evidence from this instantiation.

title: Budget-aware Correspondence-driven View Selection for Real-time 3D Perception of Mobile Robots
summary: 3D visual perception and scene reconstruction are critical for autonomous robots and intelligent transportation, yet real-world deployments often generate long, redundant image sequences that hinder downstream processing. This report investigates BCVS (budget-aware correspondence-driven view sampling), a pose-free view selection algorithm that offers 22+ FPS on a CPU, enabling online filtering for efficient 3D perception by mobile robots. Unlike existing approaches that rely on full structure-from-motion (SfM) pipelines or camera pose estimation, BCVS employs a purely correspondence-based scoring strategy that prioritizes view novelty while maintaining sufficient overlap for geometric stability. Given a user-specified budget, BCVS iteratively selects the most distinct frames and suppresses near-duplicates, producing compact subsets that preserve connectivity and minimize reconstruction loss. Extensive experiments on benchmark show that BCVS outperforms CPU-friendly baselines at tight budgets and remains competitive as budgets scale. Field trials with large aerial and marine robotics data further validate its practicality and scalability: BCVS reduces redundancy up to 16% while sustaining robust SfM registration and high-quality 3D reconstructions.

AI.tldr: BCVS is a pose-free, correspondence-based view selection algorithm that runs at 22+ FPS on a CPU and filters long image sequences under a user-given budget for efficient online 3D perception by mobile robots.
AI.motivation: Real deployments produce long redundant image sequences, and existing selection methods depend on full structure-from-motion or camera pose estimation, which is costly for online use.
AI.method: BCVS scores frames by correspondence to prioritize view novelty while keeping enough overlap for geometric stability, iteratively selects the most distinct frames under a budget, and suppresses near-duplicates to keep connectivity.
AI.result: BCVS outperforms CPU-friendly baselines at tight budgets, remains competitive as budgets grow on benchmarks, and in field trials with aerial and marine data reduces redundancy by up to 16% while keeping robust SfM registration and high-quality reconstructions.
AI.conclusion: A simple correspondence-based selection step is practical and scalable for reducing redundancy in mobile-robot 3D reconstruction.

title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
comment: 30 pages (12-page main text, appendices A-H). Code: this https URL
summary: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether nearest-of-m training is enough for one-step world models on frozen DINO tokens and proposes a random-codebook account that predicts how the number of candidates m shapes memorization, mode coverage and dispersion.
AI.motivation: One-step stochastic world models avoid mode averaging without the many network evaluations of diffusion or flow matching, and recent work conjectures that a small m suffices and that an energy score should replace the hard minimum.
AI.method: The authors train one-step world models with nearest-of-m (conditional IMLE) matching on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens and evaluate on benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated, and they interpret the objective as the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws, deriving three predictions on memorization, mode probability flattening and under-dispersion.
AI.result: Under mode-like uncertainty nearest-of-m with m=16 covers enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching at about 1/30 of its latency and better than one-step flow and energy-score generators at matched parameters, and per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant, but planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates.
AI.conclusion: The random-codebook view explains nearest-of-m behavior and bounds the method on continuous high-dimensional outcomes such as real robot video, and the planning negative result is reported with its diagnosis.

title: Shaping Useful Noise: Energy Distributions Predict Visual Pretraining Quality
comment: Accepted as an oral presentation to NeurIPS 2026 (Sydney)
summary: Synthetic data can scale visual pretraining, but current selection criteria only partially explain which datasets train strong representations. We propose using the energy profile of a dataset--the distribution of log-probability levels it occupies under a normalised real-image density model--as an audit and curation principle for synthetic data. To operationalise this view, we introduce Energy-Level Distribution Distance (ELD), which compares real and synthetic energy distributions. Real images span sparse high-likelihood scenes and dense low-likelihood textures, so useful synthetic data should cover this energy range rather than collapse to likely but low-variation samples. Across diverse synthetic datasets, ELD exposes mismatches missed by FID and predicts pretraining performance beyond FID, LPIPS variation, and feature-space recall, including across CNN and ViT self-supervised settings. We then use ELD to resample and mix synthetic sources, matching the real-image energy histogram while preserving diversity and improving downstream transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the energy profile of a dataset, the distribution of log-probability levels under a normalised real-image density model, as a principle for auditing and curating synthetic pretraining data, and introduces Energy-Level Distribution Distance (ELD) to measure mismatch with real data. ELD predicts visual pretraining performance beyond FID and related metrics.
AI.motivation: Current selection criteria for synthetic visual pretraining data only partially explain which datasets yield strong representations. FID and similar feature-space measures miss energy-range mismatches, and synthetic samples tend to collapse onto likely but low-variation images.
AI.method: Real-image energy distributions are compared with synthetic ones through ELD, using a normalised real-image density model to compute log-probability levels. The energy histogram is then used to resample and mix synthetic sources so that they match the real energy histogram while preserving diversity.
AI.result: ELD exposes mismatches missed by FID and predicts pretraining performance beyond FID, LPIPS variation and feature-space recall across CNN and ViT self-supervised settings. Resampling and mixing with ELD matches the real-image energy histogram, preserves diversity and improves downstream transfer.
AI.conclusion: Covering the full energy range of real images, from sparse high-likelihood scenes to dense low-likelihood textures, is a practical criterion for auditing and curating synthetic data for visual pretraining.

title: MUTE: Multi-Level Alignment Uncoupling Against Talking-Head Exploitation for Voice Protection
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 33 pages, including appendix and checklist. Project and code: this https URL
summary: Talking-head generation models, which synthesize realistic facial animations from audio, are increasingly vulnerable to misuse in multimodal deepfake scenarios. Protecting such systems remains challenging, as talking-head models fundamentally rely on precise audio-visual alignment, while effective audio protection methods remain largely underexplored. In this work, we propose MUTE, an audio protection framework that uncouples the underlying audio-visual alignment through a multi-level strategy. Specifically, MUTE combines (1) Alignment-level Disruption, which directly perturbs cross-modal attention to disrupt structural alignment, and (2) Representation-level Degradation, which perturbs temporal audio embeddings to degrade their representations. To improve robustness, perturbations are constrained in the STFT domain to high-energy regions, making them resistant to post-processing, denoising, and adaptive attacks. An optional speaker-level objective further mitigates potential bypass via TTS-based resynthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MUTE consistently degrades lip synchronization across both white-box and black-box talking-head models while preserving perceptual audio quality. The proposed method remains effective under real-world transformations and can be combined with image-based approaches to provide stronger multimodal protection. The source code and project page are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MUTE, an audio protection framework that disrupts audio-visual alignment in talking-head generation models to prevent deepfake misuse. It combines alignment-level and representation-level perturbations that degrade lip synchronization while keeping audio quality.
AI.motivation: Talking-head models rely on precise audio-visual alignment, yet protection methods for the audio modality are largely unexplored, leaving these generators open to multimodal deepfake misuse.
AI.method: MUTE pairs Alignment-level Disruption, which perturbs cross-modal attention, with Representation-level Degradation, which perturbs temporal audio embeddings. Perturbations are constrained to high-energy regions of the STFT domain for robustness, and an optional speaker-level objective counters bypass through TTS-based resynthesis.
AI.result: MUTE consistently degrades lip synchronization against white-box and black-box talking-head models while preserving perceptual audio quality. It remains effective under real-world transformations, post-processing, denoising and adaptive attacks, and can be combined with image-based protection.
AI.conclusion: Multi-level audio perturbation offers a practical route to stronger multimodal protection against talking-head deepfakes.

title: DPGS-SLAM: Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Dynamic Visual Sensing
summary: This paper presents DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM) for dense mapping in environments containing dynamic objects. Dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction in visual SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping). Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Our proposed DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB SLAM framework that supports provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds through asynchronous diffusion-based background completion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2 (segment anything model 2). For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while Metric3D v2 predicts metric depth from the completed images to initialize provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Experimental results demonstrated competitive camera tracking, with average ATE RMSE values of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D. On StaDy4D, DPGS-SLAM improved average PSNR by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using only monocular RGB input.

AI.tldr: DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for dense mapping in scenes with dynamic objects. It completes occluded static backgrounds with a diffusion inpainting model and tracks provenance so that generated primitives do not affect camera pose estimation.
AI.motivation: Dynamic objects violate the static-scene assumption of existing 3DGS-SLAM systems, which then become unstable. Excluding dynamic observations can leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained.
AI.method: Dynamic regions are found by optical-flow motion discovery and mask propagation with SAM2. For keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model completes occluded backgrounds, and Metric3D v2 predicts depth to initialise provisional Gaussians. Provenance labels separate generated primitives from observation-supported ones, and generated primitives are removed once the background is observed.
AI.result: Camera tracking is competitive, with average ATE RMSE of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D. On StaDy4D, average PSNR improves by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using monocular RGB only.
AI.conclusion: Provenance-aware separation of generated and observed Gaussians lets diffusion-based background completion improve dense mapping in dynamic scenes without corrupting tracking.

title: Leveraging High-Activity Post-Therapeutic I-131 Scans for Deep Learning Reconstruction of Extremely Sparse Planar Images in Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
summary: Background: Diagnostic I-131 whole-body planar imaging in differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) is count-limited by low administered activity, and quality worsens under rapid acquisition. Models trained on such data struggle because their targets lack photon statistics. Purpose: To test whether high-quality post-therapeutic (PT) I-131 scans can serve as superior training references for enhancing sparse diagnostic planar images, using transfer learning and input-image addition. Methods: In this single-center prospective study, 111 patients were enrolled in PT training (n = 19), diagnostic follow-up (FU) training (n = 58), and FU paired test (n = 34) cohorts. Five Restormer-based models were trained: FU_DLx2 on FU labels; PT_DLx2 transfer-learned on PT data; PT_DLx1+ and PT_DLx2+ with input-image addition; PT_DLx6 as a PT-only reference. Test-time processing used two-step denormalization and Poisson re-scaling to preserve noise statistics. Quality was assessed by PSNR, SSIM, and a blinded dual-reader evaluation of all 34 test-cohort patients. Results: PT_DLx2 achieved the highest PSNR (34.4 +/- 3.6 dB) and SSIM (0.81 +/- 0.07). PT_DLx1+ and PT_DLx2+ were comparable (33.8 and 33.3 dB; SSIM 0.80). FU_DLx2 ranked below the unprocessed fast scan (30.3 vs. 32.0 dB; 0.76 vs. 0.79). Subjectively, PT_DLx2+ scored highest in image quality (4.54 +/- 0.60) and diagnostic confidence (4.54 +/- 0.60), surpassing the reference standard (4.19 +/- 0.83 and 4.31 +/- 0.81; P = 0.005 and P = 0.008). FU_DLx2 and PT_DLx6 scored lowest. Conclusion: Count-rich PT scans provide effective training priors for reconstructing extremely sparse images. Input-image addition and cross-domain transfer learning from PT data outperformed direct training on count-limited diagnostic data, supporting 2x scan acceleration with quality matching or exceeding the unaccelerated standard scan for selected PT-derived configurations.

AI.tldr: The study shows that high-quality post-therapeutic I-131 scans can serve as training references for reconstructing extremely sparse diagnostic planar images in differentiated thyroid cancer. Models trained this way yield images whose quality matches or exceeds the standard scan, supporting 2x scan acceleration.
AI.motivation: Diagnostic I-131 whole-body planar images are count-limited by low administered activity, and rapid acquisition degrades quality. Models trained on such data lack reliable targets because those targets have no photon statistics.
AI.method: In a single-centre prospective study of 111 patients, five Restormer-based models were trained: FU_DLx2 on follow-up labels, PT_DLx2 with transfer learning from post-therapeutic data, PT_DLx1+ and PT_DLx2+ with input-image addition, and PT_DLx6 as a PT-only reference. Two-step denormalisation and Poisson re-scaling preserved noise statistics at test time. Evaluation used PSNR, SSIM and a blinded dual-reader assessment of 34 test patients.
AI.result: PT_DLx2 had the highest PSNR (34.4 +/- 3.6 dB) and SSIM (0.81 +/- 0.07). FU_DLx2 scored below the unprocessed fast scan (30.3 vs 32.0 dB). PT_DLx2+ received the highest subjective image quality and diagnostic confidence (4.54 +/- 0.60 each), above the reference standard (4.19 +/- 0.83 and 4.31 +/- 0.81; P = 0.005 and P = 0.008).
AI.conclusion: Count-rich post-therapeutic scans provide effective training priors for sparse-image reconstruction, and input-image addition with cross-domain transfer outperforms direct training on count-limited diagnostic data for selected configurations.

title: SPARK: Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge to Robot Control
summary: Large-scale representation learning has produced public foundation models that provide strong general-purpose visual features. However, their pretraining objectives are not designed for robot representation learning, so the resulting embeddings tend to emphasize global semantics rather than the temporally sensitive representations required for robot control. Training robot models from scratch is also undesirable due to the limited scale and high collection cost of robotics data, as well as the substantial computational burden of pre-training. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models to robot control. SPARK is built on two principles: temporal abstraction, which encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model to retain useful pretrained semantics. These objectives yield compact visual state representations that remain semantically meaningful while preserving useful prior knowledge. Experiments across multiple robotics benchmarks show that SPARK consistently improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models, and further demonstrate that these gains transfer to real-world robot manipulation.

AI.tldr: SPARK is a post-training method that adapts general-purpose vision foundation models into compact visual state representations for robot control. It combines temporal abstraction with knowledge preservation, and its gains transfer to real-world manipulation.
AI.motivation: Foundation model embeddings emphasise global semantics rather than the temporally sensitive features robot control needs. Training robot models from scratch is costly because robotics data is scarce and pretraining is computationally heavy.
AI.method: SPARK rests on two objectives: temporal abstraction, which encourages compact features that preserve temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model.
AI.result: Across several robotics benchmarks SPARK consistently improves success rates and generalisation over vanilla foundation models, and these gains transfer to real-world robot manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight post-training can convert general foundation models into robot-ready representations that keep their useful pretrained semantics.

title: LHNav: Long-Horizon Humanoid Navigation via Multirate Coordination and Physics-Grounded Action Data
summary: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. Deployment on the Unitree G1 further demonstrates single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon task execution in real-world environments, including layouts with repositioned objects. Project website: this https URL.

AI.tldr: LHNav is an asynchronous system for long-horizon humanoid navigation across successive destinations under language instructions. It splits the work into a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation and a Brainstem for whole-body execution, and it runs on a Unitree G1.
AI.motivation: Existing task decomposition does not guarantee progress throughout execution, and waypoint-based navigation does not ensure natural, route-faithful whole-body motion through confined spaces.
AI.method: Progress and arrival feedback coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction and whole-body control at different time scales. A physics-grounded data engine improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the demonstrations with rendered visual observations to train the Cerebellum.
AI.result: In simulation the navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. A VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations reaches 75.56% success on long-horizon navigation, and real-world deployment on the Unitree G1 shows zero-shot long-horizon execution.
AI.conclusion: Separating reasoning, motion generation and whole-body control across time scales lets planning proceed alongside continuous movement and extends single-goal navigation to successive destinations.

title: Harnessing Vision-Language Models for Federated Unsupervised Visual Recognition
summary: Federated learning (FL) is a promising research paradigm that enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without data sharing. To handle unlabeled data in local clients, existing unsupervised FL research has primarily focused on tasks like clustering and self-supervised representation learning, leaving the critical problem of unsupervised visual recognition largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce FedUR, the first framework designed for unsupervised recognition by leveraging the zero-shot capabilities of pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP. Specifically, FedUR addresses data heterogeneity through a pseudo-labeling mechanism with a class-aware data selection strategy. This strategy first estimates a global pseudo-label distribution, then allocates pseudo-labeled data to clients accordingly. To handle the uncertainty of conventional positive pseudo-labels, FedUR further incorporates class weights and a negative pseudo-labeling strategy. Furthermore, FedUR proposes a personalized prompt aggregation protocol where general visual prompts are aggregated on the server, and personalized text prompts encoding local knowledge are retained on clients. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedUR consistently outperforms baseline methods under both label-level and feature-level distribution shifts. We believe this work paves the way for further advances in federated unsupervised recognition. Code will be available at {this http URL}}.

AI.tldr: FedUR is a federated framework for unsupervised visual recognition that uses the zero-shot ability of CLIP-style vision-language models to pseudo-label unlabelled client data. It outperforms baselines under label-level and feature-level distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Existing unsupervised federated learning research has focused on clustering and self-supervised representation learning, leaving unsupervised visual recognition largely unexplored.
AI.method: A class-aware data selection strategy estimates a global pseudo-label distribution and allocates pseudo-labelled data to clients accordingly. Class weights and negative pseudo-labelling address the uncertainty of positive pseudo-labels. Global visual prompts are aggregated on the server, while personalised text prompts encoding local knowledge stay on clients.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show FedUR consistently outperforms baseline methods under both label-level and feature-level distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: The work opens a path for federated unsupervised recognition by combining vision-language pseudo-labelling with personalised prompt aggregation.

title: Controlling Temporal Pseudo-Label Marginals for Stable Online Test-Time Adaptation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 20 pages. Code: this https URL
summary: Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) methods update models online using a stream of unlabeled data to overcome distribution shifts encountered at test time. However, CTTA is often unstable, as it can reinforce biases in early predictions and increasingly predict only a few classes, resulting in drift or even collapse. In this paper, we identify narrowing pseudo-label class usage as an indicator of CTTA instability and quantify this behavior. Most existing methods have attempted to address this issue by either selecting reliable adaptation samples or re-weighting the loss to encourage diverse pseudo-labels, but they do not explicitly enforce a class marginal over a temporal window. Instead, we propose Sinkhorn Class-Marginal Regularization (SCALAR), a simple plug-and-play module that controls the pseudo-label distribution over a short temporal window. SCALAR works by maintaining recent predictions in a buffer, balancing their class distribution via the Sinkhorn algorithm to match a specified target distribution, and using the balanced soft targets for adaptation. Without changing the model architecture, SCALAR maintains the per-step runtime and increases the peak allocated GPU memory by only 10 MB on ImageNet-C. Our method is particularly effective on skewed, non-stationary data with severe distribution shifts, where SCALAR significantly alleviates drift and collapse when combined with existing stabilization methods based on entropy or diversity.

AI.tldr: SCALAR is a plug-and-play module for continual test-time adaptation that stabilises online adaptation by balancing pseudo-label class marginals over a short temporal window with the Sinkhorn algorithm. It alleviates drift and collapse when combined with entropy or diversity stabilisation methods.
AI.motivation: Continual test-time adaptation is unstable because it can reinforce early biases and increasingly predict only a few classes, leading to drift or collapse. Existing methods select reliable samples or reweight losses but do not explicitly enforce a class marginal over a temporal window.
AI.method: SCALAR keeps recent predictions in a buffer, balances their class distribution with the Sinkhorn algorithm to match a specified target distribution, and uses the balanced soft targets for adaptation. The model architecture is unchanged.
AI.result: SCALAR keeps per-step runtime and adds only 10 MB of peak allocated GPU memory on ImageNet-C. It is particularly effective on skewed, non-stationary streams with severe distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly controlling the temporal pseudo-label marginal is a simple way to stabilise continual test-time adaptation without changing the model.

title: VLA-MOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Task VLA Policy Consolidation
summary: Physical intelligence requires embodied agents to ground language in observations and execute actions while retaining useful skills. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies offer a shared interface, but task-specific post-training often produces separate specialists. Consolidation is difficult: mixed-task reinforcement learning provides sparse trajectory-level credit, while offline distillation may miss student-visited observations and endpoint distillation does not supervise intermediate action-generation states. We introduce VLA Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (VLA-MOPD), a protocol for consolidating flow-matching VLA specialists. After acquiring task or suite experts, a shared student collects robot rollouts and queries the instruction-routed frozen teacher at each visited observation and intermediate ordinary differential equation (ODE) state. Detached per-flow-step transition targets supervise valid action chunks through a masked local matching loss; an optional reference-policy term supports retention on other tasks. Starting from one trajectory per LIBERO task, VLA-MOPD raises mean success-once from 75.4% to 98.9%, compared with 98.15% for endpoint action distillation. It improves mean RoboTwin 2.0 success from 73.0% to 89.3%; on a Piper robot, two consolidation rounds improve average success from 70.0% to 90.0%. In a near-matched Spatial-adaptation study, reference matching limits the Object suite decrease to 3.0 points, versus 13.2 without the reference term.

AI.tldr: VLA-MOPD is an on-policy distillation protocol that consolidates several task-specific flow-matching VLA specialists into one shared student policy. It queries an instruction-routed frozen teacher at each visited observation and intermediate ODE state.
AI.motivation: Task-specific post-training yields separate specialists. Mixed-task reinforcement learning gives sparse credit, offline distillation misses student-visited observations, and endpoint distillation does not supervise intermediate action-generation states.
AI.method: A shared student collects robot rollouts and receives per-flow-step transition targets from the routed teacher at each visited observation and intermediate ODE state. These detached targets supervise valid action chunks through a masked local matching loss, with an optional reference-policy term for retention on other tasks.
AI.result: Starting from one trajectory per LIBERO task, mean success-once rises from 75.4% to 98.9%, compared with 98.15% for endpoint action distillation. Mean RoboTwin 2.0 success rises from 73.0% to 89.3%, and on a Piper robot two consolidation rounds raise average success from 70.0% to 90.0%. The reference term limits the Object-suite decrease to 3.0 points, versus 13.2 without it.
AI.conclusion: Dense on-policy teacher supervision along the student's own trajectories consolidates multi-task VLA specialists more effectively than endpoint distillation, and the reference term helps retain skills on other tasks.

title: How Many Exposures Does a World Model Need? Learning Unseen Game Mechanics at Test Time
comment: 31 pages, 21 figures, 12 tables. ARC Prize 2026 Paper Track. Code and weights: this https URL
summary: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.

AI.tldr: The paper asks how many exposures a world model needs to learn unseen game mechanics at test time. On ARC-AGI-3 it finds that a 35M-parameter vision transformer pretrained on other games learns about four in five mechanics to at least 80% accuracy on held-out games.
AI.motivation: Agents in unfamiliar environments must learn mechanics from limited interaction, yet how many observations a world model needs to predict new mechanics has not been measured.
AI.method: The authors introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from their programs and scores predictions on the cells each mechanic changes at each exposure. They build WARC, a 35M-parameter vision transformer pretrained on other games that updates all parameters after each transition. WARC-Agent pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer.
AI.result: On held-out games WARC predicts four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on changed cells and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, while without updates only one in seven does at all. WARC-Agent raises the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training, and the entry scores 0.20 on hidden Kaggle games.
AI.conclusion: Test-time updating is essential for learning unseen mechanics quickly, and roughly 80 exposures in a single play is enough for many mechanics.

title: Rethinking Radar 3D Perception: Representation Learning from Raw Spectra
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 18 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Miao Zhang and Mohamed Abdelsamad contributed equally
summary: Raw radar spectra are widely viewed as too cluttered and noisy for direct representation learning, motivating handcrafted reductions, sparse point clouds, or compact Doppler descriptors in radar perception. We challenge this assumption and argue that the main limitation lies not in the raw representation itself, but in the absence of a learning objective that separates structured signal from noise. Handcrafted reductions partially address this problem but impose rigid assumptions about what constitutes signal, discarding weak yet informative structure while retaining artifacts that fit the reduction model. Once removed, such information cannot be recovered by supervised learning. We propose an alternative: structure is the component of a radar spectrum that remains reconstructable under localized corruption, while noise is the component that does not. This perspective motivates self-supervised masked modeling for dense radar spectra without predefined signal-noise separation. We instantiate it with Leakage-aware Spectral MAE, a masked autoencoder for raw radar cubes using a corruption strategy inspired by cross-bin energy spreading caused by spectral leakage. We also demonstrate the importance of Doppler organization: treating Doppler as a primary spatial dimension in an x-y-D representation, with height encoded as features, substantially outperforms naive channel stacking and enables effective learning from dense 4D spectra. Without handcrafted reductions, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art radar-based detectors and point-cloud-based self-supervised learning (SSL) counterparts. These results establish raw radar spectra as an effective representation for 3D perception when paired with an appropriate pretraining objective.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that raw radar spectra can serve as an effective representation for 3D perception when paired with a suitable pretraining objective. It introduces Leakage-aware Spectral MAE, a masked autoencoder for raw radar cubes that treats Doppler as a primary spatial dimension.
AI.motivation: Raw radar spectra are usually considered too cluttered for direct representation learning, which has led to handcrafted reductions, sparse point clouds or compact Doppler descriptors. Such reductions impose rigid signal definitions and discard weak but informative structure.
AI.method: Structure is defined as the part of a spectrum that remains reconstructable under localised corruption, and noise as the part that does not, so no predefined signal-noise separation is needed. The masked autoencoder uses a corruption strategy inspired by cross-bin energy spreading from spectral leakage. An x-y-D representation treats Doppler as a spatial dimension, with height encoded as features.
AI.result: The x-y-D representation substantially outperforms naive channel stacking and enables learning from dense 4D spectra. Without handcrafted reductions, the approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art radar-based detectors and point-cloud-based self-supervised counterparts.
AI.conclusion: Raw radar spectra are a viable input for 3D perception when a masked-modeling objective and Doppler-aware organisation are used.

title: AutoVLA-D: Learn a Trajectory-Geometric Condition from Reasoning for Autonomous Driving VLA
summary: Autoregressive VLA planning usually predicts continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions often describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final continuous trajectory. We address this gap with TrajCond, which introduces a discrete trajectory-geometric condition for VLA planning. Specifically, we represent TrajCond as a 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory and learn it with a two-stage training framework before final continuous trajectory prediction. With the simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories, we name our method AutoVLA-D (Double). Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond, consistently improving final continuous trajectory prediction across closed-loop and open-loop driving benchmarks. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: AutoVLA-D introduces TrajCond, a discrete trajectory-geometric condition that a driving VLA generates before its continuous trajectory, so that discrete and numeric trajectories are produced autoregressively together. It improves final continuous trajectory prediction on several driving benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive VLA planners predict continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final trajectory.
AI.method: TrajCond is represented as a discrete 1D differential action trajectory and learned with a two-stage training framework before continuous trajectory prediction. Discrete and numeric trajectories are generated simultaneously in an autoregressive manner.
AI.result: Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond. The condition consistently improves final continuous trajectory prediction in closed-loop and open-loop benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A discrete trajectory-geometric intermediate condition, derived from reasoning about actions, is a better conditioning signal than the direct discrete output for driving VLA planning.

title: V3DSAM: Semantic-Geometric Loop Verification and Geometry-Anchored Persistent Instance Mapping for Feed-Forward Dense SLAM
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: To address unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence feed-forward dense SLAM, this letter presents V3DSAM, an open-vocabulary semantic dense SLAM system that establishes physical correspondences at both the scene and object levels. The system combines feed-forward geometric estimates from VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with open-vocabulary semantic observations from SAM3. We introduce semantic-geometric dual-scale loop verification, which identifies false loop closures using pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D spatial correspondences, without accessing backbone-internal features. We further propose geometry-anchored persistent instance mapping, which defines physical instances through class-constrained 3D connectivity in an optimized global coordinate system and assigns global IDs without inter-frame identity propagation. The proposed verifier rejects all four false loop candidates in our TUM RGB-D evaluation, while long-sequence ScanNet experiments show improved instance identity consistency. Thus, V3DSAM reduces dependence on internal backbone features and temporal ID propagation for robust long-term cross-view association.

AI.tldr: V3DSAM is an open-vocabulary dense SLAM system that combines VGGT-SLAM 2.0 geometry with SAM3 semantics to build object-level instance maps with consistent identities over long sequences. Its loop verifier rejects false loop closures without backbone-internal features.
AI.motivation: Cross-view association in long-sequence feed-forward dense SLAM is unreliable, and existing approaches depend on internal backbone features or temporal identity propagation.
AI.method: Semantic-geometric dual-scale loop verification uses pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D spatial correspondences to detect false loops. Geometry-anchored persistent instance mapping defines instances by class-constrained 3D connectivity in an optimised global frame and assigns global IDs without inter-frame identity propagation.
AI.result: The verifier rejects all four false loop candidates in the TUM RGB-D evaluation. Long-sequence ScanNet experiments show improved instance identity consistency.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring instances in optimised 3D geometry reduces reliance on backbone features and temporal ID propagation for robust long-term cross-view association.

title: Direct Conditioning of Audio Diffusion Transformers on fMRI Reveals Cortical Contributions to Sound Reconstruction
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 main track as a poster
summary: Reconstructing audio from brain activity remains challenging. Existing brain-to-audio pipelines typically map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis. While recent work in the visual domain has explored direct conditioning on brain activity, this approach has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models. We introduce MAAS (Multi-Area Auditory Synthesis), an end-to-end framework that conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer on ROI-wise fMRI responses without first supervising a decoder to predict an external stimulus representation.
